With such statements before us, how is it possible that the hon. members, who applauded the hon. member for 'South Lanark only a year ago when he was so severely criticising the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, should, but a few days ago, almost to a man, and the hon. member for South Lanark himself, applaud the hon. exminister until there hands were sore from pounding their desks ? I believe the hon. ex-minister never in his life enjoyed live hours more than he did the five hours of his opening speech in this debate. He had at his mercy, under his thumb, the great body of the opposition who had been maligning him and criticising him for the last six years in no uncertain language. For five hours he held them at his beck and call. When he desired them to rise to the occasion, he would make some sweeping general assertion against the government's project, and they would rise to the occasion, every man of them. But when he finally desired to produce something in the nature of a climax, when he desired one hurrah greater than any others, he himself stooped to make the mean insinuation that an honourable senator of this country had something to do with this scheme, and made them pound again like so many tin soldiers, while he himself stood laughing at
them. The hon. ex-minister has had the grim satisfaction of wiping out six years of the oposition's denunciation of him, and of appearing to them within the last week or so as a hero and the propounder and exponent of the only objections they have been able to raise in this House against this measure.
With reference to the speech delivered by the hon. leader of the opposition, it is but fair to assume that our grounds of difference in connection with this proposal are but few and slight. I believe that on the great features of the proposal we are practically all agreed. It is only in matters of detail, and in many instances minor details, that we lack a consensus of opinion. We are agreed that there is an urgent necessity for greater transcontinental railroad facilities in this country. The expanding trade and commerce of our country demands it. The rapid development of our Northwest country demands it. The want of competitive freight rates demand it. The steady onward march of commercial and industrial methods, rendering competition keener and still more keen, until the question of railway facilities and railway rates becomes not only an important but a dominating factor in most commercial transactions, demands it. That man were dull indeed who, either in this House or out of this House, would express an opinion contrary to the opinion that I believe we all share, namely, that the necessity is great, that the moment is opportune, that the ability of our country to meet her national requirements is beyond a peradventure. These being our common grounds of agreement, they are the main questions involved in the consideration of this measure. Our differences appear to arise as to the best methods of putting our conclusions into effect.
While I submit that there is not in this country to-day a condition of affairs which would justify a government in taking over the railroad systems of the country and operating them, either by a commission or otherwise, I do not despair that at some time in the future there may be such a condition of affairs as to render that sort of management possible. Certainly the management of the Intercolonial Railway system is not very encouraging as an example of government management. We have in this House an hon. member who occasionally starts on bis favourite theme of the nationalization of railroads. I refer to the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean). I do not think the hon. member has a very clear or concise idea of what he means by that high-sounding term; but time and time again, in this House, and in his newspaper in Toronto, he elaborates on what he is pleased to term the nationalization of railroads, as the only mode of relief from all our difficulties-as the only panacea for all our ills in connection with railway mat-

ters. Surely the people of this country, if they pay any attention to the statements of the hon. member for East York will say :
Now is the winter of our discontent
Made glorious summer by this son of York.
But, Sir, so far this idea, I think, is in embryo only. I look forward to the day when the matter may be taken up seriously, but I do not think that at present any one can seriously contend that we should go in for government operation of railways, either by commission or otherwise.
We know that the Conservative party always consider it a tremendous triumph that they had a great deal to do with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think that this country can look with very great pride upon the accomplishment of that great work. I know that when travelling in other countries, notably in the United States, and hearing the puffing and blowing which goes on there about their miles of railway, my own breast has swelled with pride when I thought that in a country of 5,500,000 of people, we have the greatest system of railway, under single management, in America and perhaps even in the world. I look forward to the day when we will have another such system. I believe that we are taking the first steps towards realizing that expectation at present, but I do not think that the Conservatives are entitled to the credit. Nor were they entitled to all the credit for the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That was a road which the people of Canada, as a whole, constructed. I notice that the hon. leader of the opposition, in his remarks yesterday, proclaimed to his followers, as he turned towards them with a grand gesture :	We built the Canadian
Pacific Railway. Sir, it was the Canadian people who built it, but the unfortunate feature is that although we built it, we do not own a dollar of it. Since then a radical change of procedure has taken place. That part of the new transcontinental line which we are going to build, we intend to own ; and while we do not intend to operate it ourselves, we shall lease it and allow other railway companies to have running powers over it, and operate it, in conjunction with ourselves, if we so desire.
Our hon. friends opposite say that there is a great deal of sentiment in this proposal. I am glad to know that there is, 1 have heard it claimed that there was a great deal of public sentiment behind the Canadian Pacific Railway contract, and one of the most cheering facts, in connection with the scheme before the House is that there is so much public sentiment behind it. But if therp be sentiment behind it. it is certainly a high and noble sentiment-that sentiment which we call patriotism is perhaps the highest the human heart is capable of. Long may the people of this country have that sentiment with regard to all their institutions, their great railways, hanks and public systems of one kind or another ;
and so long as that sentiment has force, Canada will be assured of a prominent place among the nations of the world.

Although this debate has been rather prolonged, Mr. Speaker, the question before the House has so much to do with the future of this country, that it is hardly necessary for me to offer any apology whatever for putting my views upon record concerning it. I think we may put from our minds altogether the expectation that we shall dispose of this question and conclude this debate at an early I day. It seems to me a question on which we may rightly expect representatives from all parts of the country to express their opinion. This session is already in its sixth month. To-day it completes its twenty-third week, and those of us who are from the extremes of this country, either in the west or in the east, feel that we have a very just cause for complaint indeed at having been kept here so long, but we consider also-that it would be unreasonable to expect this parliament, after it has sat here, from month to month, quibbling and quarrelling over comparatively insignificant questions, to dispose in an off-hand way, of a matter so important as the one now being considered.
I wish to pay some attention to the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell). I find that speech a most peculiar one-one I can well imagine he will yet wish he had not been under the necessity of making. In it he made a radical reversal of his former attitude on the principle of government ownership as applied to railways. The necessity for his doing this, he explained in an early stage of his remarks, when he told the House that he would not have addressed it at all on this subject, had it not been for the fact:
Some years ago I advocated a proposition, which has been mentioned in the course of this discussion, as a possible alternative to the policy propounded by the government. Shortly after the acquisition ot the Drummond County Railway, a report obtained currency that the government was about to purchase the Parry Sound road for the purpose' of still further extending the Intercolonial Railway and pushing it forward in the direction of the green fields of the west. It seemed to me at the time that this was a logical sequence of the steps already taken for the extension of the road to Montreal.
When an hon. gentleman has to admit that a few years ago he was advocating a system of government ownership, when he has to admit that he was advocating a policy of removing the Intercolonial Railway from the position it had hitherto occupied, of merely being operated in accordance with the terms of confederation-when he admits that he advocated making it a competing road by extending it to Montreal, and afterwards further on to Georgian bay, in the expectation of still further extending it into the west-when an hon. gentleman

has to admit that that was his position a few years ago, and that he is to-day obliged to reverse that position, I feel for him. When he finds that in the whirligig of events it was necessary for him to go back completely on the stand he took a few years ago, he has my deepest sympathy. But it is unfortunate that public men, when they are under such necessity, will not fairly and frankly tell us the real reason, and not try and explain something which cannot be explained. I am prepared to admire the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), who got up and said : I believe in government ownership, my people believe in it, we want a government road through the west, but we cannot get it, and I accept this scheme for the good there is in it, but I only accept it because we cannot get what we want. There is something to admire in frankness of that kind, but one can only feel pity for an hon. gentleman who is under tiie necessity of arguing against, his own convictions ; and I think we might very well ask such men not to render up to party what belongs to mankind.
The hon. member from Hants (Mr. Russell) laid down this proposition, as a finality on the question of government operation :	He
prefaced his proposition by telling us that human nature will have to be altogether regenerated, that governments will have to be administered on a different basis, that the general public will have to move up to a higher plane before we could consider government operation and ownership of railways as a practical proposition.
In a democratic state there never will be a government railway operated in successful competition with a private railway.
And he seems to take the position that until that occurs which he says will never occur, his argument remains good. Well, his statement is so laid that it is beyond the reach of demonstration. What would be ' successful competition ' of a state-owned railway in a democratic state with a privately-owned railway ? What would be the relative quality of success. A private railway is operated for private ends, for private profits. Its success depends on its being able to get the maximum rate and make tiie maximum profit. But with the publicly-owned road in a democratic state the object is to serve the public-it is a public end, and not a capitalistic end that is to be obtained. Success ? How can success be measured in a matter of this kind ? Well, let us take a parallel case. Speaking of railways in this country or any other country where the railways are privately owned, we should lay it down as a rule that a small railway cannot successfully compete with a big transcontinental line. That seems to be a proper way to state the question. And, until you cau show a small road successfully competing with a big one, the hon. member for Hants would not agree 286
that competition is possible. Well, the outcome of this kind of test is that the big road acquires and extinguishes the small one. That is success in the big road. What has been the experience in those democratic states and the other states where there has been public operation of railways? Every time, the result has been that they have acquired the other roads. That is their success. To make his statement good, the hon. gentleman quoted the cases of Belgium and Prussia. Now, I imagine that he did not quote them as democratic states, but it is true they did, have an experience of partial government operation and partial private operation of railways. What lias been the result ? I would direct the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Russell) attention especially to this. As he has referred to the matter, I will give him the result in these two countries :
When Prussia took over the railways (passing the law near the close of 1879 and taking the roads soon after), one of the first steps of the government was a great reduction of rates, with the result of a great increase of traffic. The policy of reduction has been continued, and the rates are now among the lowest in the world, as will appear shortly, yet the roads pay very well, indeed. Prussia is realizing a profit of $75,000,000 a year on the railways above operating expenses and interest, and in the last fifteen years she has realized a clear profit of $500,000,000 above operation and interest. The capital has been very greatly reduced. I cannot state the exact figures, but it is the policy of the government year by year to make certain payments reducing the capital, so that by the middle of the next century there will he no capitalization of the railways at all.
Is that an answer to the hon. gentleman's challenge? Is that any evidence of the success of state-operated roads in competition with private roads ? It can hardly be denied that success has been obtained, for private roads have been absorbed. Now, take the case of Belgium :
The Belgian government, at the outset, established very low rates-about four-fifths cent a mile.
Hear that, Canadians.
Later an express service was started at somewhat higher rates, but the ordinary fares were reduced from time to time, and are still the lowest in the world, except perhaps, on some of the lines in India. The average fare, third-class, in 1898, was two-thirds of a cent a mile, and on the whole traffic, including all the classes, the average fare was 0'88 of cent a mile.
And then the hon. member for Hants, to make his point good, referred to the handicap the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals was under in trying to operate the Intercolonial before it was extended so that it could compete for traffic. Well, that is "*ranted But what would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Russell) do ? He was. in favour of that extension to Montreal where the Intercolonial could compete for the whole



traffic of tfie west. But I find it is not only the principle of government ownership that the hon. member for Hants finds fault with, but he isi very sarcastic in his description of those who advocate that principle. He tells us, on the information of Mr. Ackwcrtli :
that the movement for government operation is like the scarlet fever. It is liable to attack any community and at irregular intervals to become epidemic, but its attacks as a rule are severe, only in the case of the younger and more irrepressible portion of the population.
I think, if the hon. member's statement is to be taken seriously, that there is a large amount of fever of this kind among the irrepressible, the youthful, and the folly-stricken in this country at the present time. He admits that he made an exception of the the two ex-ministers in this House. And he admits also :
Now, I must admit at the outset, that I have a great degree of sympathy with the views those hon. gentlemen have presented to the House. I have been at times seriously threatened with the symptoms of the disease with which they are afflicted.
He admits that he at one time was afflicted of the disease. But he has got better. Oh, yes. And it is to be noted that his recovery was remarkably rapid and remarkably complete. And now we are told that those who believe in and advocate the government ownership of railways are the cranks, and; schemers, the youthful portion of the population, the hopeful, the optimistic. Well, if that is true, the hon. gentleman must carry out his own logic in its application to the nations of the world. And I would like to line up the nations of the world according to the standard set by the hon. member for Hants. He can say at once, as he does say to Canada : Be quiet : Agitation cease :	You have the railways :
You have not been imposed upon by the young, the hopeful, the optimistic. Of course, you have a great deal of agitation upon this subject, but that is ail a mistake. You, fortunately, through a good deal of tribulatiou, chose the right way ; you were led by the wisdom and experience of the older heads. And he will say to Britain : This sentiment expressed for so many years in your country that you would like to'have an opportunity of again inaugurating this railway system is all wrong. You started exactly right ; your older and wiser heads were the ones that' had control of your affairs when this policy had its inception. It is true you have complained that for years continental products have been delivered at your ports, and to your interior cities, at lower freight rates than are given to neighboring towns in your own country. It is true you have had to send goods from Liverpool to Newr York and ship them back to London, because it is cheaper to do than to ship them 20(1 miles by rail direct to London. That is all very true. But you are

quite mistaken in the conclusion you draw. The great army of railway workers of Britain who are working for far less wages than those employed in other branches of industry in that country, look across to the continent and wonder how it is that understate operation there the operatives of the railway lines are better paid relatively than other labour in those countries. They may wonder how it is that it is sixty-four years since the parliamentary rate of oue penny per mile was passed and it has never been improved on leaving Great Britain today one of the highest priced countries for railway travelling in the world. They may wonder how these things are, but the member for Hants tells them * you are right, you are old and not young.' And to the United States with its marvellous railway development he says that the agitation there has been a mistake. Nearly forty state railway commissions have been called into existence for nothing, they were only dreams or were created to rectify grievances that evidently never existed. They complain there that the railway monopoly was the father, sponsor of all the big monopolies, that it has discriminated against and ruined cities and even states and that It has corrupted legislators and judges and that it Is to-day and has been for years past enabled to put a restraining influence even on the professors of sociology and political economy so that this rising generation shall not know even of the wisdom of these men who put aside all of these little follies in the early years so that wiser heads prevailed and they kept clear of state ownership and operation. It would be novel indeed to hear Chancellor Bismarck charged with being carried away with youthful fancies and follies. He was wrong, the member for Hants says he was wrong, that he was foolish in 1876 when he told Prussia that it was-time to put a stop to the exploitation of the public for private interests, when he said that the carrying ou of these roads was to all intents a public service and when he said it should be done by the public and for tlie public. He was wrong, the member for Hants told us so.
Hear, hear.

And Australia, democratic Australia, you started wrong. The successes that you achieved are bad, you have started wrong, you have allowed your young men to prevail, those who would prefer to run Australia for the benefit of the people who are in Australia, you who have got a railway system to which as a matter of fact we do not pay much attention in Canada. Great Britain and the United States, because it compares favourably under state ownership with our own. You have been mistaken. Nova Scotia is willing to correct you.
And democratic New Zealand, New Zealand who have been so remarkably successful

ill sociological experiments that other nations have not dared to attempt. In New Zealand where you have at last found out a way to construct branch lines to districts where there seem to be no call for them whatever, where it is being done now by contract with settlers that come to settle upon the lands which the branches shall serve. These men enter into a contract with the government that in addition to clearing the lands and planting crops they shall also construct the right of way and grade up everything ready for the metals and do it at so much a day. Thus living right there they construct their lines even in the districts that are so poor-and they have many districts poorer than ours-too poor to support a good line of railway, but they have these railway branches built in this way and have thus a sufficient supply and service to meet their needs and they have arrived to that extent at the very forefront of democratic operation and ownership of railways. But the member for Hants says if you do not fall in with his theory, you are behind the times.
What shall I say about Switzerland V Surely here is a case of the old growing young, a nation that started wise becoming foolish. A country, remember, composed of more, varying peoples, languages and religions than are settled on any other spot of similar size, who have been able to so govern themselves as to live together in peace, as to be a model for the continent in which they are located. These people have been getting worse. They started with private roads and it was only five years ago, only in 1898 I believe,' that by popular vote by two to one these people showed evidence of this youthful fever and converted every private railway within their bounds into a public railway and are to-day operating them themselves with remarkable success.
Well, are there no others ? Yes, surely there are others, there are two others. There is Spain and there is Mexico. The hon. gentleman will like his company. Take Spain for instance. I can imagine the hon. gentleman telling Spain that she is the model of wisdom, that her people are the old heads, that they are not feverish and I can imagine the candid man in Spain replying to the member for Hants, ' yes, we" have been before reminded that we are a back number.'
And Mexico. Well Mexico is in our class. The member for Hants has said so. And China. Here is proof positive that they are in the sear and yellow leaf of wisdom for they have not only refused to operate railroads, not only have they given such railroads as they have over to private control and private profit, but they have kept to this principle with the post offices and have left them to private control. China indeed. China must be the apex of the hon. gentleman's logic.
2861 [DOT]
And, Sir, I forgot to mention in passing in connection with the case of Great Britain that the gentleman to follow out his reasoning would commend them for their system although they so bitterly regret that is was ever started on the private system. This country that has confusion worse confounded in the railway world is the country that has been most successful in operating a post office system, one with an adaptability and elasticity and usefulness to the people of the country that make it a model to all democratic people and this applies not only to the post office but to the telegraph service as well. You find them here, these two principles operating on the same ground and operating so diversely and how the hon. member for Hants feels so sure in congratulating that country on the private ownership of the railroads is more than I can understand.
In passing let me mention one point from which the hon. gentleman extracted much fun, and why he did so I cannot imagine. He wanted to know whether, if we nationalized this road or any other -road, we in Canada who are not used, as a matter of fact, to very large salaries, would be prepared to sit quietly and see any commission or government hire railway operators or managers at $40,000 or $50,000 a year-yes, $50,000 a year, and they go all the way up to $75,000 a year, I believe. It is true that men do get these salaries

five, six and seven times as large as are. paid to the Prime Minister of this country. I wonder that the hon. gentleman did not see that that was one of the evils of the very system he was defending. These men cannot earn as much as $70,000 a year at such employment. Are these experts in this business so vastly superior to men who are fitted and well fitted to be the Premier of this country; to be cabinet ministers or judges, or to take up the leading positions of life, that they can command ten times the salary paid to those occupying the high positions which I have enumerated ? It seems to me that the argument is against the hon. gentleman. If we did take over these roads, if we did at the present time proceed with a national policy of railway construction and operation, perhaps we might, and perhaps we would have to, and perhaps it would be profitable for us, to pay the high salaries that others pay. It seems to me quite likely that we would have to do as other roads do, and we would find ourselves doing what has become too common a practice in this country, going across the line to the United States and giving to the citizens of that country all the big salaries that we have to pay. We might have to do that, but I believe we could soon train our own people to be more successful managers than we could get from amongst the people to the south of us who would not be acquired with the system in this country. I believe we could very well train men in this country to take

provincial governments for subsidies and grants of moneys and lands of large proportions for these corporations ;
And Khereas the policy of bonusing with money and bestowing the public lands on such corporations is vicious in principle, and has resulted in grievously burdening the settlers, and provides all the incentives for corruption in political life ;
And, whereas another development of this system is becoming prominent in the transferring of large blocks of land to irrigation companies ;
Therefore, be it resolved, that we reiterate our opposition to all proposals for the continuance or extension of the iniquitous bonusing policy, or pledging the public credit for private interests, and affirm our belief that this is an opportune time to enter upon an unqualified system of government acquisition and construction of railways, including the extension of the Intercolonial Railway through to the west.
That was the invariable conclusion of these resolutions. That resolution was Passed at a meeting in Winnipeg on March 12, the day on which this House met.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay a little attention to the contract we are discussing. My principal objection to that contract is that it is a contract, made by the government of Canada with private persons who seek to secure the carrying out of a public service. As an advocate and supporter of the government ownership of railways, my principal objection to this contract is that it is a contract. For that reason I do not compare it with the old Canadian Pacific Railway contract. I have never been accused of saying much that could be construed as being favourable to the government or the parliament that endorsed that contract. It seems to me that it would be absurd to rejoice over a contract that gave $35,000,000 in constructed works, $25,000,000 in money, 25,000,000 acres of land, exemption from taxation for twenty years and an absolute monopoly for twenty years, wholly into private hands, practically without any reservation or real control. In addition to this, the right to interfere with rates was put absolutely beyond our control. It was stated that the rates should not be interfered with until the company earned 10 per cent, and I suppose for all practical purposes that time will never come ; the company will see that it will not. In that respect the country must have been saved a lot of trouble in regulating the railway, because we contracted ourselves out of it.
I have never felt, even considering the times and the circumstances in which that contract was made, that the right and proper thing was done. I regret that when the country stood ready to do so much, it should not have done all-that evqn if it put into private hands the operation of the railway, it should not have retained the ownership, which it could almost have done with the money it put into the railway.
The present contract has been before the country for some weeks, and it is remark-

able what little attention it is attracting. This big work and this big line of policy that has been outlined, does not touch the popular chord by any means. What a difference there would have been if there had been laid before the country a proposal for the construction by the government of a railway from the east to the west, the government retaining the ownership and control. As a matter of politics it would have been one of the most popular things that could have been devised. It would have got the assent of more people in this country than anything else that could be named. I recognize the objections which are urged against a course of that kind. The political objection is this, that the people, e' cn though you serve them, do not remain constant; that although you do what they desire, they forget ; that other questions come up, and they deal with them as they arise. The corporations do not. The corporations never forget. They never forget a friend. We have had experience of this in our province, and also in this Dominion. But that simply strengthens my position- my belief not only in the feasibility, but in the imperativeness, in the interest of good government, and of the country generally, of our owning and controlling these large services.
Looking over the clauses of this contract, and tracing the projected line, one is struck -and I do not care who that is or where he sits-with our intense ignorance of the country through which the greater part of this road is projected. It may be better than we suppose. We hope at all events that the country to the north of us is good country, that can be settled, and is worthy of development. Perhaps it is ; but whatever it is, we can never be disappointed or surprised, because we know nothing about it. It is best to acknowledge at once that we do not know what this north country is. If it turns out well, we shall be gratified. If it does not, let us hope that a railway will not be put through it. That I believe must be the ground on which this contract is entered into. This question of knowledge before action is a very important one. You know, Mr. Speaker, that the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was not a success. Had there been more deliberation, at all events had a proper route been chosen, the development of our western country would not have been retarded twelve or fourteen years, as it was. The country is developing now, people are going in, and it is taking the position we expected it to take. But for twelve or fourteen years it looked as if that were not going to be the case. We practically stood still during those years, and I cannot imagine that that would have happened if the Canadian Pacific Railway had been constructed through one of' those passes through which this contract contemplates that this new line will be taken. It was a

serious mistake to make in the first instance. If the Canadian Pacific Railway had been taken to Edmonton, probably by this time it would have been advisable to construct a line along the route where the Canadian Pacific Railway is now ; but the result of putting it there at that time was to retard the development of the country for twelve or fourteen years. We ought to have been in a far better position than we are to-day. The men who were in this country then know that their expectations for many years were not realized. If the Canadian Pacific Railway route had been better chosen, Canada would have been to-day far different from what it is. This is an important question, and I hope, whatever may be the necessities of the government, after this contract is ratified, if it is ratified, that they will not be led, notwithstanding the taking idea of rapid construction, to start constructing this line until they thoroughly understand where it is going and what is going to be its general condition. I must say that I think that that would be the right course to take, and one which would meet the necessities of the case. What is wanted in the immediate future is government connection between Winnipeg and the great lakes, and from the east of the lakes to the Intercolonial Railway. Giving those connections, we will be able to handle the traffic that will offer until we are certain that this road not only can be constructed, but will be constructed in the place best calculated to give the best results.
The hon. member for North Norfolk, (Mr. Charlton) attracted a good deal of attention, and properly so, but for the amount of ' ifs ' which he made use of in discussing the character of this proposed route between Quebec and Winnipeg. He did not at all commit himself to any statement that the ' ifs ' could be carried out. If the grades, if the general conditions of the country, and so on were of such a character, it might be possible to transport grain from the prairies of the west to St. John in the east. That was as far as the hon. member would go, and that simply confirms the opinion I am trying to put before the House that we should not allow ourselves to be carried away by any idea of rush in this matter. It is better to provide the required facilities to the lakes and then from the lakes to Montreal and the eastern coast rather than start this work, which it will take years to complete in any case, and which, when completed, may enable the hon. member for North Norfolkj to say : You did not consider my ' ifs,' and the road is not fulfilling the purposes for which it was intended.
The hon. member for North Norfolk gave all his attention to the section from Winnipeg to Quebec. True he was dealing with that because that is the government constructed portion ; but as far as the traffic is concerned-and the great object of this
proposed line is to give an outlet to the traffic of the west-why should not the government construct and own the whole line from the east to the coast ? The hon. member for North Norfolk, however, left the west to take care of itself. But the far west, which is the new west that is being developed, is too far west, and St. John and Halifax are too far east, for us to pay attention only to the grades ou the eastern section. The waters of the west are too near the far west, and if the position be such-and there is hardly any doubt that it is-that it will be practicable to take the products of the far west to the waters of the west, it would be suicidal to allow any private company to refuse to overcome the grades and the obstacles that exist in the Rocky mountains for the sake of forcing traffic right across this continent to the seaboard of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. However much sentiment there may be in the matter-and by the way our shippers in the west do not pay much attention to the sentiment of an all-Canadian line, it is the freight bills they look after-it would not be to our advantage, as a nation, to attempt to force traffic over a continental haul to eastern ports, if that is going to cost more than to send it across the Rockies and put it on board ship at a Pacific port. At present the products of the western states are being exported from San Francisco. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Morrison) told us the other night that as the chain of mountains in British Columbia go north, they also go west, so that our western country is nearer the Pacific ocean than are the western states. If the transcontinental railway is going to be the benefit to Canada which it can be, no expense should be spared- and I doubt if a private company would most effectively do this-in keeping the grades through those mountains down, so that our traffic from the west would be able to go a few hundred miles into Fort Simpson. The products of the western states are carried around Cape Horn, and the products of British Columbia and west of the mountains, are to a large extent, carried around Cape Horn. But that is not always going to be the case. How long will it take to complete this projected work ? Five years is the first estimate, but suppose we say eight years, in that time the United States expect to have the Panama canal constructed. That canal is going to make a vast difference in the Pacific trade and also to our western ports. It is going to make it impracticable to ship grain 3,000 miles by rail when you are within a few hundred miles of Fort Simpson. Yesterday's cable news gave the information that the Colombian senate had rejected, for the time-being, the contemplated treaty with the United States for the acquisition of this tract, but they have simply given the Colombia government power to make the

necessary treaty, and the supposition is that they are simply expecting to get some concessions. The United States have got their preparations made and have parties organized ready to go down to the Panama canal, and expect to complete that work in eight years. And as the cost is only $150,000,000, there is no reasonable doubt that they will carry the work through as soon as they get the necessary rights. But even if they do not. they will then build the Nicaraguan canal. This was the canal which they had selected, and which would have been in proceess of construction by this if the old Panama Company of France, had not offered its old works at a reasonable price. In all probability this Panama canal will have an immense influence on the western traffic of this country. It will reduce the time to the old country tremendously and at once put freight rates, for the products of the west, far below what we may expect, even with the low grades to be hoped for over 3.000 miles of rail haul. I am surprised that the hon. member for North Norfolk should have overlooked this matter of grades in the west. Surely if we are goiug to guarantee a line in the west, there must be some importance in that question. The reason why a great deal of trade has not already gone through the Canadian Pacific Railway to the port of Vancouver is the excessive grades on that road, owing to the ill-judgment of the locators in constructing it through the Kicking Horse pass.
As regarls the running rights under this contract, I have heard them discussed from every point of view, and an ordinary person would be excused for saying that the possibility of various railways exercising running rights over one line depended altogether on who was speaking. But looking at the contract, I see that all railways are to have just about the same rights as they have under the Railway Act. They have running rights, if they want them, under terms that are favourable to the company that grants them. But the Intercolonial has special privileges over that road, which, if hon. gentlemen on the other side were not attempting to reduce the character of the Intercolonial, might at some time be used to make the Intercolonial a trunk line. But I do not think there is any intention of doing so, and the cause to which I have referred will probably never be taken advantage of. But this does not begin to meet my views of a government trunk line. I can thoroughly understand that many hon. gentleman would not be prepared to support my views in favour of the nationalization of railways who would yet commit themselves altogether to government ownership of the trunk line. So. it seems to me, I have a right to look in this contract for a proper scheme of a government trunk road. Taking the plain meaning of the contract and the circumstances under which it was drawn up, we can only Mr. PUTTEE.
conclude that the object to be attained is this : There is a large section of this country in which we fear there will be no local traffic, but through which must be hauled the grain of more prosperous districts. If the government builds that road and so controls the capitalization, it can keep down the rates on this non-productive and costly7 road to the actual cost of construction and hauling. That appears to me to be the proper meaning for me to take out of the contract. But if this is the object, it seems to me the government should build the road from Quebec to Winnipeg and put it in charge of an operating company and keep that as a trunk road for the use of all parties who want to use it. The operating company would have nothing to do with individual shippers or with freight bills or collections. It would simply take the cars from the companies delivering them at terminal points or branch line points wherever indicated. It would provide the motive power of course, and the necessary staff to pass over that trunk line all cars that were given into its hands. There would be no duplication of authority ; there would be no question of running rights; no question whether it would be possible, or practicable or profitable for the operating company to grant running rights to other companies. They would be an operating company only, and there would be no possible friction. Early in the history of the road, it could be demonstrated what it actually costs to haul a car a mile, and that would be the basis of the price to any one who wanted to send a car over the road. If local trade should be developed, some arrangement could be made with another company to pick it up, or the operating company itself could pick it up. Outside of that, all traffic should be passed through in bulk, in carloads. This, it seems to me, would be a proper government trunk road. If run in this way it would be of some use to the west. For any districts in the west that were settling up, if the companies for any reason did not see fit to put in a branch line, or if the people did not want to be in the hands of a large corporation, the people themselves could form a company or a small body7 of capitalists could construct a road to the point where the freight would be handed over to the trunk road, and they would send their traffic over that road on equal terms with all others. It would be understood exactly7 how much it would cost to pass a car over the road, so that the charge to all would be known to everybody, and the other roads would simply give their price to haul to Winnipeg where the traffic could be handed over to the trunk line. This, it seems to me, would be a proper plan for a government-constructed and government-owned trunk line. I am surprised that it has not been adopted in this case, that is, while recognizing the fact

that the government does not believe in government ownership and is not prepared for the nationalization of the railways, yet wants to do everything possible to develop the country and to avoid putting it in the hands of railway corporations. That, it seems to me, would be a proper way to spend the people's money on a trunk road.
Now, Mr. Speaker, other gentlemen far more competent than I am, have dealt with the matter of guarantees and the general bonding privileges of this road. I have not much to say on that subject. But I have listened attentively to the explanations that have been given by others. We are to pay all the money for the construction of this expensive, non-productive eastern section, and we are to guarantee 75 per cent of the balance of the cost from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada guarantees the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for the other 25 per cent. The government, I suppose, gives the first guarantee, and I do not quite understand what is the value of, or necessity for. the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. For the last few years, the company has been in better shape than formerly, but I do not regard its position as superior to that of the government. Just what is the use of their guarantee I do not quite understand. It reminds me of a few lines the poet put together in this form :
In Klon, that town of monks and bones, And pavements fanged with murderous stones,
And hags and rags and hideous wenches,
I counted two and seventy stenches All well-defined and separate stinks,
Ye nymphs that reign o'er sewers and sinks, The River Rhine, it is well known,
Doth wash your city of Colonge ;
But tell me, nymphs, what power divine Shall henceforth wash the River Rhine.
And when this guarantee was explained to the House the question struck me : Who is going to guarantee the Grand Trunk ? The country is, of course. Well, if we have to guarantee everything, for there is no doubt that practically the credit of the government is involved in these railways; why do we not construct them and own them ?
How does the account of the Dominion of Canada stand with regard to its railway operations ? I take from the Statistical Year-book the following facts :	Bonuses
granted to railways, 852,831,000. Suppose we strike an average between the estimate of the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific and add $70,000,000 for that. Then, the government roads owned and operated by the government represent an expenditure of $74,194,000. This makes a total of $197,026.000 in money spent on the railways- the greater part of the national debt. The number of acres of land granted to railways is 58,288,092. Of course, about 8,000,000 acres have been granted by the province,
but all out of the public domain. But we will say 48,000,000 acres. The bigger part of the national debt and 48,000,000 acres of land and what have we got for it ? Surely we ought to have a lot, the biggest part of our national debt Is on this debtor account of the railway ledger. What have we got ? Well, in two or three generations we shall have, provided these corporations do not get so large as to be able to negotiate with us beforehand, in two or three generations we shall have a trunk road there, to hand over to posterity. It will have no branch lines and no connections but there will be a road. Of course the bonds will have to be floated again, it has to be bought about that time but we shall have the road ; and then we have the Intercolonial and the Prince Edward Island Railway. The Intercolonial as far as it is possible and practicable seems to me at present to be a first-class railway. There has been a good deal of money spent on it, and I believe the late Minister of Railways and Canals is justified in boasting that he has brought that road up to the condition of a really useful practical railway of first-class character. We are going to relegate that to a second-class character, and then all we have got is our interest simply as users of the other railways of the country when we have to travel and we have to pay a high rate for that. I believe that our passenger rate is practically higher than on any other extensive system in the world. We have given the bigger part of our national debt, we have given a kingdom in lands and that is the way the ledger stands at the present time. Why, Sir, 1 never feel that I have to apologize, that I have to plead my youth or my rawness or my optimism when I say I am in favour of national railways, and at this time, when the opportunity presents itself and has to be met as perhaps never before ; it seems to me that this is the opportune time, to start on the method that lias been tested the world over and proved successful, the method of the government not only paying for and constructing and owning but also operating its own roads.
Mr. Speaker, I came to this House four years ago an advocate of the nationalization of railways. There is a good deal of opportunity during the protracted sojourns that we have in this city for a man to try his theories, to test his beliefs, to hear and to read the other side. The magnificent library in connection with this parliament is of great value in this respect particularly. We can not only see and read and understand what we have in our own country but we can understand and become acquainted with what has been done under other systems in other lands and other continents. I say that for four years I have watched the work of this House. A greater part of our time has been taken up with struggles in the Railway Committee especially, with all kinds of Bills, some legitimate enough, some

good enough considering our policy, and some bad enough. I have noticed that the promoters of the worst ones have generally tried to get a certain following on one side of the House and then to make it a party question when their Bills would often not stand close straightforward criticism; they try to make it a party measure so as to get it through the House. I have seen during this time, every member has seen it, and must liave been impressed as much as I have with the amount of time and the amount of trouble and even I believe the amount of loss to public rights that has been caused by the passage through this House time after time, session after session, of railway Bills. I have seen too the lobbies filled with railway men, with their lawyers, the very best lawyers. They have their business to do under our system. I am not complaining while we follow the practice of granting charters, I am not finding fault with them, but I see they are here, they are the most prominent, outside the members themselves, the most prominent and most constant and the most devoted to their duties
And the most aggressive.

Yes. and the most aggressive of all those that are around this House, and I say that I have noticed these things. I have opposed every time the Subsily Bill. I am opposed to subsidies and these things have not made me more favourably disposed to them, and, Mr. -Speaker, I believe that my temperament is such that it inclines me, impels me often to take no part in a discussion or a debate for the fear perhaps of being considered as posing, as seeking simply to get a little notoriety, but I say I have the consent of any little intelligence that I have got in saying that this whole system is wrong, that it is an imposition on the people who sent us heite to look after their interests and their interests alone. It is a giving away of prerogatives and privileges, of property and resources that should only be used' and exploited for the public good and we give them for private good and for private benefit. I say we become forgers of fetters, creators of taskmasters for the very people of whose interests and whose interests alone we here as the parliament of Canada ought to be preservers and protectors. Believing that, Mr. Speaker, -believing that that principle is right, believing that it is practically unassailable, I think, and I have thought, that at this time at this change of the policy of the country that it was right and proper for me to put these sentiments of my own on record and to state exactly where I am on that railway proposition and those that have in the past come before this House.
Now, I want to deal shortly with the question of government ownership as it is before us, and although the hon. member Mr. PUTTEE.
for Hants seemed to think that those who proposed to advocate this principle were the few, were the cranks, the schemers, the youthful unreliabl-es and although 1 have not come to that conclusion by observing the members of this House during the last session. I have come to the conclusion and I believe there is a very strong feeling among the members of this House in favour of a new policy of this kind and that is one reason why I regret that this contract is brought down here as a contract so that it closed the mouths and changed the current of thought and changed the method of expression that would otherwise have been given by the members of this House.
But I am not so lonely, I quote here for instance from the hon. the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) who said :
My decided preference is for a government owned and government operated railway across the continent.
That is mine too, and the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, a man of experience, a man who has never that I can remember been in the habit of coinciding with the hon. gentleman who was last Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) the Hon. John Haggart, during this debate said :
There is no probability of this parliament acceding to any such thing as a government railway, although in my heart I believe, judging from the experience of other countries, that a government railway can be managed and run as economically as any other railway. My experience upon the Intercolonial Railway was that you could get a service as cheaply and buy supplies cheaper than upon any other railroad in Canada.
I do not feel as lonely as the hon. member for Hants would have the House believe.
I have quoted statements of two men whom we may look upon as being experienced in railway matters, as we have a right to do. A man who has been Minister of Railways and Canals for seven years and a man who has been in that position in previous years certainly have experience in these matters, and I consider that in this parliament we are bound to accept their opinions as having greater weight than opinions which are not based upon actual experience. The right hon. Prime Minister said :
I formed my opinions some years ago, and perhaps I may he permitted to relate a personal experience which went far to form my own conviction in this regard. In the fall of 1896, Mr. J. R. Booth, of this city, invited me to visit his railway, the Canada Atlantic Railway. which was then in process of construction. I accepted the invitation. The road had been built almost to the shores of Georgian bay, perhaps within half a mile of it. When we left the train we walked to the shore of the lake, a bleak shore with not a building upon it. Mr. Booth said : this is the terminus of my Railway. I asked Mr. Booth : Where is the trade to come from ? His answer was : I have to create it.

One of the first and most expensive and boldest tilings Mr. Booth did to create that trade was to construct the Canada Atlantic Railway. Is that not the experience in every case ? You have to provide the service first and if you do provide the service you can get the trade. Did the hon. exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), when he extended the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, go down there to create the trade ? No, he went there to accept the trade, he made it a success and the acquisition of that piece of road was the one thing that put the Intercolonial Railway in a better position than it had ever occupied before. The question which is now presenting- itself to us is really the one of ownership vs. control. We are now proceeding upon an attempt to control. Without going into the matter. I want to say that this has been a very thorny road to tread. It has not so far been* attended with any alarming amount of success. In the United States they have spent millions, they have had some forty state commissions and they have their interstate commerce commission, and yet they have been able to make no very great success out of it. We attempt to control railways for the sake of keeping the rates down, for the sake of serving our people better and for the sake of drawing the claws of the railway companies; of trying to hold them down, trying to prevent them from taking too much from us, but from all the experience that we have had in efforts of this kind this attempt is likely to be expensive as well as unsatisfactory. It would be better to face the alternative at once and adopt a national policy in railway operation.
Some hon. members have expressed themselves in favour of government ownership and they have told us that this contract is in itself one step towards government ownership. Well, it may be or it may not be. Probably it will not have this effect ; certainly it has not had this effect so far because hon. gentlemen who have hitherto been supporters of the principle of government ownership are obliged to go back on their records, to go back on the arguments put forward by themselves in former times in favour of this principle and as a believer in it I do not accept this proposition as one step towards government ownership. Then, there is another reason to commend it, and it is this : If the operating company, the Grand Trunk Pacific, default, if they cannot pay the interest, the contract becomes null and void and the road becomes our own. not only our own to have and to hold, but to operate. In other words, if it is a success it belongs to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, but if it is a failure it belongs to the people of Canada. I was speaking of the account of the Dominion of Canada in regard to railway business. The opposite side of the picture is disclosed by our publie reports, which show that $03,000,000- the hon. Minister of Justice mentioned $S3,-000,000, and he is probably right-have been spent on our canals. We own our canals, because they are not interest earners. They do not produce interest and profit and therefore we own our canals. If the Grand Trunk Pacific is not a paying concern we will have all the duties of government ownership thrown upon us.
The hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), who advocated very strongly the principle of government ownership this session in the Railway Committee has spoken on this question, but he has also found it necessary as an advocate and sympathizer with government ownership to change his position. He regrets that it is not practicable. He regrets that he finds it necessary to part with his hope of constructing and operating a transcontinental railway bv the government. This is the reason he gives :
Another feature of the government embarking in a general scheme of ownership of our lines of railway would be the questions that might arise in the future as to the construction of additional lines and of branch lines. There would also be involved, by reason of the pressure that might be exercised upon parliament. the question of the duplication of railway lines. There might be too tight a rein exercised, or it might be too free. It would all depend on the political pressure that would be brought to bear. To the extent that this might operate either in the one direction or the other, it would be productive of injury to the public interest. You could not be too stinted ; and it would not be in the public interest to have too free a hand. The interest of communities not served by railways, or not having the advantages of government lines, would always be brought to the front and parliament would be besieged time and again for the duplication of lines, in order that these communities might share in the advantages of government-owned railway's.
His objection to advocating this principle is that it would be impracticable, unprofitable and unsafe, because the government would be open to influences, that the people would use their influence to get lines constructed, deflected or duplicated. That is a line of argument that has been urged and sometimes it has been urged with some effect. But, what is the reverse ? Is it a defect that is inherent in public ownership ? I say not. It is merely a defect that is peculiar to our present system. I have never been along the line of the Intercolonial Railway, but I have carefully noted all that has been said in this House by men who know, and my firm belief is that there can be no reason for the construction of the new line from Quebec to Moncton, except that very political reason which the member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) has urged against the policy of government ownership. That line may be profitable, and in the future necessary, but from the day the private Bill of the Grand

Trunk Pacific Railway was introduced until now, tlie only vital reason that has been given for the construction of that portion of the line, whether it parallels the Intercolonial Railway or not, is the reason that it is a political railway. That being true, and I submit to every reasonable man that it is true, there is no argument in it against the public ownership of this road. Indeed, it is an argument in favour of public ownership. I am opposed altogether to any system that would be open to abuses of this kind, and that could be effected by influences of this kind. The sad truth is, however, that railway matters do mix up with politics in this country. They meddle with our political institutions and, they meddle too effectively. There are too great interests involved in the private ownership of railways, and under our system of government these interests are altogether too powerful. There is no doubt that we often legislate in opposition to the general consensus of the opinion of this House, and against the intelligence of this House. We often legislate on railway matters in a manner that we would not legislate, if railway interests were less powerful than they are.
The trouble is with many of us that we are slaves to the thing that is ; that we have been reared, in contact with, the tiling that surrounds us, and that we are apt to believe in it just because it exists. We found it in existence here; we were born in it, some of us ; we cannot imagine anything else ; it is the thing that is, and we are committed to it. Last year I had the pleasure of meeting a gentleman who was then outside of Australia for the first time. He had been able to visit leisurely a great part of the United States, and he had travelled to a considerable extent through Canada. I met him on the steamer as we were leaving Canada for the old land, and finding that his comparisons between democratic Australia and the United States and Canada were most interesting, I asked him :	What strikes you as the most remarkable thing in this country, and he replied :	' The most remarkable thing to me
is that your railways are controlled by private individuals. I was born in Australia, where the railways are under public control, and having lived under that system it seems to me that in a great democratic country like this which declares that all men are born equal, and which provides that its citizens shall be well protected, 1 believe that the government itself should be the owner of the railways, and not tremendous railway corporations. It seems* to me, he said, although I do not know it, that these corporations must wield a powerful. and I would suppose, mischievous effect on the body politic. He was convinced that the wealth and Strength of these corporations. in promoting their own interests, which must necessarily sometimes be antagonistic to the interests of the public, must have a very pernicious effect on our political system. I have said we are slaves to that which is ; we are slaves to the things we are used to. Iin that instance this gentleman had been used to exactly the opposite system which we pursue in this country, and it was the strangest thing that he had met with on this continent.
Now, Sir, I want to lay down the proposition that railway transportation is properly a government function. When that is conceded, as conceded it must be. it tlieu becomes a question of expediency as to whether we should delegate our powers to private parties or whether we should exercise them ourselves. It never occurred to me but that this definition of the character of a railway would be properly understood, until I heard the hon. member for Westminster (Mr. Morrison), a gentleman of the law, speak the other evening. He said :
The whole contract discloses the fact that the Liberal party have apparently, for the first time recognized the cardinal principle which seems to underly our constitution, and one which heretofore has been ignored by hon. gentlemen opposite, namely, the subordination of transportation corporations to the sovereignty of parliament.
He was of the opinion-and I do not blame him for not holding that opinion before, except that he may be blamed for having taken so long to learn it-he was of opinion that parliament is sovereign, that this matter of transportation is a function of government. We have wandered so far away from the recognition of the principle that even a lawyer is struck by the fact that we are coming back to it. In 1876, Bismarck explained that railway transportation was a function of government, and he proclaimed the doctrine for economic as well as for state and military reasons. John Stuart Mill, who is generally accepted as an authority who cannot be gainsaid on such matters, distinctly lays down the proposition that the operation of railways is a government function. Indeed, when we pass a railway Bill in this parliament, we put in a clause delegating our powers, when we state that the Act is for the general advantage of Canada. We recognize that we give to private parties powers that by right belong only to the government. The railway commissions of the United States in their reports to their various states and to the central government, are continually reiterating this principle. It seems as if they are doing it in a spirit of despair, for time and again they have to draw attention to the fact that the powers they are trying to control are powers that should belong to the government. And, Sir, that principle, conceded as it must be conceded, I lay down the further proposition that this power can be exercised by government aside from the influence of politics, and that it can be used by the gov-

eminent for the public benefit without the damaging influence and interference of partisan politics. If this is a power that belongs to the government, we should not delegate it unless there are good and sufficient reasons. If it is a power that can be used by us and exercised by us properly for our own benefit, then I say it should be exercised by us for our own benefit. That it can be so exercised I am going to show by simply taking the experience of the colony of Autralia, as given by Mr. H. H. Lusk, who has been forty years in that colony, at one time being Secretary of State of New Zealand, and who has lived in the United States for three or four years, long enough to form a fair opinion of the system there.
What are you quoting from ?

I am quoting from a report of a hearing before a Senate committee of the United States in 1900, given to Mr. Lusk, whom the hon. geutleman will recognize as an authority on Australian matters :
In Australasia altogether there are 15,000 miles of government railroads, and they are operated to the entire satisfaction of the people. There are no complaints whatever as to any favouritism as between one class of persons and another. There are no complaints as to discourtesy or want of attention on the part of officials, and there has absolutely, during the last ten years, been no complaint that politics has interfered in any way with them, and my only wish here is to state what our experience has been and, as far as I may, why it has been so. Now, I think that our experience, both of the efficiency of the service and of its absolute freedom from political abuses may be referred to the mode in which the service has been organized. You see, it is not merely that we have experts from the outside to manage it, but it is that every employee of the railroad is a civil servant of the government. Not one of them can be dismissed except for cause. Not one of them can be defrauded of his right of promotion if he deserves it, in his turn. Their rights in that way are strictly preserved to them by law. If complaint is made, the employee has a right to a public investigation before he is punished by degradation or loss of office. Up to a certain age, different in different colonies, they are entitled to remain in the service and in most of them, if not in all, there is a provision made for retiring allowances at an age which is fixed. :	.	.	. With regard
to the question of politics, there is no possibility of exercising governmental influence to make the men vote one way or the other.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is pretty difficult to get them to vote against the government ?

Not the slightest in the world. Sometimes they do vote against the government. I remember one case in New South Wales in which the vote of the operatives of the railway was regarded as being very strong against the government, owing to certain legislation that was supposed to be opposed to the labour interst, and they naturally went for the most part in favour of the interest of labour, and they were certainly not in favour of the government at that time.
Then, referring to New Zealand and the question of political control there, he says : The thing would have been a dead failure if any attempt of that kind had been made ; but rio attempt was made.
I could make other quotations along the same line, blit I will not take up the time of the House with them. At the same time,
I believe that the matter which I have introduced from this report is valuable, and I have not seen it referred to before in this country.
I would like to call the attention of those hon. gentlemen who are opposed to this principle of government ownership on the ground that it is impracticable, to the similarity between the conditions existing in Canada and those In Australia. The people of Australia live under a government similar to ours, they speak the same language, they have the same sentiments, the same regard for their rights and the same business methods. They have practically a continent to govern, as we have. Their population is sparse, and it is important to them, as it is to us, to have lines of railway connecting the different parts of the country with each other. The mileage of their railways is large, as ours is. So that the comparison between the two countries is very apt. We have a population of over 5.000.000; they have a population of about 4.000.000. They have 15.000 miles of railway owned and operated by the government. We have over 18,000 miles. If I had time. I could quote from Mr. Lusk, to show that their experience of government railways has been altogether satisfactory. After living in tlie United States, where private ownership of railways is supposed to have reached almost the flower, he claims that the service there is not better than the service in his own country. In Australia, the value of money is not quite so high as it is in Canada ; but the rates on their railways 'are about the same as ours, except passenger rates, which, as in almost every other country, are far below ours. One thing that should not be forgotten is that on government railways, practically in all countries, school children are carried free. That country, which boasts of having made such a success of its railways, has a debt of $600,000.000 on account of the 15,000 miles of railways owned by the government-a good many of them constructed by the government, but the major portion of them, I believe, purchased from private parties, with all the disabilities that are incident to their construction and ownership by private parties. In Canada with between eighteen and nineteen thousand miles of road the liabilities are over a billion of dollars. It is not fair to contrast the United States railway system or even the British system, with that of Europe. The comparison between Canada and Australia is about as fair a one as can be made in a matter of this kind, and that comparison

is undoubtedly in favour of the government ownership and operation of railways. My great objection to private corporations operating railways under special privileges, and using powers delegated by the government, that properly belong to the government, is, after all that the system results in erecting vast private enterprises, which are naturally first and foremost for private interests, and not for the public interests. That is to a large extent the reason for my opposition to these private roads. I believe, too. that these private corporations do meddle in politics a great deal more than they care to admit and that the cause of good government will gain by not encouraging the formation of these corporations. The interests of good government lie altogether in the public ownership of our great railways. But, we are also far behind in our civil service, in the way we operate it, in the influences exerted upon it, and it seems to me that if we could reform that system, which is badly in need of improvement, it would be a good secondary result of a plan of government ownership.
Then, there is the question of discrimination-a question that can never be buried under a private railway system, a question that comes up now and again more strongly than at other times, that flourishes all the time in the United States, and is never absent from this country. The question of discrimination can never be settled except by the national ownership of railways. Then there is the other matter of fair and equal service to all. This is something which is no less important than low rates.
Before I close my remarks, I want to advocate what I think would be right and what I have advocated before in this House, and that is that questions of this kind should not be settled off-hand even in this parliament. This is a question which affects every citizen of this country. I would be prepared to support a policy of expending our own money on our own roads with the idea of keeping these roads and using them for our own purposes. But when we are making a contract with private parties, when we are giving them either our credit or large sums, when we are following a policy which, X am confident, the majority of the people would not approve, opportunity should be given to the people to declare their opinion on this policy before we finally adopt it. In my opinion, the people would gladly escape from this policy of bonusing and subsidizing and guaranteeing, which makes more distant the policy of the people owning and operating their own roads. Before committing the country to a contract of this kind, before committing it to the large expenditures involved in this contract, it is only fair that the people should have an opportunity of declaring whether they are in favour of it or opposed to it. I am a believer in the principle of the referendum. I believe that

we would not be doing anything derogatory to the dignity of this parliament if this contract were sent to the country and submitted to the vote of the people. The question before the people would be this contract or public ownership. I believe that the people should be given the opportunity of declaring themselves on this question, irrespective altogether of partisan influence. I do not mean simply the return or the defeat of the government at a general election. At a general election all sorts of questions are discussed-separate schools, bonding privileges and railway policy, tariff, and each of these has more weight in some constituencies than it has in others. But what I submit is that this particular scheme should be referred to the people for tbeif sanction or rejection. As I have said before, I believe in the nationalization of railways. I have never seen the necessity for government ownership so strongly as I do at present, and I am going to place in your hand, Sir, an amendment declaring what a really national railway policy would be.
I beg to move, therefore :
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted :-
By reason of growth in population and the rapid development in the productiveness and trade of Canada, and especially the western part thereof, the time is opportune for 'he adoption of a definite policy of government construction and operation of railways, under a properly safeguarded civil service system, put entirely beyond the influence of partisan politics.
