Instead, however, of bringing the report upon that Bill before the council of the board of trade, the gentleman who had charge of the committee, who was chairman of the committee, and vice-president of the board-and I may say that my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell), who also has the honour of sitting on the council of that board, was present, I believe, at the committee meeting-and my hon. friend1 from West York with others decided to bring in a resolution regarding the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway project. This resolution was brought in on the 23rd of June, when there was very little known about the project, when there was very little about it in the newspapers. But in some mysterious way or other, those gentlemen who supported this resolution, got an inkling of what the government intended to do, and in order to strengthen the hands of the government, a resolution was framed and rushed through the council, contrary to the practice which has prevailed for many years in matters of this kind. In all such matters, the usual practice has been to refer them to an open meeting of the board of trade, to which the public and the press are admitted. But in this ease, there was a star chamber inquiry, and this resolution was rushed through, although it was not at all adopted unanimously. This resolution was in favour of an outlet by the shortest and Mr. KEMP.
cheapest route for the productions of the North-west. But it seems as though tbe committee must have been informed that the government would perhaps go further than they desired, for at the end of the first paragraph I see these words :
And tbe advisability of competition without the extravagance of the duplication of lines.
They seem to have been possessed of the idea that the government intended to duplicate the Intercolonial Railway. They were afraid that the government would do something silly, and so guarded themselves in this way. What happened afterwards V Mr. Peleg Howland, of Toronto, who is a good supporter of this government, and who also helped to put this resolution through the council of the board of trade, came out in an interview a short time ago, in which he said :
I am strongly opposed to building a line from Quebec to Moncton, and I think for the present at least the Intercolonial Railway is sufficient. Personally I am not fully convinced that the time has arrived when a line should be built from Quebec to Winnipeg, but if so, then I believe it should be built and owned by the government, and running privileges given all roads desiring the same.
In an interview, Mr. J. D. Allen, vicepresident of the board of trade, and who was chairman of the sub-committee, which investigated this question and brought in this resolution, heartily approved of the government's decision. But when I say that Mr. Allen, who is a good friend of mine, was the defeated Liberal candidate from West Toronto, I think I have said enough on this subject to show how it came about that this resolution came to be passed. It did not by any means, represent the opinion of the board of trade, and I believe the board of trade would not endorse the project to-day under any circumstances whatever.
Now, in regard to the matter of the transcontinental railway the Prime Minister seemed to rest his ease mainly on two points, the question of the bonding privilege, and the question of carrying the products of the North-west to the seaboard in a more economical way than has been possible in the past Take the question of the bonding privilege first. The right hon. gentleman seems to have been seized of the importance of this part of the question, and he represented to us that it is absolutely necessary, because of this bonding question, to have this railway built, although- a point which seems to have been largely overlooked-we have now two railways going through New Brunswick, the Intercolonial and tbe Temiseouata line, from Riviere du Loup to Edmundston, and from Edmund-ston to St. John by tbe Canadian Pacific Railway. Tbe right hon. gentleman refers in bis speech to the discussion which took place in this House in regard to the short line through the state of Maine to St. John,

New Brunswick. He tries to lead us to believe that the resolution which he moved at that time, had it been carried, would have prevented this railway from going through American territory. I confess, I cannot so interpret that resolution. The Prime Minister said in his speech introducing this Bill :
I am sorry to say that this motion was defeated. If it had not been defeated, if the policy which was there enunciated had been implemented, probably it would not be my duty today to ask this House to vote money for the building of another line between Quebec and Moncton, for the line would have been built oh the very ground where we now propose to locate it.
The right lion, gentleman took up a great deal of time in dealing with the bonding privilege as one of the arguments in favour of this project. We all agree with the loyal sentiments he uttered. We are all loyal Canadians-it is not necessary to say that, for that is taken for granted. But I would point out to the House the position which the right lion, gentleman took with regard to this bonding question on a previous occasion. The right hon. gentleman took part in a discussion on the contract to the Canadian Pacific Railway syndicate, and his position then was directly the opposite of that which he takes to-day. The right hon. gentleman spoke on December 21st, 1880, and this is what he said, according to the 'Hansard' report:
The only point on which there is any disagreement is as to the expediency of building the whole road at once, or only as rapidly as the wants of the country require. I think it must be perfectly manifest that this section on the north shore of Lake Superior is not required at the present time, that its construction might be advantageously postponed until some future period, and that it would be quite sufficient, at present, to build the eastern section as far as Sault Ste. Marie. The fertile plains of the west are separated from the east by an extent of barren territory in the region north of the lake, while it happens that the route along the southern shore would pass through some of the best lands on the continent -through several of the most important states of the Union. Would it not be better, under these circumstances, to bring the road immediately to Sault Ste. Marie, tap the American system of railways, and secure not merely the trade of our own North-west, but a large share of the traffic from those states. This is so evident from a geographical point of view, that I will not stay to discuss it.
The policy enunciated by tbe l-iglit lion, gentleman on that occasion was not to build tbe railway north of the lakes. He was perfectly willing to take his chances on the bonding privilege, and he was also perfectly willing to cut off our great Northwest from eastern Canada by making our railway connection through the United States. And he comes down now, when there is not a sign of trouble with the United States, and urges the danger of the abrogation of the bonding privilege as a
justification of the whole scheme. My impression is that the Prime Minister made a great mistake in making so much of this bonding matter. It was not a good thing for us to raise the question. It is undoubtedly a great benefit to this country to have the products of the United States come to our seaports for shipment; but it is a greater benefit to the United States to have our products go to their ports. There were times in our history when signs were not wanting that the American people might cancel the bonding privilege. But those days have long gone by. The people of the United States tried to coerce this country with a high tariff, the McKinley tariff-advocated, I am sorry to say, by some Canadians as a means of coercing Canada-they tried to force us into a commercial union with their country. But the Americans now are convinced1 that this policy of coercion will not succeed. They are more friendly with us now than ever before. They are holding reciprocity conventions and passing resolutions favouring closer trade relations. We have the Michigan Central Railway running through Ontario, which would be very seriously affected if the bonding privilege were withdrawn. We have the Wabash Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway also. Then it must not be forgotten that the people of New England are interested in the maintenance of this bonding privilege and would protest most strongly if it were withdrawn. We have all these railways running through Canada, helping to bring business to American ports and helping also to reduce the charges for the transportation of American . products which go to the New England states. In days gone by the United States tried all their experiments of foreign policy upon this country. Now they have Cuba and the Philippines and they must have a more conciliatory foreign policy. The fact that they have launched out into colonization in this way is a guarantee of their good behaviour. In discussing this bonding question the Prime Minister laid a good deal of stress on what the New York ' Sun ' had said in days gone by in reference to this question. Therefore I take the liberty of reading a few words from the New York ' Sun ' to show what it thinks now on this question. A few days ago the New York ' Sun ' said :
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Canadian Premier, addressed the parliament at Ottawa on July 30 and formally committed the ministry and the Liberal party to the support of the Grand Trunk Pacific transcontinental railway project. Mr. R. L. Borden, the leader of the Conservatives, replied on behalf of his party, and it is quite evident that Mr. Borden had not a little the best in the argument. Sir Wilfrid's speech was of considerable length, filling in solid type an entire page in the newspapers.
We have already commented upon the merits of the proposed railway plan. A point of more important immediate interest to the American people appears in the speeches of Sir Wilfrid

Laurier and Mr. Borden in reference to the bonding privileges extended to Canadian goods in transit through the United States. Upon that question Mr. Borden had much the best of the discussion, both in point of fact and of patriotism. Sir Wilfrid advanced an argument in favour of the proposed line, evidently Intended as an appeal to the patriotic sentiment of his people, that the government laid it down as a principle upon which they were willing to be judged by friend and foe alike, that Canada should have a transcontinental railway ' with its terminus on Canadian waters, and every inch of it in Canadian territory.' With all respect to Sir Wilfrid, this savours of gallery play, an oratorical display for effect only. The United States has no transcontinental railway from sea to sea, unless the ' Sunset Route,' the eastern terminus of which is at New Orleans, be counted as such. We have systems and connecting lines which make up such a route, but no through single line from ocean to ocean. Although she has only one line where we have several, Canadians or Canadian products can now go from Vancouver to Halifax without touching an inch of our soil.
From this false premise, Sir Wilfrid argued Canadian dependence for transcontinental transportation upon the good-will of the United States in maintaining the bonding privilege over American lines to American ports. Having highways of their own	
Whatever Canada ships through the United States is just so much an advantage to the United States. There are also articles produced in Canada whereof an increased shipment to the United States would be of mutual advantage.
Now, the Prime Minister took the liberty of quoting from the New York ' Sun,' and I take the liberty also, and I think it shows there is very little agitation or no agitation at all and no hope on their part that the bonding privilege will be cancelled, and I think so far as that excuse for this great project is concerned it falls to the ground. At all events the hon. gentlemen on thie opposite side of the House who have spoken since on that subject have referred very gingerly to this aspect of the subject as enunciated by the Prime Minister.
It was said by the Prime Minister that the eastern part of this railway would cost the country $12,000,000 and not one cent more than $13,000,000 and that the cost of the western section would not exceed $3,780,000. In this connection I would like to know why no mention is made in the contract of what the grades on this railway are to be and what the curvatures are to be ? it seems to me that this is a very important thing. Supposing this railway is not built to the satisfaction of the Grand Trunk Pacific can they not say afterwards that they cannot carry grain over this line because it was not built to the proper standard ? It seems to me that will be the position they can reasonably take. The argument of the Minister of Finance is that the government is going to build a cheap railway and he makes ills figures fit into a cheap railway. The Minister of the Interior says it is going to be a first-class railway and is going into Mr. KEMP.
competition with, and will carry grain as cheaply as it is carried over any railway in the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have made up the cost of this project and I am prepared to give the details of my figures and to have them open to criticism. The first cost that . I made up I thought was a little high; I had calculated the interest at three and a half per cent. I think it will cost the government more than three per cent to get money. A very large amount of money will be required and with expenses and everything I think it will go over three per cent. I do not know that it will go quite three and a half per cent, but I feel justified in stating that my figures should bear three and a quarter per cent interest. A good deal has been said about the cost of this railway from Moncton to Winnipeg. An hon. member on the government side speaking in the House to-day put the cost at $35,000 a mile. From what inquiries I have made on the subject I do not believe that a railway such as it is contemplated to build for the purpose of carrying grain with grades such as a road of this kind requires can be built for anything like that. This railroad it must be remembered runs at right angles with the rivers. There will be a great amount of bridging; the country in many places is rocky and the rocky ridges or mountains run at right angles to the route of the railway and I believe the cost will be not less than $40,000 per mile. I believe that is the figure that will be necessary to build the railway. Calculating the distance from Moncton to Winnipeg at 1,825 miles at $40,000 per mile gives the cost of that section at $73,000,000. Calculating the interest as I have said at 31 per cent for seven years (compounding once a year)-and in this connection I want to say that I have not brought to my help an actuary as the Minister of Finance did,
I have simply figured this matter in the way I figure ordinary business transactions and the way I have been taught all my life; I cannot understand the way the Minister of Finance explained it; it seemed to me he was juggling with figures-I figure the interest on $73,000,000 for seven years at 31 per cent (compounding that interest once a year) at $18,317,345; and then there is an additional three years during which we are likely to have to pay interest and I assume we will have to pay interest that will make in all $27,513,282.
Then we give this road to the Grand Trunk for forty years, and they pay us 3 per cent. Now, supposing they pay 3 per cent, supposing the revenue of that road is sufficient which I doubt very much-I believe it will be found that the cost of maintenance will take everything and I do not believe the Grand Trunk Pacific will be able to pay 3 per cent, but even if they are able to pay if we have to pay 31 per cent that leaves in the forty years $7,300,000. The five years

of construction figured as two and a half years and 3i per cent compound interest on $73,000,000 will give $6,086,715.
Then we have the mountain section. The Prime Minister stated in the House that the length of the mountain section would be between 600 and 700 miles. The Minister of Finance makes it less and 1 am taking the figures of the Prime Minister at 650 miles. Taking this at $30,000 per mile we have a cost of construction of $19,500,000 and the interest on this for seven years at 3 per cent (compounded once a year) is $1,482,540. Then for an additional three years making in all ten years we have interest of $6,706,368.
I take the Quebec bridge and terminals at $5,000,000 and this totals up to $125,606,365. not including any depreciation on account of paralleling the Intercolonial.
Then we have a liability or what perhaps some might call an indirect liability of the guarantee of bonds of the mountain section 650 miles at $30,000 per mile, $19,500,000 and 1,150 miles of the prairie section at $13,000 per mile which comes to $14,950,000, these two guarantees coming to $34,450,000. This gives a grand total of $160,056,365 including cash expenditure and liability or in other words not taking into consideration the liability but only the cash payment a debt against every family in this country of $114 calculating five to a family on our population.
1 would like to point out in this connection, Mr. Speaker, to show the magnitude of this thing that the paid-up capital of all the chartered banks in this country is $76,660,301, but this railway, this project according to my figures will cost $125,606,365, leaving an excess over the paid-up capital of the chartered banks of $48,946,064.
Now, Sir, something has been said about Canadian produce going over this line and two clauses, clauses 43 and 44 have been referred to as ' the pious clauses,' and I believe that they are so in every sense of the word. I think that they cannot be enforced. I do not think it is possible under these clauses to oblige the Grand Trunk Pacific to take grain from Winnipeg to St. John and transport it to a Canadian port and I believe they will not do it.
In passing I would like also to draw attention to the fact that the distance from Montreal to St. John by the Canadian Pacific Railway is 481 miles. From Montreal to St. John by Riviere du Loup and Edmundston, the line in existence to-day is 585 miles and I do not believe that the government if they build this railway through New Brunswick will get a shorter line from Montreal or Levi>s" to St. John, New Brunswick, than the existing lines. There was a point which was referred to in this debate by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker). He gave it in a very graphic way when be said that Mr. Hays in the Railway Committee was willing
to do almost anything that the committee wanted him to do.
He was willing to promise to build the road anywhere and everywhere and at any time and all times and to change his route on the suggestion of any particular section and to go on a thousand miles on the mere hint of some member of the committee.
As the hon. member for Hamilton pointed out that was the attitude of Mr. Hays before the Railway Committee, and while Mr. Hays was willing to extend this railway to Quebec or to the maritime provinces in committee he was downstairs later in the day making a bargain with the right hon. leader of the government that the government should build the road and assume the whole responsibility for its cost.
There is also another question about which we have not heard very much from our hon. friends opposite, and that is the arrangement made with the Grand Trunk Pacific as to running rights over the Intercolonial Railway from Moncton to Halifax and St. John. It has been said, and said very truly, that this policy of the government when carried out will largely control the policy of the Intercolonial Railway. I remember that, when a few years ago the question of selling the Intercolonial Railway to another railway company was brought up, when it was suggested that the Canadian Pacific Railway could operate the Intercolonial Railway to better advantage than the government, the people of the maritime provinces rose up in protest against any such proposition. I would like to ask if this proposition does not give the Grand Trunk Company as much control over the Intercolonial Railway as the Canadian Pacific Railway would have had if it had assumed control of the railway, and whether the Grand Trunk Railway are not going to assume control over it ?
The question of paying 3 per cent on the capital expenditure on this railway is a very important one and I have wondered if the government ever expect the railway reallly to pay this 3 per cent. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have to pay the expense of maintenance, to pay the officers' salaries, &c., and they have to put $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock upon the road which at the present prices of locomotives, freight cars and passenger cars would mean that they would put on 100 locomotives, 3.000 freight cars and 60 passenger cars. At present prices, that number of locomotives, freight cars and passenger cars would amount to $5,000,000. The ordinary rental that is charged by one railway to another for the hire of a locomotive per dav is $10. for a box freight car 75 cents, and for a passenger. car $4. That gives a total rental on the basis of the number of locomotives, freight cars and passenger cars that I have mentioned of $3,490 per day. I would like to find out -what the agreement says in regard to the prices

the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are going to charge for the hire of their rolling stock to be used upon the railway and to ask if they cannot charge almost any price they like. If they charge at the rates which I have mentioned, the total of which is .$3,490 per day, it would amount in one year to $1,273,850, or 3 per cent on $40,000,000.
Now, I come to what is perhaps the most important part of this discussion-the question of freight rates. I have said that the government have largely built up their case on the bonding privilege and on the question of being able to handle the grain of the west and I have observed that the members of the government who have spoken upon this question have referred very gingerly to tbe_ question of the bonding privilege. I noticed also that the members of the government who have spoken, with one or two exceptions, have hardly touched the question of the cost of transporting grain. The hon. Minister of the Interior, however, was willing to tackle that question and he approached it with the courage of a Napoleon. You will have noticed that a lawyer very frequently, when he expresses his opinion in regard to a question of law, is very careful as to what he says, but when it comes down to a question of this kind we have an example of a lawyer expressing his opinion in regard to a matter of this importance in a very reckless manner indeed. The hon. Minister of the Interior gave us two or three illustrations of the way he figured out this matter of transportation. He had found somewhere or another-I do not know how he came across it-but he had found, he said, that grain was carried from Kansas City to Chicago for 5 cents per 100 pounds. I understand that he gave the page of the book in which he found that statement. It is not, however, to be had in the library and I was anxious to have seen it to have found out what explanation there was for such a statement, because, as a matter of fact, no such rate exists from Kansas City to Chicago. The rate from Kansas City to Chicago is 14 cents per 100 pounds, not 5 cents per 100 pounds. The average rate from Kansas Citv to Chicago is not less than 12 cents per 100 pounds, and I do not think it has been less than 12 cents for a long time past. That is more than half a cent per ton per mile. The hon. Minister of the Interior then went on to say that if grain could be carried-and he built up his case on that-from Kansas City to Chicago for 5 cents per 100 pounds, you could carry it from Winnipeg to St. .Tohn for 111 cents per bushel. It seems to me that there should be a limit to what a minister of the Crown should say in this House and can send forth to the country.
I challenge the hon. gentleman to produce anything to contradict the statement I make that the rate from Kansas City to Chicago is 14 cents per 100 pounds and that the

average rate is not less than 12 cents per 100 pounds. The hon. gentleman also referred to the rate on the New York Central from Buffalo to New York as being 21 cents per bushel, but later on he said that":
I talked with a prominent member of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange the day before yesterday, and I asked him, how that 10-85 cent rate would compare with the rates which he Is now paying from Winnipeg to New York by lake and rail. He tells me that, taking into account the rate by lake and the rate by rail, and a small additional charge for extra insurance which they have to pay by reason of this mixed carriage, the rate to-day from Winnipeg to New York is 164 cents.
He states at the top of the column that the New York Central rate is 24 cents per bushel, and here he says that the statement which was made to him by a prominent member of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange was that the rate from Winnipeg to New York was 16* cents per bushel. We all know that the rate from Winnipeg to the head of the lakes is 7* cents per bushel. We all know' that the rate from the head of the lakes to Buffalo is not more than 2 cents per bushel ; 7-1 cents added to 2 is 94 cents, and 94 cents subtracted from 164 cents is 7 which, therefore, according to his own figures is the rate per bushel from Buffalo to New York. So that, he actually says himself that the rate is 7 cents from Buffalo to New York ; yet,, he figures out a rate of 10-56 cents a bushel from Winnipeg to St. John, on the basis of a rate of 24 cents per bushel on the New York Central. He then comes to the Canada Atlantic Railway and he makes up this rate of 10* or 11 cents a bushel on the basis of the rate at which the Canada Atlantic Railway carries grain for. There is a very low rate existing at the present time on the Canada Atlantic Railway to Montreal. There is very little grain offering for carriage as last year's crop was shipped by the first of July, and the boats on the lakes are trying to get a little return cargo, they are cutting each other's throats and in that way they have got the rate down to a very low figure. In the fall when the new crop comes to be handled the rate will go up to 4 or 44 cents a bushel from Parry Sound to Montreal. The government have built their case up largely on the basis of being able to carry grain from Winnipeg to Quebec and to Halifax and St John. Even if we could carry grain over this road upon the most favourable conditions that it is carried over the American roads, could we attempt to compete with their lowest rates in face of the climatic conditions in winter in northern Canada, which renders the motive power of a railway engine, often from 25 to 33 per cent less, than if that engine were operating under favourable conditions on an American railroad, not taking into consideration the long rail haul over this proposed railway. We have some evidence' as to what it costs to carry grain. There

was an inquiry made a few years ago by a special comfuittee of tbe Senate, and the evidence was published, and I have tbe testimony here of Mr. G. A. Thompson, of Duluth, a man who is well posted in regard to the cost of carrying grain by water and by rail, and this is what Mr. Thompson says :
There has been a magnificent reduction in the rail rates corresponding to this table which I have shown you here, but suppose we turn now to the water rates. We find that on the Erie canal the rate is very much less. Turn to the lakes. There at the outlet of Lake Superior the records are kept very close, and in 1896 the average price received for the transportation of freight which went through the canals at the outlet of Lake Superior was ninety-one hundredths of one mill. We can state the fact broadly by saying that in general the cost of deep water transportation is only about one-tenth the average cost of rail transportation. Suppose I go, just for a moment into a little further elaboration of the figures. During that same year, according to a statement made before a meeting of the Lake Carriers' Association, the average rate of freight transportation on all the great lakes was only eighty-five one hundredths of a mill, and that mainly because there was deeper water in some of the channels below than in the St. Mary's canal and some of the outlets in that neighbourhood. Let us now- find the ultimate limits of competition :n order to discover the cheapest known form of transportation. A careful series of experiments conducted on the Grand Trunk Railway here in Canada some years ago showed that the actual net cost of transportation, that is exclusive of interest on bonds, &c., was five mills per ton per mile. The average net cost in 1896 on the . railroads of the United States was Bomewhat larger than that, being nearly six mills per ton per mile. There are a few coal roads where practically all the loads are carried by gravity, and the engines are used merely for the purpose of running the empty cars back again, and on these the average cost is three and half mills per ton ; but the best rate in actual railroad transportation under ordinary conditions is four mills per ton per mile.

speechtext: Does that include the long and the short haul ?

Yes. The road on which freight is carried at that low cost is the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway. Coming back to the story I was starting to tell you about the two railway presidents, I may mention the name of one of them. The western man was Mr. James Hill, president of the Great Northern road. He said [DOT]	' I have built some
steamships myself. Those steamships are built to the full draught of water at the Sault. This was before the larger canals were opened. They carry twenty-seven hundred tons of freight, and they make the run from Duluth to Buffalo in three and half days, and cost ail average of $120 per day. Now, in round numbers, almost as exactly as we can name it the distance from Duluth to Buffalo is 1,000 miles, and working that down we find that the cost is fifteen one thousandths of a cent per ton per mile. Turning that into figures that business men understand better than they cannot understand these microscopic rates, it means one-twenty-seventh of four mills, and that is the absolute net cost of carrying freight on the great lakes. That is to say. we do on the great lakes for $1 what it cost the best situated
railway in the United States $27 to do. Therefore, without going further into these figures-
I could give them by the hour, if necessary- you will agree with me in my conclusion that water transportation is the cheapest, and therefore if economy in transportation is the chief factor in the prosperity of nations, that nation which enlarges its waterways and developes them to the greatest possible extent will have done for its citizens, its producers and its consumers alike, the very best which can be done. But -we are not through with these interesting matters.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to place one or two illustrations before the House as to what it means to carry grain at so much per ton per mile, as is referred to in that evidence. Certain hon. members have dealt with this subject on the assumption that there is no basis of cost in regard to matters of this kind. They have proceeded under the assumption that railroads have been running in Canada and the United States all these years, and that they have not yet got down to any figures as to what it costs to transport grain, and as to what they have to pay for wear and tear, for coal, for the wages of men, and for all the things that enter into the operations of a railway. This report says that the figures Mr. Thomson gives do not include the interest on the bonds. Now, if it were possible to force the grain out of the North-west over this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to the seaboard, I would like to show what it would cost to the people of the North-west, basing my calculations on what is the actual cost of transportation. As was pointed out by the leader of the opposition yesterday, the cost to the Grand Trunk Railway for hauling freight where they have return cargo, and where they have plenty of traffic, is five mills per ton per mile. I will first take the calculation at five mills per ton per mile and then I will take four mills per ton per mile, although it is quite certain that this new road can never attain to the position in this respect of the best American roads, and this gentleman says in his evidence that the best-situated railways in the United States can haul for four mills per ton per mile. I will take the calculation at five mills per ton per mile, or, a half cent per ton per mile. From Winnipeg to Quebec the distance is 1.425 miles, and at five mills per ton per mile that would mean $7,121 cents per ton, or 36 cents per 100 pounds. The present rate from Winnipeg to Port Arthur is ten cents per 100 pounds, and from Port Arthur to Montreal eight cents per 100 pounds. I am assuming that the rate from Port Arthur to Montreal is not 31 cents per bushel, which is a cut rate, but I am taking five cents per bushel as the rate from Port Arthur to Montreal, which I know' is the current rate under normal conditions this year. Therefore the rate from Port Arthur to Montreal is eight cents per 100 pounds, and the rate from Winnipeg to Montreal would be. as 1 have shotvn, eighteen cents per 100 pounds.

The all-rail rate half a cent per ton per mile from Winnipeg to Quebec would be 36 cents per 100 pounds, whereas the present rate from Winnipeg to Montreal is eighteen cents per 100 pounds, which would leave a difference of eighteen cents per 100 pounds in favour of Montreal, as compared with any possible rate that could be charged on the new railroad to Quebec. That would mean that a bushel of wheat in Winnipeg which at present is worth eighty-five cents would only be worth 74-20 cents if carried by this new^ line of railway. If we had an export of 50.000,000 bushels of wheat, and if it were posible to force wheat over this railway to the extent of 50.000,000 bushels, then, at a loss of 18 cents per 100 pounds it would mean a loss on that amount of wheat of 85.400.000 to the farmers of Manitoba and the North-west, at the rate of half a cent per ton per mile. Now, making the basis of the calculation four mills per ton per mile, instead of five mills, then from Winnipeg to Quebec the rate would be $5.70 per ton, or 284 cents per 100 pounds, and that is a difference in favour of the present rate to Montreal of 104 cents per 100 pounds. That would mean on an export of 50.000,000 bushels a loss of $3,150,000 to the farmers of the west. Now, if we attempt to force to St. ,Tohn, N.B., 25,000,000 bushels of wheat over this new line, then basing the rate at five mills per ton per mile, there would be a loss on that quantity exported of $4,350,000. and on the basis of four mills'per ton per mile there would be a loss of $3,000,000, calculating the present rate from Port Arthur to Montreal at 18 cents per 100 pounds. The idea of hauling grain from Winnipeg to Quebec over this road would be just ns reasonable as if the Canadian Pacific Railway would talk about-hauling grain from Winnipeg to Montreal to compete with the water route, with this exception, that the new railroad might possibly be a better railroad for transportation, and that is the only advantage which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railroad could possibly have over the Canadian Pacific Railway. But be that as it may. the Canadian Pacific Railway would never think of doing anything of the kind.
I have made, the calculation as to the carriage of this wheat to St. ,Tohn. N.B., and if it could possibly be carried to Halifax the distance would be 100 miles greater, and the cost proportionately greater. I have read to the House the statement that it costs $120 per day to run one of these vessels carrying 90.000 bushels of grain, and lion, gentlemen can see how infinitesimal that cost is as compared with the expense of keeping up a railway.
It lias been said that grain could be carried from Port Arthur to Port Colborne or Buffalo in one of these large vessels carrying 250:000 bushels, at from 1} to 14 cents per bushel, but I believe that grain can be carried nearly a thousand miles from Port Arthur to Port Colborne at one cent, and Mr. KEMP.
from there to Montreal for two cents more, so that grain could in the' near future be carried from Port Arthur to Montreal by water for a sum not exceeding three cents a bushel. In this connection I would like to say that it seems to me that it should be the policy of the government to eqttijp Port Colborne, to build elevators, and to make further improvements there, in order that we may be able to compete with Buffalo, for the grain will come to one or pther of these ports.
The Prime Minister referred to the possibility of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway carrying the products of the North-west, but the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) admitted candidly, that it was not possible to carry grain to Quebec by this road. He said there would be other things to carry. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman, has there been any demand in this country that there should be a railway built for the purpose of carrying the manufactures of this country to the North-west ? What business of that kind will there be for this road that any other road in existence could not carry without any increase of rolling stock or of capital or anything else ? This road will not decrease the cost of carrying manufactured products to the North-west by one cent. The existing lines could carry six times as much of those products as they are carrying at the present time.
The right hon. Prime Minister made a great point of the importance of the proposed road for the shipment of manufactures to the North-west. I would like to read what he said on this point:
For one, two, three generations, at least, and perhaps more, these new settlers will grow cereals, and probably nothing else. They will have need of everything that is required by civilized men. They will have need of clothing, furniture and every other kind of manufacture. Then, Sir, what shall we do ? Shall we allow them to be supplied by our American neighbours, or shall we provide a railway which will enable our manufacturers in Ontario and Quebec to supply them with what they shall require ? There is one thing above all which will be their chief need, and that is lumber. They must have lumber for their houses, their barns and their stables, and all their buildings. Where are they to get it ? Not from the section of country where they live and work. The lumber is not to be had in that section.
But luckily for us, the other section of the road, the section between Moncton and Quebec, is rich in lumber of every kind ; and the moment the road is open, there will be established an important trade between the older sections of the country and these newer sections.
Now, Mr. Speaker. I think I have dealt sufficiently long with the bonding question and with the grain question, and I would like to take up this question of lumber very briefly. The Prime Minister proposes to take lumber from New Brunswick to build barns for the farmers of the North-west.
I wonder what the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who knows some-

thing about the lumber business, -would say of this suggestion. The hon. member for North Norfolk ventured to go as far east as the Timiskaming district in northern Ontario for lumber, but he thought be had better stop there, and not go any further east. The price of common pine in Winnipeg to-day is $19 per thousand feet. The cost of transporting lumber from the province of New Brunswick to the prairies beyond Winnipeg would be more than lumber is worth in Winnipeg. We all know that lumber cannot be transported any great distance without great cost, because it is such a cheap and bulky product; and yet the Prime Minister suggests that the people of the province of New Brunswick are going to send lumber over the proposed railway for the purpose of building barns for the settlers in the North-west. Why, the Lake of the- Woods district, which is only a little over 100 miles east of Winnipeg, is full of lumber, and there will be no lumber whatever going from New Brunswick to the North-west, a distance of 1.600 miles. I merely mention this to show some of the astounding arguments which hon. gentlemen opposite have resorted to on this question.
Now, I feel very much interested in the building up of the St. Lawrence route. Some people ask, how is it that our canals do so little business, and that our great St. Lawrence waterway is not utilized to a greater extent than it is ? Well, Sir, the reason is very clear. For many years we had no Canadian bottoms on the lakes, or at least very few, to move the grain from the west. The Americans had the business, and they managed to keep it, and it has been going to Buffalo. I have here a letter which was written to me on the 3rd of June, 1899, by a gentleman who used to be a member of this House, the late George H. Bertram. That gentleman, in the conduct of his business, and in this House, advocated the consideration of this transportation question on broad lines. In this letter he said :
I am quite satisfied in my own mind from a thorough examination of the whole question, that the St. Lawrence route via the Welland canal will ultimately be the controlling route, as to rates, provided there are sufficient Canadian vessels to do the business, and ample facilities at Montreal for receiving and exporting the grain of the west.
I quite agree that a greater necessity than ever exists to increase ' the number and capacity of Canadian bottoms at present engaged in the grain-carrying traffic upon the great lakes,' and that the government should encourage in some substantial way, the creating of a large Canadian marine capable of hauling the North-west grain.
Mr. Bertram was very anxious that the government should give a bounty on The registered tonnage of Canadian vessels to offset the duty on the fittings of vessels which come into this country, while British
bottoms come in free of duty. He did not succeed in convincing the government of his views. Other gentlemen have urged the same views on the government. If the government adopted that policy we would have more Canadian bottoms on the lakes than we have at the present time. However, through private enterprise we are getting a Canadian marine together by slow degrees. There have been imported into Canada from Great Britain this year for service on the lakes thirteen new vessels, a large number were imported last year, and there have been three vessels made in this country this year. But what the government should do is to encourage by a bounty the building of Canadian vessels for service on the lakes, and if we succeeded in building up a Canadian marine, we should be able, with the improvements in our canals and waterways between the head of the lakes and Montreal, to carry our own grain at least. The situation is very encouraging at the present time. The increased tonnage of the Canadian marine is showing its results perceptibly in our exports. In the last few years the total tonnage of seagoing vessels which left the port of Montreal from the opening of navigation up to the 1st. of August in each year was as follows : In 1900,	644.312 tons :	in 1901.	719,082 ; in 1902,	726,820 tons, and in
1903, 922,911 tons. But what is more encouraging is that the total tonnage of inland vessels arriving at the port of Montreal from the opening of navigation up to the 1st of August was as follows : In 1900, 774,729 tons ; in 1901, 743.926 tons ; in 1902, 852,761 tons, and in 1903, 1.956,949 tons. So it will be seen that what wTe have long hoped for, namely, the development of the St. Lawrence route and the diversion of the grain traffic from the Buffalo route, is coming about. I have always claimed that the St. Lawrence waterway will be the regulator of freight rates, and that we shall not be obliged in future, as we have been in the past, to say that the Erie Canal and the New York Central Railway are the regulators of freight rates. But what we have to do is to equip the St. Lawrence waterway so that we shall be able to carry our own grain in competition with the Buffalo route, and when we have done that we will get American grain also, and carry that to our own seaports. The grain of the North-west is bound to come out of the country by the lakes and the St. Lawrence waterway, or by the Georgian bay, and then on by rail to Montreal ; and if the Prime Minister would be a_ little patient, and instead of forcing on this railway to Quebec, would devote himself to improving the means of transportation by water, he would accomplish in that way what he will never accomplish by this railway. We have heard it said that grain has been carried to Quebec for 31c. per bushel. There

is no doubt that Quebec will be a great port in the future. I am as much an admirer of Quebec as any bon. member of this House; but we do not want to go into the great expense of this proposed railway at the present time just because of the solicitation and the earnest appeals of the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister, who, rightly, no doubt, because their constituencies are in Quebec, advocate this project. If the government desired to do something of real benefit to the farmers of the North-west, let them follow the example of the Manitoba government, when they said to the Canadian Northern people, You will have to reduce the cost of carrying grain from points in the west to the head of the lakes 2, 3 or 4 cents per 100 pounds. When this bargain was made, the rate from Winnipeg to the head of the lakes was 14 cents per hundred pounds. It has since been reduced to 12 cents per hundred pounds, and on the 1st of September it will be 10 cents. If this government had undertaken, in connection with this deal, to find out what the average rates were, and said to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway : ' What you have to do is to put before us a scheme whereby the cost of carrying grain to the sea-board will be reduced one, two or three cents per hundred pounds, such a policy would have interested the people of the North-west, and carried the country. This does not in any way relieve the conditions of the North-west. It does not reduce the cost of transportation to the farmers of that country one-millionth part of one cent. But whatever this proposal may accomplish, it has led to a very interesting debate, and we have had from hon. gentlemen supporting this project demonstrations of how you can force water to flow up hill. I have given a very full statement of this question of grain rates, and challenge any member of this House to contradict anything I have said. You cannot compete with the water system of the St. Lawrence by a railway paralleling it, and I have every hope that the great bulk of the grain of the Northwest will go out by way of Georgian Bay or Welland Canal, and the St. Lawrence route in the future, as well as a large share of the grain of our neighbours to the south.
When I interrupted the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) this morning, by calling his attention to the fact that this road could not carry grain in competition with the water route, he admitted my statement, but he said that manufactured products would go over it. But that will not be of any benefit, because the rates will not be reduced, as the railways now in existence can carry much more freight than they are able to secure. He also said that the Intercolonial Railway would not be handicapped because freight from the west to the maritime provinces would still go over that line. How does he make that out ? The Grand Trunk Railway has a system Mr. KEMP.
which gridirons Ontario, which gathers the manufactured products from most of the cities and towns of Ontario, and the Grand Trunk Railway will take that freight to L&vis, over its own road, and will not haul it over the Intercolonial Railway. It will do what it can to earn the interest it will have to pay the government.
Again, it is said by hon. members that if we cannot take grain over this road in the summer, we surely will take it in the winter. But grain does not go out of our Northwest or the American west in the winter time to any great extent. The transportation rates are so high that it pays better to store it away until the spring. Grain is sold for certain deliveries, and as much as possible is forced out of the country in the fall. What is left is held in the elevators, and the cost of carrying it in the elevators is very much less than would be the cost of taking it out in the winter.
The hon. Minister of Justice said that the day was dawning when the city of Quebec would get justice. Well, I want to see that city get justice, and I believe that the port of Quebec will benefit by the transhipment of grain, and the increased tonnage of ocean vessels which will go there. But I say that it will not be practicable to send grain to Quebec by this route. What the government should do, and what I would urge the hon. minister to advocate, is to improve the St. Lawrence system, so that vessels may go to the St. Lawrence ports just as easily and as safely as to any port on the continent, and also to improve our canal system. If that be done, the port of Quebec will be sure to reap a large share of profit.
The government have no mandate to push through this scheme at present. I believe that they should proceed along the line they laid down at the opening of the session, and appoint a commission. I look upon the government as occupying the position of trustees, and I cannot see how they are going to justify themselves before the people, when they have rushed into this project without having any expert knowledge of the cost of carrying the grain and other products, and of the capabilities of the country through which this railway will go. The have absolutely no knowledge of the conditions except the meagre information which they have placed before us, and are therefore not justified in going on with this project.
A good deal is said about diverting traffic and making it run from east to west or west to east, instead of from south to north, but in this connection you must not consider railway facilities only. In fact railways only occupy a minor position with regard to this matter. You must have your tariff so arranged that the products of the United States will not go from the south to the north. You must adjust your tariff to suit Canadian industries, and then you will have traffic for your railways

running east and west Tlie questions of fiscal policy and transportation policy go hand in hand, and the government will do well to consider these two questions as one. I am sorry to say that the government are weak on the tariff question, just as they have shown themselves weak on the question before the House. They would not have shown themselves weak with regard to the project before us had they followed out their original policy of appointing a commission to inquire into the whole question of transportation. A good, deal has been said about wild speculation. We have heard of loan companies and private individuals going into wild speculations and gambling in stocks ; but I would like to know if a more impulsive unconsidered thing was ever done by a private individual than has been 'done by this government, when, in a few weeks, it jumped to a conclusion and placed the project we are now discussing before this House. I would like to know if there is any record of anything of the kind having ever before been done by the government of any civilized country. If you take the cost of the railway at $125,000,000, and add that to our national debt, it brings our national debt up to the sum of nearly $400,000,000. It makes the liability to which we are committing ourselves in one session of parliament, including the guarantees we have assumed, including the estimates of this session, which I put at $65,000,000, including the guarantee of the Montreal harbour bonds, and the Canadian Northern Railway bonds, including all these, it makes a liability which we are incurring in one session, of $237,350,365. What I would like hon. members on the other side to give their attention to, when discussing this question, is the appointment of a commission on the transportation question. I would like them to explain why it was not appointed. Let us know the reasons which made the government go back on that policy V I would like to have them also show, if they can, that the figures I have given of the cost of transporting grain to the sea-board are wrong. I would like to know also how lumber can be brought from New Brunswick to points west of Winnipeg, and how the grain which the Grand Trunk Pacific. Railway will bring from the lakes is going to Canadian seaports. I would like to have the government show how the farmers of the North-west are going to be benefited to the slightest extent by this project ? Where the grain and the other produce of the North-west are going, while the eastern section is being constructed, and after the western section has been completed ? I would also like to know if it is necessary, in connection with a great national project of this kind, that a corporation should come to this government or any government with terms, conditions and schemes. Surely if we were going to build a great transcon- j
tinental railway we should have had an opportunity of making our own plans and specifications and asking for tenders on those plans and specifications in a businesslike way.
Mr. Speaker, I must apologize for having taken up so much of the time of the House. I did not intend to speak so long. In bringing my remarks rapidly to a close, I would say that there are two things which it is desirable to keep in mind. The first is to send Canadian goods through Canadian channels to the seaboard, and the other is to provide low rates in favour of the producer of the west. The result of the government's policy will be to send goods for years by way of Chicago, as the line to Quebec will not be built, and, even if it were finished, it would not be able to take the business. Moreover, the scheme will not reduce the cost of transportation. I shall be glad to have any Ontario members like my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) defend this scheme from an Ontario standpoint. I am especially interested in seeing some of my friends on the other side from Ontario attempt to defend this scheme along the line on which the government have attempted to defend it.
I am in favour of providing the west with all the transportation facilities necessary. We must adopt a generous policy with regard to Manitoba and the North-west Territory. As this scheme stands, the most objectionable part is the eastern portion of the line. That is an impracticable scheme; the road will only be a sink-hole for all time to come, and a burden upon the country. What the country wants is adequate transportation facilities to the North-west and cheaper rates. This road will be a burden upon the people of the North-west as well of the rest of this country ; it will not realize the millioneth part of a cent, so far as reduction in freight rates is concerned. The effect of it will be to place the Intercolonial under the control of the Grand Trunk. The distance is not likely to be materially shortened between Montreal or Quebec and St. John or Halifax. Even if there is a shortening of the distance to the extent of 60 miles on a transcontinental railway 3,600 miles in length, this shortening of the distance will be of no practical value. The people have not shown that they are in favour of this scheme ; they have not petitioned for it. There is every reason to believe that they are against it. If the government reduced the freight rate two or three cents a hundred, that would have pleased the people and would have been a good business proposition. The result of the policy of the government with regard to this scheme will be that the western part of the road will be in operation many years before the eastern part. A channel for trade through the United States will be established, a channel that we do not now use. And even when the whole railroad is

in operation, it will not lie able to carry tlie grain in competition with the water route. I would also like to refer to sections 42 and 43 of the contract which I have referred to as the pious clauses. I would point out that there is a dispute between the Grand Trunk- and the Intercolonial in reference to the wording of the traffic agreement now existing between them. I believe that the Grand Trunk will interpret that agreement strictly according to the legal and technical wording of it, and I think that nothing less can be expected than that they will do so. What I would do would be to improve the St. Lawrence water-way so as to take a large share of our trade to tlie seaboard, and, when this was done we could get a larger share of the American trade. This is not a party question. It it too serious to be handled in that way but impartially and carefully. I again appeal to the government to reconsider the question of the eastern portion of the road. That portion will not answer anything that is expected of it as an addition to the transportation facilities of this country. I hope that in the interests of the country, in regard to that part of the scheme, at any rate, the government will see their way clear to reconsider it, and, having withdrawn it, will secure expert evidence which will enable them to develop a plan more in accordance with the interest of the country as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, from certain articles I have seen in the newspapers and from information received from other sources, I am led to believe that a good deal of misapprehension exists in the minds of some persons in the province from which I come in regard to this national transcontinental railroad. I deem it my duty, therefore, to remove, if I can, some of this misapprehension. In my judgment the strongest and ablest-certainly the strongest-speech in this House against the proposed scheme, was that delivered by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair). I believe that it was the speech that had the most effect in the country. This was not entirely due to the speech itself, but was, in my opinion, due to the fact that the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals had been for many years associated with the Liberal party and had been for seven years a member of the government and the head of the Department of Railways and Canals. The part of that speech which appeared to the hon. gentleman himself, I think, to be the strongest, that part at least, on which he laid the most emphasis, was the part in which he alleged the undue haste, unwarranted and unexampled haste with which this project had been sprung upon parliament and the country. He said there had been no demand, from any party or any province of the Dominion, that there was no need of the railway, and he could not understand what induced the Mr. KEMP.
government to proceed with it. In order that there may be no misunderstanding on this point, I will, with your permission, read a short extract from the hon. gentleman's speech, which was delivered on the 11th day of this month :
The government of this country, realizing the enormous magnitude of this measure ; realizing that it is perhaps a measure without parallel in the history of this country ; realizing that no question so momentous in its nature, and involving such large responsibilities on the country had ever been presented to parliament since the confederation of the provinces of British North America ; realizing also that this decision and determination to carry this project through, if it could be carried through this parliament, and if the assent of the country could be secured for it ; realizing all this, my right hon. friend very naturally felt that the people of the country would expect that some satisfactory explanation should be furnished, as to why, with such unusual and such unexampled haste a measure of this magnitude and this character had been pressed upon them. My right hon. friend, realized this as any one with the same responsibilities and occupying the same position would have realized it, and therefore, we observe that the very first feature of this whole question to which the Prime Minister directed his attention, was to repel if possible the charge, or to answer if possible the accusation which must have entered into the mind of almost everybody from one part of Canada to the other, that this question had been sprung with undue haste and without deliberation. The right hon. gentleman undertook an answer to that phase of the case, and I will give the-House in his own words the answer which he gave. Let me tell the House in the first place, however, wherein it was that the right hon. gentleman did not offer an explanation of his course. He did not deny that there had not been deliberation ; he did not aflirm that the government of the country had availed itself of all proper sources of information, and had waited until they had exhausted all the means in their power-to ascertain what the conditions were in the various portions of the country which this road was to traverse ; he did not tell us the need which had arisen for us to jump headlong into a scheme of this kind ; he did not tell us that he had summoned to his assistance the wisest counsels which the country could afford ; he did not tell us that he had sought the assistance of experts in order to know what the traffic conditions were which would make this railway desirable ; he did not even pretend to tell us that he had done these
things	I have been a willing listener to
any demand of this kind, .and I am hound to say I have not heard any great outcry for another transcontinental line from ocean to-ocean. I do not know where the cry was made that it reached others. It was not made, at all events, so that it reached me	
I make bold to say that there is no evidence that the people of this country demand this legislation. I will commence with the province of British Columbia and ask you :	Is there any
call, loud or weak from the province of British Columbia that another railway should be put through the passes of the Rockies and carried to Fort Simpson ? If there is, I have not heard it. vince of Ontario ? Have we heard even a whisper of it before this thing was suggested?

But was the hon. gentleman of that opinion a few months ago ? There is no country where the soil is more fertile than in the millions of acres in Canada which the plough has not yet touched, and which man has not yet invaded. If we are to invite the people from the world outside to immigrate here, they have a right to expect that the government can assure them the means of transportation. pire.' On that day the ' Mail and Empire ' correspondent ' asked the minister to-night if he had at the time in his mind the possibility of the extension of the Grand Trunk to the Pacific coast,' and Mr. Blair replied :

The government would then have to hustle to provide traffic for two roads instead of one. Would that not injure the Intercolonial Railway if it could be injured ? Under the present arrangements when this road is built and leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the government need not worry any more about it. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has to provide traffic for that road and the government can turn its attention to the upbuilding of the Intercolonial Railway, and surely the government will be as efficient in the future as it has been in the past. The hon. leader of the opposition last night stated that he was not opposed to the building of a line from Quebec to Winnipeg but he said he would make it a colonization road. Surely, it would be well if the road were built to make it both a colonization and a transcontinental railway. Why not use it for both purposes V Would there be any objection to having transcontinental freight going over it and at the same time making it a colonization road? The hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken appear to be in favour of building a line from Winnipeg to North Bay. That would have no effect at all in accomplishing the object we have in view. The traffic that the Grand Trunk Pacific under these circumstances would bring down as far as North Bay would find its way to Montreal and Toronto and ultimately to Portland. Would that be a desirable thing? That is what we are anxious to prevent. If we can carry that traffic to our own country and ship it from our own ports would that not be a desirable thing to do ? Particularly as the road from Winnipeg to North Bay would cover about three-quarters of the whole distance would it not be well to go on and build the other fourth and thus complete the road to Quebec, an ocean port on the river St. Lawrence, especially as this road will bring Quebec as near to the wheat fields of the North-west Territories ns Montreal now is with the existing lipes. In addition to that Quebec is 180 miles nearer the ocean than Montreal and the traffic that goes over the Grand Trunk Pacific as far as Quebec must either be shipped by Quebec or sent on to some maritime province port. It cannot then go out to a foreign port. But, it has been said that it will be impossible to carry grain by this line from the North-west Territories. Sir Wm. Van Horne has been quoted as saying something to the effect that no railway would voluntarily carry grain from the wheat fields of the North-west to Montreal and to the ocean ports. As a matter of fact, according to the statement made by the hon. Minister of the Interior and even by the hon. leader of the opposition himself, large quantities

of grain are now being carried by rail from the North-west Territories. Although he is an experienced railway man Sir Wm. Van Horne is not the only man in Canada who is an authority upon these questions. There are other railway men who are second only if they are second to Sir Wm. Van Horne. There is the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway, Mr. Hays. He surely has had some experience. There is Mr. Wainwright and Mr. McGuigan who assist Mr. Hays in the management of the Grand Trunk Railway and they claim that grain can be carried by this route. They do more than make that claim; they are willing to put their money into the enterprise and back it up by their reputations as business men and railway men, and according to the ex-Minister of Railways they will put 828,000,000 of their own money into the undertaking. Whether grain can be carried or not, certainly, in the estimation of these men, sufficient traffic will go over this road to enable this company to pay interest on the cost of construction for forty-three years out of the fifty. That to my mind is the strongest possible proof that can be adduced in favour of the building of this road. When you get a company, like the old Grand Trunk Railway Company of this country, and when you get capable railway managers, like Mr. Hays and those who are associated with him, going into this enterprise and agreeing to operate the road, to keep it up to a high standard of efficiency, to pay all the operating expenses and to pay interest on the cost of construction for forty-three years it shows that in their estimation, at all events, it is going to do business. We need not worry very much about what kind of business it is going to do. It must not be forgotten that there are other kinds of trade in Canada besides the business of carrying grain. There is another industry in the North-west Territories that is perhaps second only to the business of grain growing. I refer to cattle raising. The great ranches of the North-west Territories are only beginning to be used and when better facilities are given to the people who are in the ranching business for getting their cattle out to the markets of the world, an enormous development will take place in that business as it will in other businesses in which the west is engaged. Last year ten million dollars worth of cattle were shipped out of the country, and a large portion of the cattle shipped from the North-west could not find sufficient railways to carry them east and. I think, 30,000 head had to go through the United States and be carried by United States railways to the seaboard. Is that a desirable state of things ? It is possibly true that grain during the summer months will take the lake route in preference to the rail route, but cattle cannot be carried by way of the lakes. The cattle must travel by rail the whole way from the point where they are raised to the point where thev are embarked 288i
on the ocean, and it is therefore necessary that we should provide facilities for handling this large traffic. Then, there is another industry that would be very important as far as this railway is concerned and as far as the settlers in the North-west Territories are concerned. That is the lumber industry. It is impossible, according to the information that I have received, according to information that has been given to this House and according to what we know, that the North-west Territories can be settled, that immigrants can go in there, and live unless they can get lumber with which to build their houses and barns and other buildings that are necessary for them. This road when built will go through the great lumber regions of northern Ontario and Quebec, and through the mountain districts of British Columbia and will be enabled to carry lumber to the settlers on the plains. This of itself will give rise to Important industries. The establishment of mills on these rivers in northern Ontario and in British Columbia where this lumber would be manufactured, will give employment to thousands of hands and call for the investment of ten of thousands of dollars.
But. the point which most concerns the province from which I come and for that matter the other provinces, I suppose, is the financial aspect of this question, and that is the point which has been most misrepresented by hon. gentlemen opposite. The Minister of Finance went pretty fully into this question and anybody who followed him closely ought to have a good knowledge of the financial side of this proposition. I need not say that the words of the Finance Minister will be accepted in this House and in this country pretty generally. He showed conclusively that $13,750,000 now invested in interest-bearing securities would provide sufficient money to meet all the demands the government would be bound to meet in connection with this transcontinental railway. There is another way of looking at the question. It appears to me that our friends opposite ignore the fact, wilfully ignore the fact, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will meet its obligations. There is no doubt in the minds of sensible men in Canada that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will meet the obligations, because it will have deposited with the government before it commences its construction at all, a guarantee of $5,000,000 in cash or in securities that will remain in the hands of the government until the road is completed up to within $5,000,000 of its total cost. That money will only be released by the government in instalments in order to enable the company to finally build and equip its road. In addition to that, the company puts at least $30,000,000 of its own money into the enterprise. The government guarantees the bonds on the prairie section, but is not responsible for any interest in any shape or manner as regards

that section, so long as the company will meet its obligations. The government guarantees the bonds on the mountain section to the extent of not more than $30,000 per mile, or three-fourths of the cost, and it will pay the interest on that guarantee for seven years.
Now, Sir, let me refer to the part of the road which will be built by the government itself from Moncton to Winnipeg. It is said that that road will be between 1,700 and 1,800 miles in length, and I will take the longest mileage on which to base my calculation. The ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) estimated that it would cost $35,000 per mile to build that section. In criticising the project from his standpoint, it1 was to his interest to put the cost of the road as high as possible, and I think most people in the country will come to the conclusion that he did so. Experienced railway men have said that it will not cost more than $25,000 per mile, but be that as it may, I will take the figures given by the ex-Minister of Railways. Now, 1,800 miles of railroad at $35,000 per mile would amount to $63,000,000. I am sure that !n the opinion of every reasonable man in this country, that will include the interest during the time of construction and everything up to date when the road is finished. The cost of that portion of the Quebec bridge which can be debited to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, according to the estimate of the Finance Minister, will not exceed $2,000,000. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier estimated that the total cost of the Quebec bridge is $5,000,000. but as four or five other railways will use that bridge, that portion which can be debited to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ought certainly not exceed $2,000,000. We have then as the total cost of the railway, and bridge included, $65,000,000. The interest on this amount at three per cent for seven years is $13,650,000. That is the total charge the government will have to meet, because at the end of seven years the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway takes over the road and pays the interest on the cost of construction from that time forward for the balance of the fifty years.
The mountain section is estimated at 480 miles, and supposing it is 500 miles long, then at $30,000 a mile or a total cost of $15,000,000 and the interest on that for seven years would be $3,150,000, or a total cost to us altogether of $16,800,000. That I submit is the largest amount for which the government of this country becomes responsible. It is the outside figure, because at the end of fifty years, when the bonds for the building of this railway will have matured, does any intelligent or reasonable man in Canada suppose that the railway will not then be worth a great* deal more than it cost, and if the government of that day sees fit to operate the railway, will it not be worth more to the government than it has cost ; or if the government of that day will
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.)
operate the railway they will certainly get a rental for it far in excess of three per cent, and possibly twice that amount. The development of the country by that time will have been such that the railway wilt certainly be more valuable than when it was constructed. Now then, would this $16,800,000 be an enormous sum for the people of this country to meet ? Suppose we take it over and divide the population of Canada into it. The population of Canada at present is upwards of 5,500,000, and before we are called upon to pay any large contribution to this railway our population will have reached 6,000,000. That would just amount to $2.80 per head. If the people of this country had to pay $2.80 per head in one year, would it bankrupt them ?
Not much.

I think it was the hon. member for East Grey who said that the burden placed upon the people of this country by this proposed railway would precipitate his constituents into the yawning abyss of financial ruin.
Oh, my.
I did not make any such) statement.
Well, the statement of the hon. gentleman was a very strong statement in that direction.

I said that according to the estimate I made of the obligations incurred by us, it would represent from $100 to $125, standing against each family in the country, which might fairly be regarded as a mortgage on the farm of every farmer as long as the youngest member of the fam-t ily was alive.
I cannot possibly see how $16,800,000 would represent a mortgage of $125 on each family in the country.

Does the hon. member pretend to say that the eastern section can be built for $16,000,000 ?
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.) I do not say that, but I say that that sum will be the interest for seven years.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that we must borrow the money ?

Yes, lam aware of that. Well, now. we are not called upon even to pay this $2.80 per head in one year,-because it will be spread over a period of fourteen years, and we will be asked to pay it in fourteen annual instalments which will amount to just 20 cents a year for each' one of our population. Twenty cents a year per capita the people of this country will have to pay in order to provide a transcontinental railway from Moncton to the, Pacific ocean.

Cheap enough.

Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) Yes, it is cheap enough; it is an excellent bargain. I do not think there is a man in this country who will have to mortgage his farm in order to raise that 20 cents. I do not think there is a farmer in Ontario who will have to do so; I know that there is not one in Prince Edward Island. But shall we have to pay the 20 cents even? No. Before the 14 years will have expired, our population will have at least doubled. Some people think it will have trebled. I believe that kon. gentlemen opposite agree that it will at least have doubled; and consequently our per capita contribution to this railway will be cut in two, and will be down to 10 cents. But during a portion of that time our population will be no more than 6,000,000, so that I suppose it will be fair to strike an average, and say that our contribution during the 14 years will be 15 cents per capita per year. What do we get for that ? We get a transcontinental railway, a railway from ocean to ocean.
But this is not all of the financial aspect of the question. This railway will pass through 1,200 miles of fertile territory in the North-west, throwing open to settlement from 25,000,000 to 50,000,000 acres of land. It will be a conservative estimate to put upon that land the value of $3 an acre. The hon. Minister of the Interior the o+her evening stated that he felt justified in saying that before ten years will have elapsed, the Interior Department will have sold 20,000,000 acres of land to settlers for at least ?3 an acre in consequence of the building of this transcontinental railway. So that the railway will return directly to the treasury of this country from the land sales alone three or four or five times what the people of the country will be called on to pay for the building of it. That money will remain in the treasury or be used for the necessary public works throughout the country, and at the end of the fifty-year period, if the people of the country had to pay the bonds on which the money to build this railroad was borrowed, long-before that period would have elapsed the money that would come from the land sries in the North-west in consequence of the building of the railway, would more than provide for the lifting of those bonds, and the railway would not therefore cost tbe people of this country one Cent.
