The increased value of the lands through which the railway will pass will more than pay for the railway.
There is another way of looking at tbe matter. Will any man in this House deny that this country will do a largely increased business in consequence of the building of this railway, that it will induce immigration to come to this country, and $100,000,000 of capital? Surely this will give a great impetus to the trade and commerce of the country, and what will be the profits the people will derive from that increase of
trade? I am inclined to think that it will be at least three or four times what we shall be called on to pay. The position appears to me to be something like this. If a farmer or a merchant or a manufacturer, or any man doing business in Canada, were morally certain that by enlarging his plant, increasing his machinery, putting up more buildings, perhaps doing a little judicious advertising, his business would be so much increased that the profit on the increased business would more than pay the interest on the expenditure, would any progressive business man hesitate to make that expenditure ; and that to my mind is the position of this country with regard to the financial aspect of this railway.
It was said that this will parallel the Intercolonial ; but that cry has been dropped, and it is said now that it will duplicate it. As the hon. leader of the opposition has said that he is not opposed to the building of a railway from Quebec to Moncton, the statement that this road will parallel and destroy the Intercolonial will certainly have to be dropped or modified. But are there any other places in Canada where railroads parallel or run close to each other which have been built by the people of this country ? There are certainly many cases, and yet we never heard this cry raised before, that the railroads wiere paralleling or destroying each other. The Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk Pacific from Quebec to Moncton will average sixty miles apart. Bet us compare them with other railroads which run close to each other. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canada Atlantic from Ottawa to Montreal are on the average sixteen miles apart. The Canadian Pacific, when it had only one line from Ottawa to Montreal, was not satisfied with that, but built another line: and there is also river navigation between these two cities. So that there are three lines of railways and the river between Ottawa and Montreal, and I suppose they all find trade. Then the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk between Montreal and Toronto are on the average only twenty-five miles apart, less than half the distance between the proposed railway and the Intercolonial. The Grand Trunk and the Canada Atlantic from Montreal to the Georgian bay are on the average sixty miles apart; the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern between Winnipeg and Port Arthur are on the average sixty miles apart; yet, these railways are not said to parallel one another.
It may be said, and it has been said, that the people of Prince Edward Island will get no benefit whatever from the building of this railway; but I have this to say, that the province of Prince Edward Island is an integral part of the Dominion of Canada, and the people of that island, if I understand them, and I think I do, are willing to pay their fair share of whatever is

required to provide the necessary public works throughout the Dominion of Canada for the development of the trade of the country, knowing and believing that their fellow-Canadians in the other provinces will give what is fair and reasonable to enable them at least to overcome the natural disadvantages and difficulties which are incidental to their insular position, and to provide the necessary public works in that province.
There are some things that we greatly require in Prince Edward Island, and I take this opportunity of presenting in a few words some of the needs of that province. At the time of confederation it was stipulated in the terms of union that we would have continuous and efficient steam communication, winter and summer, between Prince Edward Island a"hd the mainland, and an efficient up-to-date telegraphic service. Well, Sir, reasonable efforts have been put forth to provide these requirements in the past; but I must say that these stipulations have not been carried out in their entirety. We are not unreasonable in our demands. What we require now is a third winter steamer. Our trade has grown so fast and I am sure the members from the other provinces will be glad to hear that the development of Prince Edward Island is going on as rapidly as that of the other provinces of the Dominion; so that where a few years ago we required only two steamers to accommodate our trade we now require three. The cost of a third steamer will not be large, and she could be used in the fishery protective service in the summer, and for communication between the island and the mainland in the winter. We have been demanding improved telegraphic communication for several years. Our present telegraphic service is open only twelve hours out of the twenty-four on week days, and is closed every Sunday. In that respect we are a very' exemplary people. And if costs one hundred per cent more to send a telegram to or from the island than it does on the mainland. These are grievances that ought to be removed and removed quickly ; and while we are willing to contribute our fair share to the construction of public works necessary for the development of the other provinces, we ask our brother Canadians in those provinces to contribute sufficiently to overcome these difficulties to which I have referred and which are incidental to our insular position. In addition we require a few more miles of railway accommodation in order to carry on our business, and I would impress on hon. members, what many of them do not seem to know, that the people of Prince Edward Island built and paid for their own railway at the time of confederation. Consequently, when we are contributing to the construction of railways in the other provinces we
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.)
have a claim on them for reasonable railway accommodation in our own.
But will the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific be of any direct advantage to the farmers of Prince Edward Island ? I believe it will. It will certainly develop the coal, iron and steel business of Nova Scotia such as nothing else could do. We know how valuable the markets of Sydney and other towns of Nova Scotia have been to our farmers during the last few years. We know that anything which will build up the towns and cities of Nova . Scotia and New Brunswick and thus provide a market for the products of Prince Edward Island, will be of the greatest advantage to the farmers of that island. The larger markets which will be given to us in Nova Scotia, Cape Breton and New Brunswick, by the construction of this railway, will repay us three or four times at least our contribution towards its construction. These are the chief reasons why this project appeals to my support.
The leader of the opposition last night laid before this House an alternative proposition. He proposed to extend the Intercolonial to Georgian Bay or to purchase the Canada Atlantic Kailway and then build from Georgian Bay to Sudbury. He proposed also to acquire by purchase the Canadian Pacific Railway from North Bay to Port William, and to spend large sums on the improvement of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Port William to Winnipeg and on improvement of the Canadian Northern from Port William to Winnipeg. He did not tell us, nor has any gentleman opposite told us, what all this would cost; but in my judgment it would cost at least as much as this transcontinental line. To improve the Canadian Pacific Railway, its grades and curves, from North Bay to Port William, would certainly cost a large sum of money. To buy the Canadian Northern Railway to Parry Sound or Geogian Bay would cost a heavy sum. The country to Sudbury is said to be a very difficult one to build through and very expensive. But even when that would be all done, we would have no more railway transportation facilities than we now possess. The facilities might be improved, but they would not be increased. But the hon. gentleman was not satisfied with that. He said lie was in favour of building from Quebec to Winnipeg and from Quebec to Moncton. He was not afraid to spend money. In fact he was willing to promise anything and only invited the people to ask for whatever they wanted. He was going to improve the docks and terminal facilities at Halifax, make Montreal a free port, improve the harbour facilities at Quebec, and in fact all along the lakes. I .have no doubt it would take $300,000,000 or $400,000,000 to carry out all the improvements which the leader of the opposition \dvocat-

ed last night, and as he unfolded his scheme,
I could not help feeling compassion Cor the misery which the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) must have suffered when he thought of his constituents and the mortgage that would be put upon them and the farmers of Ontario before half these improvements were carried out.
These improvements would be carried out for half the cost of the government undertaking.
Give us the figures.

I think my hon. friend will find out that I have not exaggerated. The scheme submitted by the government commends itself to my judgment. This proposed railway will extend from Moncton through the central part of New Brunswick and give railway accommodation and development to that province. It will extend along through the southern portion of Quebec. It will extend from Quebec westerly and northwesterly and through the northern part of the province of Ontario, opening up in that province great mineral wealth and giving access to valuable timber areas and rich agricultural lands. It will give depth to our country as well as length, and we will no longer be a fringe of settlement along the international boundary. It will provide a living band of men and women in that portion of country which is not now inhabited, that is between the east and the west, and extending on on to the Pacific coast. These are desirable things to accomplish and which cannot be accomplished in any other way.
But there is something else which commends this proposition to my approval. If the time should ever come-and it will not come through any fault of ours-when we may have to stand shoulder to shoulder in defence of our country, our institufons and our laws, think what a sense of security this continental railway extending from the impregnable fortress of Quebec in the east to a fortified fort on the Pacific ocean, will give us. Our troops could be easily transferred from the west to the east or from the east to the west and placed at any intermediate point where danger might threaten. Should that day ever come,, as there ',a man in Canada who would begrudge this contribution of 15 cents a year for fourteen years for the power and security which such a line of communication would afford ? Mr. Speaker, the people of cities yet unbuilt will rise up to do honour to the men who had the ability to conceive and the courage to carry, through, in spite of the opposition of friend and foe, this great national undertaking, an undertaking whiijli will do much to make of Canada a nation among the nations of the earth.
Mr. ,W. H. BENNETT (East Simcoe). I move the adjournment of the debate.
It it only eleven o'clock, and it seems to me we ought to go on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen on that side of the House, two or three times since this debate commenced, have asked for an early adjournment. We have been running pretty late for some time, and I think the government might consent to the adjournment now. I do not think it would prolong the debate if we adjourned.
I would suggest that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) might go on, as has been done by other hon. gentlemen, deliver part of his speech, and finish tomorrow.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when, towards the latter part of 1902, it was announced in the public press of the province of Ontario that certain gentlemen were about to undertake the construction of a transcontinental line, that announcement was hailed with considerable pleasure by people of the Dominion generally. We all had faith in the future greatness of the country and felt that a second transcontinental railway was not only a desirable project in the interests of the Dominion, but one that would probably be a remunerative undertaking to those who projected it. The announcement made at that time was a business proposition. And forthwith the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which really stood as a sponsor for the undertaking, caused to be circulated among the business men. of this country a book called ' Facts concerning the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.' At the same time they caused to be circulated throughout the Dominion a map showing where the projected line of railway was to run. And when one looks back over those six months, it seems impossible to reconcile the proposition now before parliament with the proposition announced by these gentlemen. A few words from this book issued by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will show what the proposition was which they had in view at that time. I quote from page 2 of this book :
The proposed Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, which will extend from Quebec to the Pacific coast by way of North Bay, the present junction of the Grand Trunk Railway, a distance of about 3,025 miles.
So, it is plain from the prospectus that there was no intention on the part of these gentlemen, no thought present to their minds, of building from a point further east than North Bay in the province of Ontario. Further than that, in the maps that were issued by these parties at the time, it was plainly shown that the construction was to

commence at North Bay. The public will naturally wonder why, after the lapse of two or three months such a striking departure has been made from the original scheme. A reference to the ' Canadian Gazette ' of that time-the original notice, I think was given about the 15th of December-shows that it was to be built from North Bay to the Pacific ocean, with branches to Winnipeg and Calgary. There is a little history concerning the change of base by these parties, and I am going to refer to it briefly.
Some year or two ago, there was granted by the parliament of Canada a charter to certain gentlemen of the city of Quebec for what was known as the Trans-Canada railway. That was a railway that was -to run from the city of Quebec westward away to the north of Lake Winnipeg and through to the Pacific coast. After that charter had been issued, the proposition known as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway came up. So, the government were face to face with a difficulty. They had a proposition with the large backing that was behind the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, not only the magnates of the Grand Trunk, but such men, high in the councils of the Liberal party, as Senators Cox and Gibson. The government were alive to the fact that if these two charters were to he gone on with, they would have to face two gigantic railway subsidies. What were they to do ? At once, efforts were made to bring the parties together and head off either one railway or the other. Of course, it would be utterly impossible to do away with Senators Cox and Gibson, owing to the great power they have with this government. A gentleman who is a member of the government from the province of Ontario saw at once the position in which the government would be placed. One subsidy was bad enough, but what was to be done if two railway subsidies had to be paid to two distinct corporations ? The month of December went by. The application of the Grand Trunk Pacific was in, and it was well understood that the granting of a charter would be followed by a demand for a subsidy. A charter had already been granted to the Trans-Canadian people, and, of course they would make application to parliament for a subsidy. One must cast his eye over the situation in the province of Quebec to see the strong position held by the Trans-Canada people. We have all seen what has been going on for the last six or seven years in the city of Montreal. Thanks to the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) great works have been going on in the harbour of that city with a view of attracting and handling the trails-portation traffic of this continent.. Now, I would recall to the minds of hon. members the fact that two years ago the members of this House and of the Senate were treated in the most royal manner in the city of Mr. BENNETT.
Quebec by the city council and the board of trade there. On that occasion, at a magnificent banquet that was tendered to us, it was pointed out that the great city of Quebec was being side-tracked. We were told that the Great Northern and Canada Atlantic Railway systems, by an arrangement, had succeeded in attracting a large portion of the grain trade to that port. And it was an open secret that the people of the city were loud in complaints, that the Premier, representing one of the constituencies of the city of Quebec and the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) representing the county of Quebec had not been able to prevail upon the government to secure any desirable improvements in the port of Quebec, but that all the improvements were being made in the port of Montreal, and that the whole trade was tending in that direction. Plainly, if things were to continue as they then were, the city of Quebec, would be left in the background, to the great advantage of the city of Montreal. The Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) knew full well that the Trans-Canada charter had been granted and that the Premier and the Minister of Justice would not stand idly by-dare not stand idly by-nor would the other members from the Quebec	district remain quiet,	and seethe Trans-Canada railway charter left without	being supplemented	with asubsidy.	The	Postmaster General sawthe dilemma-two applications for subsidies, one on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific and one on behalf of the Trans-Canada.	And	the Postmaster	General
thought he would come to the front, and so on March 24, at a banquet tendered in Toronto at which the Postmaster General spoke he saw the necessity of breaking the ice in order that the government might at once be placed in a position to bring these two rival companies to an arrangement. Speaking in Toronto on that occasion the Postmaster General who had been discussing at that time that question of transportation generally in the Dominion of Canada said as reported in the Toronto 'Newts':
For example, were a railway to be built direct between Winnipeg and Quebec city, the latter would be within less than 1,300 miles of Winnipeg, as against Portland's over 1,700 miles. Boston's nearly 1,800 miles and New York's 1,900 miles. We have also a corresponding shorter ocean distance to Great Britain.
Further on he said, and this was the point at which the Postmaster General desired to make himself solid with the public, and more particularly with the province of Ontario :
Public opinion to-day appears to be more or less against subsidizing railways. Is there any prospect of capitalists out of their own capital alone building a line over the thousand miles of country to which I have alluded, which for many a year will fail to supply any reasonable return on the capital invested ? Capitalists are

not philanthropists, but expect a return upon their investments. Shall we proceed to subsidize the various railways that are now proposing to extend their lines to Manitoba ? Shall the country extend the Intercolonial Railway, say, from Quebec to the Pacific Ocean, not only investing the capital involved in the work itself, but also operating the line, or shall we simply build a railway highway available under proper regulations, as would be a canal, for the traffic of all railways between Manitoba and, say, the city of Quebec, with its branch connections with intermediate provinces, or shall we fold our arms, shrink from discharging our proper responsibilities, and let the country drift ?
There are those who, forgetting that the progressive Canada of to-day is not the old, unprogressive Canada of half-a-dozen years ago, think her affairs can be managed now as then. There are others who, for party purposes, would paralyse our action by endeavouring to deter us from having the courage to meet the altered conditions of to-day. Neither of these classes, I think, represents true Canada. There is a third, a more broad-minded* progressive, enterprising and patriotic section of the people, an ' Onward Canada ' party in effect, who, recognizing the unparalleled progress our country is making to-day, demand that, instead of deterring the movement by inaction, we should take occasion by the hand, and wisely and masterfully grapple with, and if possible successfully solve, the problems growing out of Canada's great and unprecedented development.
A Serious Problem.
One of the most serious of these problems is the railway question to which I have alluded. The wise solution of this problem as, for example, by direct railway connection between Manitoba and Quebec city, means much for Canada.
Now, Sir, what was plain ? It was plain that the Postmaster General saw the dilemma facing the government, the Trans-Canada Railway Company with its powerful influence which would be exerted in its behalf demanding a subsidy, and the company headed by Senator Cox and Senator Gibson. The Postmaster General at once rushed into the foreground with his idea of putting both of these railways to one side if possible, and at all events if uot putting both, at least putting one of them to one side. Then what happened ? That was the position of matters until parliament met, and when parliament met the Grand Trunk Pacific Company came along with their notice and asked then that a charter should be granted them' in the terms upon which they had originally applied, namely from North Bay and North Bay alone, as the eastern point to the Pacific coast. We all know what happened in the Railway Committee, when the committee met about the 8th of May, Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Charles M. Hays were present as representing the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and then, not to the amazement of lion, gentlemen in this House, because it was pretty well known to what extent matters had gone, the company at once threw up their hands and said : 'We have changed our plans, we are not going
to build a railway to North Bay, but we intend to make our eastern point exactly what the Postmaster General said it would be, namely, the city of Quebec.' What happened then ? There was the dilemma hon. gentlemen had to meet with their party friends, the maritime province men up in arms one and all. We all remember the hon. member for Westmoreland and the hon. member for Cumberland as they each in turn addressed Sir Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays, and what was the result ? Sir Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays both made the positive and distinct statements that the railway would not go beyond Quebec, and the hon. member for Queen's, N.B. asked, ' Why stop at Quebec,' to which Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson answered :	' We have an agreemen with the government for the maritime ports of St. John and Halifax, and I think that answers the question.' The answer there, no doubt, referred to the arrangement that existed between the Intercolonial Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway. Further on the hon. member for Cumberland asked if they would build to the maritime provinces. Mr. Hays' answer to that was most emphatic:	'We will certainly not build
there.'
And they will not either.

Here was the party confronted with the dilemma that their maritime province members were to go on strike unless the government came down from their perch, and agreed to meet the wishes of their supporters from every part of the Dominion. There cannot be a doubt that as a business proposition the Grand Trunk never intended to build east of North Bay, but were driven into that by their supporters from Quebec, and after their supporters from the province of Quebec had succeeded in driving them to build it to the city of Quebec then, pleased with the prospect of what could be done by driving, the maritime province men followed suit, and the result is that to-day the people of Canada are being saddled with what was very properly termed by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals a political railway, and not a practical railway or a business railway at all.
So much, Sir, for the inception of the road, and the position it has reached to-day. We need not here go into this fact that at about that time, when the Bill was before the committee, the government had not succeeded in dragooning the Ontario ministers into accepting the Moncton proposition. It is a notorious fact that it was only at the point of the pistol that the ministers from Ontario were driven into this arrangement, and I believe to-day that the clause that exists in the contract that parliament can at any time stop the work at this end, was the last peg upon which the ministers from Ontario are hanging their caps to-day, and that there is no intention on the part

of the government ever to build one mile east of Quebec. X say that the Minister of Customs and the Postmaster General, when they go into the campaign this fall which was announced by the hon. member for South Wellington to-day, would be held this fall, I say that every one of their ministers will pin his faith to that clause and point out to the province of Ontario that that contract contains a clause that they need not build eastward from Quebec at all, but that parliament will have the right and have the power to stop the construction of the work from that point at any time.
Now this debate was opened by the Prime Minister, and that hon. gentleman made a very lengthy speech, a speech that is being franked not by thousands, but by thousands of tens of thousands, into every province from end to end of the Dominion, and I hope and trust that a great many of them may be sent into East Simcoe. I haven't much to say about that speech, but I shall do it the courtesy of referring to it at great-fer length than his followers have done to-day. We may take the speech and read it under its different heads. A great part of it is devoted to the fact that this is to be an all-Canadian route, and that Canada must have an all-Canadian route. There is not the humblest back bencher on the government side who will rise and repeat his language in that regard, because it has been exploded. Every one knows and every school boy knows that there is a Canadian system of railways irrespective of this one, from end to end of the Dominion, and no single word has been heard and no single word will be heard further in this debate as to the question of an all-Canadian railroad, and as to the filling of that long desired want.
The next point in it was the bonding privileges and to-day we heard two or three gentlemen on that side of the House, and not a single one of them has mentioned the bonding privileges. There is no hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, who when he rises in his place, and I am sure no minister who speaks on this question frofn this on, will urge as a reason for the construction of this railway the necessity of preserving ourselves in such a position that there may be no abrogation of the bonding privilege on the part of the United States of America. Now, the fact of the matter is that the government has * been driven from pillar to post on this question. In the first place the influences of Senator Cox were so great that they had to bow to them. In the next place, the influence of Trans-Can-' a da Railway Company were so great that they had to bow to these also, and being met, as they would be met, with requests for two subsidies by these two rival roads, when they found themselves able to deal with only one, the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock), and I congratulate the hon. gentleman, that for once he Mr. BENNETT.
has had his way, apparently has driven the government into this scheme for the construction of a part of this railway system, and as a result the Dominion of Canada is in the position in which it finds itself placed to-day. We have heard from the other side of the House some very lengthy speeches,' and all of them have been tinged with one thing and one thing in particular. The ministers have seen fit not to abuse the horn ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, and soj they have delegated that work to the backbenchers and each little back-bencher seems to think it incumbent upon himself to say everything he can of an abusive nature of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and, Canals. Abuse is all very well in its wayi but the people of this Dominion want something else than abuse. They want argument, and I can tell hon. gentlemen opposite that abuse an'd vituperation of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals are not] going to raise them in the estimation either in the people of this country or of the mem-t hers of this House. Sir, common gratitude should prompt some of these hon. gentlemen to speak in a proper manner of the hon. exMinister of Railways and Canals. Can any) one imagine that the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) three months ago would have risen in his place and told the great big exMinister of Railways and Canals that he was not fit to untie the shoes of the right hon. Premier ? I can only fancy this, that if the hon. member for Hants had said that the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals would have at once propounded this question : If I am not fit to unloose the latchet of the shoes of the right hon. Prime Minister of this Dominion, in the name of all that is good what menial service should the hon. member for Hants perform for that great man ?
Now, Sir, there has been a great deal said in the public press on this question and more particularly in the independent press of this country. I am going to quote some of the statements that have been published.; Nobody expected to see the ' Globe ' newspaper go up against this proposition. Who could imagine, in the name of all that is good, that the ' Globe ' would say one wrrd disparaging o.f it ? Who could imagine that the ' Globe,' after having seen the Crow's Nest deal through, the greatest iniquity that this government has ever perpetrated in the interests of the ' Globe,' could for a moment rise up and try to beat from the public gaze this great proposition of Senator Cox ? We will take the ' Farmers' Sun,' which is a pretty good paper. The ' Farmers' Sun ' says in a recent issue :
There is no justification for imposing such a burden on the farmers of Ontario and the west. They have grain to sell. They must sell it in Britain. Nothing could be more natural nor more profitable than that they should seek their market by the cheapest route.
And then we find that the government has

been unfortunate in this, that while it has the able assistance of the ' Globe ' newspaper in perpetrating any scheme upon the public, unfortunately it is not always able to control the Montreal ' Witness,' and the ' Witness ' says :
Curiously enough nothing is said about these branch lines in the contract, or has been announced concerning them. Yet these three are all obvious necessities. The one to Fort William would carry more freight than the main line as most of the grain will still cross the lakes by water. That to Montreal would make Portland as tempting a port as it now is to the present Grand Trunk Railway system, there being a constant tendency to take to the water as soon as possible.
Weil, that seems to be different from the government, because most of the members of the government have taken to the woods and the hon. member for Hants, if all reports are true, is to have a judgeship at an early day as a reward for holding a brief in defence of this iniquitous proposition. The great question as affecting this proposition to-day is the question of the railway haul of the vast products of the west. Last fall I had great pleasure in visiting the province of Manitoba and a good portion of the North-west Territories, and any hon. member of this House who may journey to the west to see that great country must be struck with the unlimited possibilities of its resources. One of the needs, and it seems to me the growing need, if one can listen to what is said by the settlers, is more railway accommodation for the country. What particularly strikes one in listening to their complaints, is that they do not complain so much of the absence of railway systems but rather of the fact that there has been a congestion of trade due to the fact that they did not have a sufficient number of cars or sufficient amount of locomotive power. To-day the question in the west, as far ns we can see and as far as all can see. is the question of getting the crop out to the seaboard in the quickest possible way, and also at the least possible rate. In all lines of business and in all walks of life the success of those engaged in similar undertakings should afford a guide and criterion for others, if we look to the western trade of the UnitPd States what is the lesson taught by it ? Go to the north-western states, to Dakota, Minnesota, and all that line of north-western states, go to Illinois, and the states that lie west and south of Chicago, and you will1 find this fact that with all their large railway accommodation in that country the grain is not carried from the west to the east by the all-rail route but it is carried by a mixed system of water and rail, and therefore I say that to-day in Canada it has been demonstrated that the proper way of bringing out the grain from the North-west is to pursue the system which is being pursued by the people of the United States. We have that very system in this country in
carrying grain from the west to the east. I recall to mind, which is in the history of the last parliament, because it was the subject! of a debate in this House, that upon one occasion the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals attempted to carry 300,000 bushels of grain to St. John from the North-west. What was the result ? That grain was brought from points in the north shore of Lake Superior to Parry Sound, it was taken down over the Canada Atlantic Railway, the Great Northern Railway and the Intercolonial Railway to St. John, and the result of the carriage of that grain for that long distance was that there was a loss of $10,000 on one cargo of 300,000 bushels. If it is a fact that on one single cargo, because that amount would only make up the cargo of one of the laege freighters on the great lakes, there was a loss of $10,000, how is it possible to carry grain from the far west to the east over a long grain haul, and in the case to which I have referred it was not 'as long a grain haul as it would be in the ease of the Grand Trunk Pacific, because the grain was put into the cars at Parry Sound ? If this project is ever to go into effect, how is it possible to carry grain over this long haul from the west to St. John or Halifax ? The people of Canada to-day have in St. John and Halifax large grain elevators, and it is a notorious fact that although the Halifax elevator cost this country some hundreds of thousands of dollars not a single bushel of grain has ever been passed through it.
As to the St. John elevator, I do not think it ever held a bushel of grain outside of these 300,000 bushels. In the face of this experience the government tell us that they are going to turn the whole tide of transportation, and carry grain by rail over this immense distance from the prairies along the north shore of Lake Superior, and clear through to the tidewater of the Atlantic. Let me call the attention of the House to this fact. Toledo is only 250 miles from Buffalo, and yet they carried by rail last year about 7,000,000 bushels of grain to Toledo and there transferred it to vessels and took it to Buffalo. That proves beyond all doubt that there can only be a successful grain carrying trade on this continent by water and by rail. From Chicago to New York the distance is 950 miles, taking the average of the different railway systems connecting the two cities, but only a trifling quantity of grain is carried by allrail between these two points and that only during the winter season. Last year's report of the Buffalo Merchants' Exchange shows that Buffalo received the immense quantity of 124,626,434 bushels of grain, and of grain reduced to flour 60,133,080 bushels, representing the total receipts at Buffalo, 184,759,518 bushels for the year. This shows that the people of the United States have made a success of the grain carrying business. I regret to say that in

this quantity of grain sent to Buffalo it embraces not only United States grown wheat, but 10,648,865 bushels of wheat from Fort William, and 542,000 bushels from Port Arthur.
This transportation question is not new' to the government or to this parliament. I myself had the honour of moving two or three resolutions asking that the government should deal -with it in a businesslike way, but I was always met with the answer that we were going to rely on our mixed system of transportation by lake by rail and by canal. We have the opinions of masters of transportation in this country as to how grain should'be carried from the west to the east. Sir Win. Van Home recently stated in the city of Toronto, that the long haul around the great lakes was dreaded because it was unprofitable, and that the bulk of the grain brought by that route was carried in the winter months and used by the millers in Ontario to keep their mills going during the cold season. Let us assume that the output of Manitoba and the North-west last year was 40,000,000 or 45,000,000 bushels of grain, and Sir Win. Van Horne's statement is demonstrated to be correct when we find that only 2,500,000 bushels of that was carried by rail around the shores of Lake Superior. Mr. Robert Meighen, president of the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, has given this opinion :
We want low-grade, double-track railways from the Georgian bay ports to Montreal. When this is accomplished you will freight wheat across the lake from Forf William to Georgian bay ports for one cent, and from there to Montreal for three and a half cents, or less, per bushel winter and summer. Do not forget that our canals are closed for six months of the year.
The opinion of those competent judges is that we have in Canada to-day a system for the carriage of grain which if we could only utilize it would bring the most successful results. The lake ports on the Georgian bay have a most decided advantage over Buffalo, from the fact that vessels plying to Midland and Parry Harbour can make three trips in the same time that they make only two trips to Buffalo.
Hear, hear.

That is an immense advantage in the fall of the year. There are vessels plying on the great lakes, and we have seen some of them in Midland, which carry 250,000 bushels of wheat, and assuming that the rate in the fall of the year is two cents per bushel-and I have often seen it higher-a vessel will make $5,000 more in freight because of the additional trip which it can make to a Georgian bay port than if she were plying to Buffalo. And yet we are told by gentlemen opposite that the experience of the United States i.s to be brushed aside and, that the lake route is not to be utilized, because forsooth the

Minister of the Interior quoted some figures here which were not substantiated by fact, and which are not figures that would be endorsed by men who know the business. Let me tell the House that the carrying trade which we have established on the Georgian bay is only to-day in its infancy. Last fall an arrangement was spoken of and was about to be put into force between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, which would have resulted in millions and millions of bushels of grain being carried from Midland to Peterborough by the Canadian Pacific Railway and thence east, and carried by the Grand Trunk Railway to Belleville, and (Prom that point to Montreal. That arrangement was a joint user of what is known as the Midland division of the Grand Trunk Railway by these two rival railroads. It has been argued in this House that there could not be a user of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway by other companies, and it might be said that there could not be a user of the Midland division by the Canadian Pacific Railway, but the answer to that is that this piece of road is only about 90 miles long, and because of its shortness the difficulties could be overcome.
How many miles ?
Between 90 and 100.
It is 100 miles.

, It is not quite 100 miles, and if the road were straightened as contemplated, the distance would be decreased by ten miles. But even suppose it is 100 miles, if that arrangement had been carried out immense quantities of grain would have been carried over the line. Any one who passes over that portion of the Grand Trunk will see proof that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway never intend to carry any grain by all-rail to the east, except, of course, the trifling quantity that might be taken out during the winter months. The Grand Trunk Railway are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on the Midland division to-day, with the object of carrying their grain from Port Arthur or Fort William to Midland and thence to the east. Every one in Midland knows that even after this proposition was launched last fall, the Grand Trunk Railway owned every available foot of water frontage in that town for a distance of over two miles, and it is an open secret that the Grand Trunk Railway intend to send their grain trade to that point. What we want in this Dominion is a first-class outlet for our grain from the west, not by rail throughout, but to the head of the waters of Lake Superior.
The province of Ontario lately had the honour of a visit from Premier Roblin of the province of Manitoba, and what did he say ? I take it that anything coming from that gentleman should carry considerable

weight and authority. Premier Roblin has everything to gain by pointing out fairly and honestly the necessities and requirements of the west; it is not to be expected that he would come down to the province of Ontario and make statements which would be inimical to the interests of the people of Manitoba and the North-west; and the whole tenor of the statements made was that any congestion of trade in the west happened between Winnipeg and the head of the lakes, and that the great and pressing necessity in the west to-day was for more railway equipment and an easier and better passage for grain to the head of the lakes.
It has been urged by the government that very prompt action should be taken on this question. I need not repeat what have been termed the hysterical remarks of the Premier as to the necessity of haste. Why, Sir, what do we see ? We see this government lying dormant, not moving its hand, for six years. What were they doing V Taking up the ends of the canal system which had been left as a legacy by the late government, and from time to time effecting improvements upon them. Beyond that this government has not lifted its hand. It could have gone to the Grand Trunk or to the Canada Atlantic Railway people, and, by perhaps offering a bonus for the carriage of grain when it reached a large amount, they might have diverted a large part of the grain trade now going to Buffalo, both that of Canada and that of the United States. But this government have stood still; they have done practically nothing for the last six years. And now at once we hear these hysterical screeches, without any surveys being made or any reports being had, to the effect that this country must be plunged into an expenditure ranging anywhere from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000 for the construction of this railway. And through what part of the country is it to run 1 There has not been laid on the Table of this House the report of a single engineer who has ever gone over that territory. We have heard reports from missionaries and from other gentlemen who have seen parts of that country; but in the prospectus issued by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company itself the following language is used with reference to this very country :
The unanimous report of all explorers who have travelled over the territory north of the Georgian bay and Lake Superior, is to the effect that it will not in the immediate future furnish business sufficient to support a railway, and it would not, therefore, be a business proposition to build one there, it was used as a link to reach the more fertile lands of Manitoba and the North-west ; the mileage through the unproductive section is estimated as 1,000.
There is the prospectus of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company condemning the very territory that is to be traversed by this railway. In the face of this fact, should not the government, before they plunge
the country into this enormous expenditure, do one of two things-either submit to parliament next session or in a subsequent session a full and complete survey of that country, or, as they are going to the country this fall, after passing this Bill, if they can pass it, go to the country, and we challenge them to do so, on this very question. Speaking for myself I have rather a hard constituency; but I tell the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches that as they are going to the country this fall, it would be more manly and more fair to the people of Canada, before they manacle them and tie them down with this immense debt around their necks, to give them a chance to say whether they will accept it or not of their own free will. But the government know that they would be hazarding too much on that throw of the dice; and therefore they propose to pass the Bill as it is, and then go to their party friends and say to them : What is the use of turning tis out ? The contract is executed, the bonds are signed; if the Conservative party come into power, they cannot upset what has been done. That is the position these hon. gentlemen are in.
With regard to the canal system of this country, on which we have spent an enormous sum of money, why do the government not insist on the people of this country recognizing that the future transportation trade of thie country should be done by the Georgian Bay and the connecting railways to the east ? They have certainly at all times led them to believe that our canal system was to be the solution of the transportation question, not only for the Dominion of Canada, but for a great portion of the western states. Already we have expended some $70,000,000 on that canal system, and I am gratified to be able to say that by the removal of the tolls this year, a greater quantity of grain has gone to the city of Kingston than in any previous year, and that a greater quantity has gone down the St. Lawrence system than ever before, and I think twice as much as went up to this time last year. 'So keen has the competition been that the fact is advertised that grain is being carried from the head of Lake Superior clear through to the port oif Montreal for four cents a bushel. That is cheap transportation. When hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches have been from time to time consulted by the representatives in this House as to what their stand was on the question of transportation, what has been their answer ? I am going to quote from the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) as reported in ' Hansard ' of 1901, at page 1,106. That hon. gentleman said :
It may be three or four or five years before we get into full swing, but there is no doubt, in my mind, that the improvements which are. in contemplation at Port Colborne, properly and efficiently carried out, and in the harbour of Montreal and the route perhaps below, will

make the St. Lawrence superior to any other route.
What have we done since that time 7 We have loaned to the harbour commissioners of Montreal vast sums, which have been expended on that harbour on the strength of the assurance of the government that the canal system would be perfected. On the strength of the expenditure of millions of dollars there, we have gone further. What have we done 7 You, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Archibald Campbell), I believe, are a member of a company which, with laudable energy and commendable enterprise, is seizing the occasion to construct elevators at Port Colborne. I congratulate you upon your energy, and I hope and trust that your best expectations will be realized. What is the calculation at present 7 We are unable to take past Port Colborne boats carrying over 70,000 bushels. We have already expended upwards of $3,000,000 at Port Colborne-for what purpose 7 To construct there a huge harbour, dredge it to a great depth, and construct great docks on which it is intended that capitalists shall build elevators. It is expected that vessels carrying 300,000 bushels of grain can land at the docks and deliver their grain to the elevators, where in turn it will be delivered to smaller boats, which will carry it through the canals and the St. Lawrence river to Montreal or Quebec. But these hon. gentlemen tell the enterprising vesselmen of this country that they are going to place before the public of Canada a transportation scheme that is to put all others into the background. They are going to raise in this country a spirit of disquiet and unrest among men who are proposing to go into the grain carrying business. Further on the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals said this :
We will see with Montreal properly equipped that there will he no reason in the world why shippers should not prefer the St. Lawrence to any other route.
Yesterday, in the course of the debate, some hon. gentleman quoted the Minister of Agriculture as having last year, in the debate on the motion of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. McLaren), in reference to transportation, practically made use of the very words of the then Minister of Railways and Canals, and endorsed in its entirety the canal system of Canada. But on the assurance thus given, these hon. gentlemen went through the country and defended the expenditure of these millions at Port Colborne and these hundreds of thousands on the St. Lawrence canal system. Let me read what the Postmaster General said at the city of Hamilton on the 26th of September last:
As you know, the task of providing a sufficient and adequate water route from the gulf of the St. Lawrence to the upper lakes is no easy one, but from the moment of our accession to office until this date, it has been continuously Mr. BENNETT.
prosecuted with all possible speed. When we shall have completed the improvements at Port Colborne next spring, we shall have made that port a safe harbour where grain can be received and shipped to our maritime ports.
Yet this hon. gentleman was forced to come to this parliament and say that all these predictions as to the carrying trade by the St. Lawrence canals and the mixed trade of the upper lakes by rail and water were things of the past.
During the course of this debate we have heard some very wonderful statements as to the cost of this railway. The last gentleman who resumed his seat (Mr. Hughes) said that the cost would be 15 cents per head during fourteen years for every person in the country, and had time only permitted, I have no doubt he would have been able to show that instead of our taxpayers having to pay anything, every one of them would receive a bonus from the construction of this road. We had first the statement of the Prime Minister that the cost would be $13,000,000. That statement nobody has since repeated. Nobody will do the right hon. gentleman the honour of repeating the statement made by him. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) would rather trust himself to the fickle member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) than to the First Minister. But those who have trusted the hon. member for North Norfolk in the past know what a broken reed he is for any one to lean upon.
What is to be the actual cost of the railway? We heard a few days ago the statement of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, and I have heard so many conflicting statements in this regard that I thought, in order to be up to the times, I would make an estimate myself. This is the estimate which I propose to submit to my electors when I shall next have the pleasure of meeting them. What will be the actual cost of this railway ? From Winnipeg to Moncton, 1,800 miles, at $40,000 per mile, (he cost will be $72,000,000. The interest during ten years at 3^ per cent will be $25,200,000. The difference between 3 and 3i per cent, which we will have to pay for 40 years, will be $12,640,000. The mountain section will cost for interest on the bonds during ten years, $7,200,000, making a total of $117,040,000. I may say, in passing, that the estimate of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals was. in round figures, about $120,000,000. When people contrast this estimate of the ex-minister with the figures of the hon. member for North Norfok, who makes the amount $70,000,000, they will ask why is there so much discrepancy ? And they will further ask : How is it possible that the First Minister came to make the statement that this road was only going to cost the people $13,000,000 7 The argument will be this, that the $13,000,000 will be the interest to be paid on a certain amount; and as the government do not ask

that the Grand Trunk Railway shall pay the interest for a certain number of years, and will make that company a present of a certain amount of interest, the right lion, gentleman estimates that at $13,000,000. And in arriving at this result, he takes good care to make the cost of the road a very trifling amount. But there is something beyond this cost of $117,000,000 to $120,000,-
000.	There is this fact, that there are certain endorsements to be made of the bonds Of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and people in the province of Ontario, particularly in the county of Simcoe, have an idea what tiie promises of the Grand Trunk Railway mean. The Grand Trunk Railway is a debtor to this country of millions unpaid. It is a debtor to the county of Simcoe of an amount which runs into several hundreds of thousands of dollars. That liability is hoary with age, no interest or principal having been paid upon it for the last forty years. Under this arrangement, we are going to guarantee millions, because on the prairie section we guarantee that we shall pay $9,000,000 interest if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway do not pay it. There is something more. Under the terms of this contract we are bound to purchase the Quebec bridge, which means an expenditure of from $4,000,000 to $5,000,000, and we have got to settle with the Trans-Canada people. I know not what that may amount to, but it is only a matter of common honesty and fairness that this government should deal liberally with the Trans-Canada, seeing that they were in the held before the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway was ever known. Then there is the question of betterments, which means that during the tenure of this lease the betterments are to be made by the Dominion, and upon these I understand they are to pay interest. Add these together. Had we accepted the original proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway, we would have granted them, in all probability, a subsidy on the line from North Bay to Winnipeg, and then guaranteed their bonds, as the government did the bonds of the Mackenzie and Mann system. This country would pay out in cold cash $i2,800,000 of subsidy, but we know where we stand. What is going to be the result of this scheme, as a business proposition, In other parts of the Dominion? First, we are to go down to the maritime provinces, where we have spent already $70,000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway, and we are to parallel that railway, and thus practically reduce it to a position of penury. We are going to put it to one side and make it useless. But there is not a word in this contract which will prevent the Grand Trunk Railway doing what they propose to do and what they are making arrangements at Midland to do, namely, to carry the grain from Midland on to Montreal and from Montreal to Portland. There is nothing in the contract to prevent their doing this. True
there is a clause providing that they shall endeavour, as far as possible, to have grain, routed to a Canadian port, but there .s nothing in the contract to compel them to do it. Worse than that. Does any man in his senses believe that when this Bill passes and the Grand Trunk Railway are entitled to receive aid they will not at that very moment commence the western soctiou ? Why, the rails will be laid, and I hope they will, from Wininpeg on towards Edmonton, and what will be the result ?	1 understand that in modern times rails have been laid at as high a rate aS' seven or eight miles a day, and even, as an bon. gentleman near me suggests, ten miles a day. So, next year we might expect to see a large portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific extended from Winnipeg westward. And when that system is extended it will garner its trade and carry it from the west to Winnipeg. Then it will be forced to do one of three things- take the traffic down under an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway to Fort William ; take it down under an arrangement with the Mackenzie and Mann road to Port Arthur, or make an arrangement with an American road and take it to Duluth. Or, either they or the government might build another line from Winnipeg to the head of Lake Superior. But there is nothing to compel them to abstain from building the road west, and, as the eastern section cannot be completed-nobody pretends it can be completed-within less than five or six years, the Grand Trunk Pacific will be free, if they please, to send the traffic through by way of Portland.
Now, this contract were it not such a serious matter, would be amusing. And in all this serious matter one wonders who has been the little joker in making up this contract. If ever there was contract abounding in silly propositions, this is that contract. We heard the Premier making the announcement with all his dramatic style that no senator or member of the House of Commons of Canada is to have a contract for the construction under this scheme. Whoever expected that any senator or member of this House would have a contract for construction work? Why it would be a violation of the Independence of Parliament Act. But there is nothing in the contract-and it would have been silly to insert it-to say that a senator or member of this House may not be a member of a construction company having a contract on this road. Need I refer to the clause respecting the purchase of supplies in Canada? It is not worth the paper it is written on, not worth the trouble it took to draft it. Then take the question of duties on imports. There is a feature of the contract which will bear heavily on our Canadian manufacturers, because it allows the importation of goods by this company free of duty so far as the government section is concerned.

I listened yesterday to the statement made by the leader of the opposition, and I must say that I believe that his policy will appeal more strongly to the people of the North-west and to the people of Canada generally than will the proposition that the government has laid before us. One great reason why it will command the favour of the people is that it does not plunge this country into such enormous expenditure. Why, Sir, whither are we drifting? To-day we have a public debt, in round numbers, of .$275,000,000. We are going to add to that at one sweep about $125,000,000, making a total debt of $400,000,000, or, as has been calculated, about $125 for every head of a family.
Our position is that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not give an outlet for several years to come for the increased product of the north-western country. Settlers are going in there in large numbers. Last year 100,000 people went in, and we hope and trust that this will not be the limit, but that the number will increase very much. Yet the government must admit, and every man must admit, that this eastern section will not be finished in less than from five to eight years, so that in that time there will only be the two present outlets to the head of the lakes, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern. The proposition of the leader of the opposition is to go to the very root of the difficulty. He proposes to expropriate either the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern line between Winnipeg and the head of the lakes. Or, if neither of these can be done, let the government take the matter boldly in hand and build a road and thus control the situation between these two points. Let this road be under government ownership, and let it be used in common by all companies that wish to use it. But I believe that every sane man will shudder at the prospect of duplicating the railway system around Lake Superior and will demand that there should be a common user of that road not only by the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific, but by the Mackenzie and Mann system as well. As to the route from Georgian Bay by the Canada Atlantic system, I have to say that that would not be as good a proposition as the acquisition of the Midland division of the Grand Trunk. If this government w7ere to acquire the road from Midland to Peterborough and to the Grand Trunk main line, not only would they put Peterborough in immediate touch with the waters of Georgian Bay and with the main line, but they would put the Canadian Pacific in immediate touch with Georgian Bay, and these two would have a quick route from the waters of Georgian Bay to their main lines running eastward.
One of the strongest reasons for condemning this proposition of the government is that it is brought before us in the dying hours of the session. On so great a ques-Mr. BENNETT.
tion, there should be no decision until the people have been consulted. It is utterly unfair to bind the country, in an important matter of this kind, without giving them a chance to speak. This government has announced to its friends in this House that they must be prepared to go before the people this fall. One of their supporters, inadvertently, no doubt, dropped a hint to-day to-the effect that this fall the members of this House may expect to face the electors. I say, in view of that fact, it would be more honest, it would be more fair, not only to this generation but to generations to come, that before thrusting upon them the heavy responsibilities of the expenditure involved by this scheme, for the government should have the courage of its convictions, if it has convictions, and meet the people face to face. Let them meet their political opponents face to face. Let them throw down the gage of battle, and let that gage be whether the country is or is not to be saddled with this great debt for. all time to come. Speaking as one on this side, I invite the hon. gentlemen to dissolve the House and go to the electors on this question, and, going to-the country on this question, we are prepared to abide by that result.
On motion of Mr. Macpherson the debate was adjourned.
On motion of the Minister of Finance (Hon. W. S. Fielding) the House adjourned at 12.15 a.m., Thursday.

Thursday, August 20, 1903.
The SPEAKER took the Ghair at Eleven o'clock.

2.	Has the government the said pension system under consideration, or has it finally adopted such a -system ?

4.	Was such scheme or any scheme of pensions submitted to the government for approval ?
5.	Has such scheme or any scheme been approved by the government ?
6.	Will gn Act be introduced this session to give effect to said system ?

The question of the pension

fund for the Intercolonial Railway officials was under consideration of the government in the time of the late Minister of Railways, but no action was taken thereon, and the matter has not since been dealt with.

speechtext:
Mr. CLARKE-by, Mr. Taylor-asked :
1.	What classes ot goods and merchandise, the product of the United States, are admitted into Japan on more favourable terms than goods and merchandise of the same classes, the product of Canada ?
2.	Have any steps been taken by the government of Canada, and if so, what steps, to secure for the products of Canada equally favourable
. treatment in the markets of Japan to that now enjoyed by the products of the United States ?

The Japanese tariff is what is called a double columued tariff ; one tariff being termed the General tariff and the other the Conventional tariff. Under the Conventional tariff lower rates are granted to such countries as have specific treaties with Japan. Canada is not one of these countries and consequently all the privileges of the Conventional tariff go to such countries as have treaties, but do not extend to Canada. The items in the tariff to which this applies are quite numerous, and I can only refer the bon. gentleman to the tariff itself which he can no doubt obtain on inquiry. One of the difficulties in the way of negotiating any treaty with Japan is, what is called, the favoured nation clause. We have had the matter under consideration, and negotiations of a confidential character have passed between the Canadian government and the government of Japan. The conditions require that if any treaty is made it shall contain what is called the favoured nation clause, which would oblige Japan to give to all other countries any privilege which she may grant to us and vice versa. As kon. gentlemen are aware, that creates some complications and interferes with our freedom, and for the present we have not been able to come to an understanding. The matter, however, is still under consideration.

Mr. CLARKE-by Mr. Taylor-asked :
1.	How many accidents, involving loss of human life took place on the railways of Canada during the fiscal year ending 30th June, 1903 ?
2.	How many human lives were lost in such
accidents, or as a result of such accidents_?_
3.	Has the government yet appointed any official whose duty it shall be to make a full and exhaustive inquiry and report, on oath, into the circumstances attendant upon, and the causes which may have contributed to all railway accidents which occur in Canada, including the system by which the traffic of the railway is operated ; the speed the trains were moving when the accidents occurred ; the condition of track and rolling stock ; the hours which the
train men, station agents, telegraph operator^ and other officials of the companies were on duty, in connection with the movement of trains to which accidents occurred ; the wages paid employees ; the sufficiency and qualification of the staff employed on the trains, and at the stations, telegraph offices, &c.

1.	As far as returns have been received, there were twenty-one accidents on railways in Canada involving loss of human life during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1903.
2.	Lives lost in such accidents or as a result of such accidents, sixty-three.
3.	No permanent appointment has been made.
