speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the House to go into Committee on a certain proposed resolution respecting the' construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, and the motion of Mr. Puttee in amendment thereto.

MACPHERSON (Burrard.) Mr. Speaker. I shall not attempt to follow the argument of my good friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) as I wish to view this question from a standpoint entirely different from his. He spoke for his own province of Ontario ; I shall speak from the standpoint of the province of British Columbia.
I would not have taken part in this debate were it not that the lion the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) made the statement in attempting to justify his action in resigning, that the province of British Columbia were not asking that a new transcontinental line be built and also that there is actually no hurry as far as the west is concerned that a new line be constructed. Either the hon. gentleman has a very short memory, or he could not have taken the Victoria board of trade seriously, when on the 8th day of October last year the following request was made to the hon. gentleman in his official capacity of Minister of Railways in the city of Victoria on the occasion of his visit to British Columbia last fall.
The board desire to place themselves on record as in favour of assistance being given to the C. N. R., so as to provide at as early a date as possible a second transcontinental line across British Columbia. They desire to point out that in view of the very rapid colonization of the prairie region, it necessarily calls for the provision of a new route whereby the grain there produced can readily reach the ocean.
Now, Sir,'there is only one of two deductions lo he drawn from the hon. minister's remarks-either his memory failed him, or he took the Victoria board of trade to be men who were not responsible for their actions, and then paid no heed to what



irresponsible people like the board of trade in one of our principal cities of tlie coast might say. From either deduction the hon. gentleman does r.ot emerge with any great degree of credit to himself. In speaking on this question, I wish to speak entirely from a British Columbia standpoint, and point out to tlie House the great good which lias accrued to British Columbia from the building of tlie Canadian Pacific Railway and building it through, possibly, the poorest part of our province. Striking into our province at the Kicking Horse pass, it finds its way through the Rocky Mountains following the valley of the Columbia river, then passing through Eagle pass it strikes the head waters of the Shuswap lake and strikes the South Thompson river valley, and following down through the valley of the Thompson until it strikes the Fraser at Lytton and from there down to the tidal waters of Bur-rard inlet. It found little to entice the imagination outside the grandeur of tlie mountain scenery And we all know that scenery will not fill the pockets nor will it suffice to stay the appetite. However, I wish to show the House what has been accomplished by the construction of the great Canadian Pacific Railway.
Prior to the advent of this railway, British Columbia was a country isolated from eastern Canada, having nothing in common other than devotion to tlie old flag and yielding homage to the same sovereign. It was a country which, from its isolation, had no natural national aspirations. But its people were men of courage and determination in that small and isolated community, and they recognized the great future of British Columbia if it could only get a railroad carried through connecting the eastern part of Canada with the west. The building of the Canadian Pacific Railway has made what was once the fishing hamlet of New Westminster a large, thriving commercial and populous city. It made a new province for Canada, one of tlie brightest gems in the Crown of confederation. It made tlie men who, while proud to say that they are British Columbians, still prouder to say they are Canadians. It made what was in 1883 a primeval forest into our present great city of Vancouver. It made it possible where 20 years ago stood only the Douglas fir and the British Columbia cedar, that a city of 35,000 people live to-day. Where not one dollar of customs revenue was collected 20 years ago, where the past year tlie sum of $1,388,709 was collected. It made possible, where banks were unknown, where to-day stand six of the leading banking institutions of Canada. Where bank clearances were unknown, to where during the first six months of the present year the clearances amounted to nearly 29 million dollars. It made the great seaport of Vancouver ai d created what last year was the fourth largest port for customs collections Mr. MACPHERSON.
in the Dominion Where ships were unknown practically 20 years ago, to-day in the harbour of Vancouver boats flying almost every maritime flag in tlie world can b * seen loading and unloading. It has made and created a new trade with the Orient. It made and created a new trade with Australia and New Zealand. It has made and created a new trade with the United States. It made and created a new province whose inhabitants are a happy and contented Canadian people. It made possible the development of a section of our mining country, which only goes to prove that we have greater than has been found. It made it possible for us to produce in the last 16 years 31.64(1203 ounces of silver, valued at $18,475,882 ; it made it possible for us to produce 280,200,S45 pounds of lead, valued at $10,447,510; it made it possible for us to produce 92.652.480 pounds of copper, valued at $12,333,200; or a total value of silver, lead and copper of $41,256,603. And prior to thenbuilding of the Canadian Pacific Railway this condition of things was unknown in British Columbia.
Now, Sir, when that which is only a small part of the many wonderful things I could name can be done in the green tree, what can be done in the dry ? If that can be accomplished by the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway through the lean section of our wonderful province, what can be accomplished by the building of another line of railroad through the fat section of our province ?
That the western part of our province- that part to be traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific-is a fat section, and that it is a section which is crying for a railroad, that the people who live there are clamouring for a railroad, that the mineral which is hid in our mountain ledges is awaiting the advent of this new road to enrich the coffers of the Canadian people. I will show and prove, and I think to the satisfaction of every lion, gentleman in the House. I will read to you a few extracts from the annual report of the Minister of Mines for the year ending 1902 ; and for fear that our good friend, the hon. gentleman who represents Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), should say that it is cooked, I will inform him and the House that the Minister of Mines is no less a personage than Edward Gaylor Prior, a Conservative of the Tory school, who was the recognized leader of the Conservative party for British Columbia in this House and a minister of the Crown. On page 45 of that report I find the following with reference to a part of the province which the Grand Trunk Pacific will traverse :
Two principal reasons seem to have deterred capitalists from investing here ; the first being the high price asked by prospectors for their holdings, and the other being the idea, widely prevalent, that the northern coast of British Columbia is locked up with ice and snow during the greater part of the year, with a conse-

quent very short working season. This is a very great mistake. With the exception of a very few days in mid-winter, there is not any portion of the Dominion, or northern and eastern United States, where a longer working season obtains. The snowfall at Port Simpson, which is the most northerly point on the coast of British Columbia, is much less than at Vancouver, the register for last winter, which' was an average one, being 14 inches. Mr. J. H. Rodgers, who spent the winter of 1901-02 at the Bonanza mine, on Observatory inlet, and who had a gang of miners working continuously, informs me that there was only one day from January 1st till July 23rd (the date on which I saw him) on which his men could not work out of doors, and that was on the occasion of a heavy snowstorm in March.
I may say that this is a report of Mr. John Flewin, a gentleman whom I know very well, who has been mining recorder in that part of the country for many years. The following refers to a part of the country which is exactly along the projected line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway :
Miners in the Kitamaat, Kitsilas and Telkwa camps are still hoping for the building of the Kitamaat-Hazel ton Railway, which will give access to the rich mineral belt of the coast and Kitsilas range of mountains, and the extensive agricultural, grazing and hydraulic areas of the Upper Skeena, the Bu'lkley and Omenica. At the present time, however, lack of transportation facilities is an effectual bar to extensive development work.
I know that country myself to a certain extent, and I know the great difficulties the miners are subjected to for want of railway communication. I will go a little further, and will read what is said about the Ptarmigan group of mines in the Kitsilas camp, which is a very rich camp :
The owners of this group, realizing that nothing more can be done to develop these claims without better transportation facilities, only employed a small gang of men during the season. Work was shut down in September, and a shipment of five tons of ore was made to test the property. The owners have applied for Crown grants for this group.
Statutory assessment work has also been performed on the Washington, Northland, Toulon, Bull-Dog, Montezeuma, Eureka,, flatzie, Golden Crown, Ruby, Granite, Golden King, Goldfinch, Golden Eagle, Golden Crown Extension, Strath-cona, Helma and Monte Cristo. I do not anticipate that any extensive development work will be prosecuted on any of these properties, some of which look exceedingly promising until railroad communication with the coast becomes an accomplished fact. The Skeena river is, at best, a very uncertain highway, owing to the sudden rise and fall of the waters ; added to which the freight rates are so high as to effectually deter any one from attempting to take in the supplies and machinery necessary for conducting mining operations on a large scale.
The following refers to the Telkwa river camp :-
In this camp only the usual assessment work has been performed on the Forrest Group, the Big Blue, Surprise and Constance mineral 2891
claims. The same difficulty-want of communication-is experienced here as at Kitsilas.
Perhaps the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) would tell these men that they have no need of a railroad. Well, I can fancy the hon. gentleman going to their camp and telling them so. If he did, I think he would find a more rapid means of transit out of that camp than he is accustomed to. I take it that these men know the value of railroad building to a mining country. Then, we travel further east to the districts of the Cariboo, Omenica, and Cassiar, about which the report says :
As for the transportation facilities for getting in supplies, &c., into the district, they have not materially changed since the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, except that the roads are much improved. Ashcroft is the point of departure from the railway. From here a stage runs twice a week in summer and once a week in winter to Barkerville-285 miles-while from the 150-Mile House stages go once a week to Quesnel Forks and Bullion, sixty miles, and to Harper's Camp, thirty-five miles. The roads are good, the numerous stopping houses are clean, comfortable and reasonable as to price, and the stages as comfortable as stages ever are. The stage company carries both mail and express, running ' specials ' whenever the traffic .iustifies it. The freight rate from Ashcroft to Barkerville is six cents per pound, and to Quesnel from four cents to five cents. These rates, of from $100 to $120 per ton, seem almost prohibitive as to heavy mine machinery, &e., anct often amount to more than the cost of the articles ; yet, while they are high, the rates are not extortionate, as at these figures there is nothing more in it than bare wages for the freighters, so that these amounts will not be materially reduced until a railway of some sort is built into the district.
In the Cariboo country alone, under these adverse conditions, placer gold to the value of $4,108,307 has been produced during the past three years. And when you consider, Mr. Speaker, that these districts are situated three and five hundred miles from other means of transportation, consequently these have to be packed on horses and mules' backs from the seaboard or from Ashcroft on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, you can readily see the immense difficulties surrounding the carrying out of the enterprise. The hon. gentleman says no need for haste. Let us look further afield, and see if we cannot find the Macedonian cry : Come over and help us.
This report, which I am about to read, is from the gold commissioner of the Omi-neca mining division, a gentleman who has been many years in that country and on whose statements we can thoroughly rely. By it you will see that there is no doubt as to the future of the country and the immediate requirement of another transcontinental line :
Now that two transcontinental railways are heading for the Pacific coast, both of which will tap the Omineca district, and one which, if the Pine or Peace river pass is chosen, will pass within a short distance of Manson creek,

which is at. present the centre of mining operations in this vicinity, the Omineca district is bound to spring into prominence, as once the great cost and difficulty of travel and transportation of supplies have been reduced, as they will be by railway communication, the hundred square miles of*country that at present are unknown and unprospected will be thrown open. A vast extent of country lying north of the Omineca river and west of the Findlay is known at the present time to contain gold in paying quantities if supplies could be got into that portion of the district, and it only requires improved means of transportation to convert this locality from an undeveloped wilderness, as the greater portion of it is to-day, into one of the richest and best mining districts in the province. A railway will place Manson, as regards transportation, in the same position as Revelstoke on the Canadian Pacific Railway Is at present. During this past season several parties of prospectors were in the district, hut on account, of shortage of supplies were unable to push their way any distance from Manson. Some, however, were so favourably impressed with what they saw of the country, that they have stored part of their outfit and intend returning next season.	'
As the transportation question is to-day the most important question before the people of Canada, every effort should be put forth to give additional transportation facilities between the great central wheat and cattle country of Canada and the Atlantic seaboard. But, in doing this I am afraid we are liable to lose sight of the fact that Canada has another gateway in the west which deserves consideration. Providence has been very kind to us in placing the great wheat and cattle country in the centre of this vast Dominion, and it is so situated that it is almost equally distant from each coast. In making this statement, I would endeavour to show that in the near future almost half the trade of the North-west Territories of Canada will, of necessity, go to the Pacific coast at Vancouver instead of coming eastward via Montreal or St. John. Vancouver, situated as she is on one of the greatest harbours of the world, is eminently fitted to be the great western gateway of Canada.
At the present time and for the past number of years a very large export grain trade is carried on between the western coast of the United State's and continental points, and at the cities of Tacoma, Portland and San Francisco, numbers of vessels are loaded each year with grain for Europe and Japan. This grain is transported by rail, in many cases, a distance of 900 miles from the coast, and what they are now doing on the western coast of the United States we can equally well do on the western coast of Canada, and in this way relieve the channels of transportation in eastern Canada at times when it is almost impossible to handle the trade.
The best transportation authorities have stated that freight can be carried four and a half miles by water for every one mile by land. On that basis I will endeavour to

show just how far east from the Pacific coast the dividing line can be. That is the line where the freight rate will divide so that part will go east and part will go west
At the present time the government of the United States have undertaken to build the great Panama canal, which they expect to have completed within eight years. When this canal is completed it will revolutionize the trade, not only to the United States, but to western Canada, and while we are in a position to-day to take advantage of the very long water route around Cape Horn, yet when this immense undertaking is completed, the distance from Liverpool to Vancouver will be reduced about 8.000 miles and the dangers of navigation will lie reduced at least 50 per cent. I have discussed this matter with ship captains, and they all agree that the dangers around Cape Horn are greater than during all the rest of the voyage. Sometimes, they say, it takes them as long as sixty days to make around Cape Horn.
Take a point 960 miles east of Vancouver which shall bring you in the vicinity of Moosejaw, and multiply that by four and a half, to bring it up to a water rate, it will amount to 4,320 miles, and from Vancouver to Liverpool via Panama canal, the distance is 8,520 miles. This gives the total distance from Moosejaw to Liverpool, via Vancouver and the Panama canal, of 12,840 miles. From said point in the North-west Territories to St. John by rail is 2,124 miles, which, when converted into water rate, will amount to 9.558 miles. From St. John to Liverpool, the distance is 2.700 miles, making a total distance of 12.879 miles, at an all water rate. This, I think will show that the time will come in the near future when the dividing line between the east and the west will be decided upon by transportation companies for their own advantage.
At the present time the greatest article for transportation from the Pacific coast to the North-west Territories is lumber. As an indication of what the trade of western Canada will be in the future, I will refer to the lumber trade as it is at present. The government of Canada are doing everything possible to encourage immigration to the North-west Territories. In doing so every effort should be put forth by the government of Canada, so that the people coming into Canada should not suffer by unnecessary hardships. It is stated that 100.000 settlers will settle in the North-west this year, and it is computed that an average* of four people comprise a family. Consequently there will be. at the very least, 25,000 families who will require houses to live in within a year. Each family will require a house say 17 x 21 feet, which, when subdivided, will make two bed rooms 8x9 feet and a kitchen 11 x 16 feet. This house if double boarded which is necessary in a cold climate, will require

5,000 feet of lumber, figuring tbe roof as lumber doubled. In addition to tbe bouse, they will require a small stable suitable for four horses, which will require 3,500 feet of lumber, making in all 8,500 feet for each family. We have estimated that there will be 25,000 families. Consequently they will require in all 212,500,000 feet of lumber. Tbe people now in the country will require for new buildings, railway purposes, elevators and the building of new towns, &c., as much more, making in all the enormous amount of 425,000,000 feet. This will load 53,125 cars at 8,000 feet per car or 5,312 trains of ten cars each, or 144 trains for each and every day in tbe year. And, as nearly all this lumber must come from British Columbia, and mostly from Vancouver for tbe present, you can instantly see that the Canadian Pacific Railway, as now constituted, have a big contract in hand to carry on this enormous business.	.
In dealing with this question of transportation so far, I have only taken up tbe part which refers to Canada and Europe.
I do not intend to omit probably the greater factor which we shall have in the near future in connection with the transportation question, and that is the trade which is increasing day by day between the Pacific coast and the orient, Australia, South Africa and India. This trade is increasing by leaps and bounds. I recollect very well when the first steamboats came into Vancouver with merchandise from the east. Their first trips were a little before my time, but I can remember when the old 4 Abyssinian ' and ' Parthian ' were objects of Interest to us, the first boats on the Pacific carrying merchandise from tbe orient to our ports. The cargoes were very small indeed. But tbe great Canadian Pacific went out for business with the orient, and they got it. And they have now five of the largest steamers of the Pacific carrying merchandise, and that trade is increasing as I say, by leaps and bounds. I would like the House to realize the immense latent possibilities in this trade. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, the half has not been told. And when the Grand Trunk Pacific with the knowledge and the capital they have, and having the desire and b)eing under the business necessity of developing traffic- when they take the field a business will be built up as compared with which that of the present will be nothing. I do not wish to be too extravagant in my estimate. But, Mr. Speaker, I can remember, in my short sixteen years of experience on tbe coast the immense development which has already taken place through the advent of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway has done immense things for our country; it has done the things that no other agency could ever be expected to accomplish. It went into the primeval forest and built the city of Vancouver. It has built opera houses, sugar refineries, and smelters. 1
Will any lion, gentleman tell me that I should support a government operated road in the face of the things I have seen and know ? I am as strong a believer in government control as any man in this House; I yield to no man in my desire to maintain intact the rights and interests of all the people. But I believe that under the contract now before us we have all the good features of government ownership and government control, without the incubus of government operation. If we were a people who would stand being policed like the people of Germany-and d do not want to make any reflection on that people, but it cannot be denied that we are more democratic than they are-we could operate state-owned roads. But until we come to understand that we must be governed by one man and rilled with the strong hand, we need never expect to have state-owned and state-operated railways in Canada. The theory of state-operated railroads is a beautiful thing, but it is idle to talk of it in the case of a people who have the sense of independence that inspires the people of this Dominion. I believe in state-governed railroads as this one, but I have got a little off the track-
You are on a good track anyway.

I was speaking of the trade that will be developed with China and Japan. It is estimated that there are 450,000,000 people living in those two countries. Up to three years ago they had not adopted western ideas, they had not begun to wear European clothing or eat such food as we eat. But Japan has taken the initiative. Japan, Mr. Speaker, is remarkable for its power of imitating other nations. But, up to this hour, Japan was simply an imitator. Nor do I wish to make any disparaging remarks about the Japanese. I do not like them as they appear in this country, it is quite true. But they are good enough people in Japan as the Chinese are good enough people in China. These people are all right in their place, but they do not make good Canadians. If the Japanese go on as they are now going it will not be many years before they will be able to take their stand with other nations of the world. They are rapidly adopting our ideas. They have begun to eat wheat flour and are putting up roller mills to grind wheat from this continent. They are already importing considerable quantities of American and Canadian flour. They are more anxious now to get the Canadian than the American article, for our good friend the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) has been over there and has shown them the excellent bread that can be made from Manitoba No. 1 hard. China is fast becoming Japanized, if you will allow me that expression. The Chinese people see that their Japanese neigh-1 hours are going ahead fast, and they are

following in their footsteps. While China may never use flour universally as a food, while there may be millions of people there who will never use it, owing to the fact that rice is so much cheaper, yet I believe that the better and wealthier classes in China and Japan will use flour. I think I am safe in saying that, within fifteen years-for we must remember that events move more rapidly than they used to do-150,000,000 millions in the orient will be eating flour. It is easy to see what that would mean for Canada. Mr. Hill, possibly one of the best railroad men we have in America says that the market for the North-western part of America is China and Japan, and that the demand there will keep wheat up to its normal price.
In addition to this, the trade between Canada and Australia, and also the trade between Canada and South America are increasing very rapidly. I have endeavoured to suggest that fair opportunities should be afforded for the trade 1 have just mentioned. For, no matter what our sentiments may be as between east and west, the trade of the country will go through its natural channels.
* But, unless you improve and develop these natural channels, the trade of the country will dwindle. For many years the trade of British Columbia went through American ports. It was not until the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway were we able to deal direct with the people in the orient.
We are in Canada peculiarly situated as it is only in Canada that any vast amount of unoccupied arable land exists. Now the great migrations of population have always been for the most part along the parallels of latitude of the north temperate zone. From prehistoric times the population of the far east has widened out in every widening circle of thousands of years. Vast numbers of people have moved towards the setting sun. At last the course of that movement to the western boundary of the old world was reached and then population moved across the ocean and during the nineteenth century Europe sent to the shores of the United States eighteen million souls, attracted altogether I may say by the wonderful free public lands offered by the American people. I take it, and I may diverge a little here that no country can be a great manufacturing country until its arable lands are exhausted. We know what immense strides the American people have made during the last one hundred years on account of the wonderful arable lands of that country. They have reached and have reached some time ago the point of exhaustion pf these lands, but we, in Canada, are in the same position as the people of the United States were seventy-five years ago. The western half of Canada equals in area England, Ireland, Scotland, Denmark, Switzerland, Germany and most of European Russia, and the production of the Canadian soil will surpass that of the corres-Mr MACPHERSON.
ponding European area. There are in these sections of Canada fully two millions of acres of land fit for production and there are in the corresponding area of Europe to which I have referred two hundred and fifteen million souls. I have not mentioned in this connection the wonderful productiveness of British Columbia which has such great food resources in her wrnters. Salmon abound in almost incredible numbers, while halibut and cod are even more plentiful. I can tell you that the British Columbia halibut banks equal any in the world and when I say that a boat can go out from the shores of Vancouver and come back in four days with a full cargo of halibut, it is almost beyond belief.
We cannot tell fish stories like that in the east.

Perhaps we cannot tell fish stories. But in the waters of British Columbia there are no suckers.
British Columbia has been for years a prospecting ground for gold and it is known that in this metal that province is wonderfully rich, then there are copper, coal and iron. It is well known that the iron mines, especially in southern British Columbia, are rich and they are placed as if nature had intended them to be for the use of man, for there are rich coal fields close at hand. I have spoken already of the vast wealth of British Columbia in agriculture, fish and minerals, and I should add that our country is particularly rich in its supply of timber, of cedar and Douglas fir. The forests of British Columbia contain over two hundred billions feet of uncut fir and cedar. It has been said that British Columbia seems destined to become the shipyard for the supply of all nations.
Now, I could go on, but I have promised the House that I will not take up its time, i wall only say in conclusion that the man who says we are not, in British Columbia, clamouring for another transcontinental line does not understand the feeling of the people of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, I was informed this morning that I would follow the hon. member for Bur-vard (Mr. Macpherson). I have listened closely to the hon. member and as far as I can see, he has made very few points either for or against this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. It seems to me that his principal arguments and language have been in favour of Vancouver or Burrard's Inlet, and it seems that the only important thing, according to the gentlemen sitting around him in that section, are suckers. Well, Mr. Mc-Craney, who ought to know all about that country, who has been there a number of years, writes me that it is not suckers but grafters, and that there are so many of them that they are really an injury and a curse to the country. Now, whatever a grafter is, I do not know. It may be a fish for all

I know, but I have to reply and speak, 1 believe, in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. But an amendment has been moved in the House, and I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that I wilbbe able to speak on that amendment, which refers to government ownership of railways. It was on this question that the election in West Elgin hinged; if I had not been an advocate of government ownership of railroads and of no bonuses to railroads unless the railroads or whoever got the bonuses were obliged to give back to the government something for the money paid to them, X do not believe that I would be here in this House, and 1 am sure that the sentiment has grown all over this vast country in favour of government ownership, and I notice that one party in this House only a few days ago pledged themselves to, or at least, enunciated their policy as government ownership. I suppose owing to the unique position I occupy in this House, my speech will not commend itself perhaps to any gentleman on this side or on that side of the House, but at tlie same time I wish to say that I do not think it would be right. I do not think it is right, for any man in this House to discuss any question in any way other than on its merits. We have heard vituperation, we have heard some of the vilest language, language such as would not be used in a common village debate, and the desk thumping and the rattling was astonishing to me when any one would make a point which members thought was for or against, them.
I do .not suppose there will be any deskthumping on either side when I have made a point. I do hope there will be no deskthumping. Those who disagree with me have a perfect right to do so, and those who agree with me have a perfect right to do so. but I do not think any gentleman has a right to abuse me because I do not 1 clong to this or that party. We are all supposed to be here to do what is best in the interests of our country, that is what we advocate on the hustings and what we talk to our constituents-country before party. Yet, in nine cases out of ten the party elects the member and expects him to be there too. Now, Sir, I am tool to no one, and I do not expect any one to be a tool to me.
Mr. Speaker. I am sure that this country and this House, too, is getting tired of this debate. We have not had a new idea advanced for the last three or four days, and it is about time that some member started out on a fresh route. Well, we have to confine ourselves to the subject.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

I have no objection to the iion. gentleman saying hear hear,- but I do not want them to thump the desk. Now. Sir, I would not speak on this question, because, as I said before, very little has been said on the question proper, but I wish to put myself on record as being strongly in favour of government ownership. This plan that the government have introduced may be better than my plan, but at the same time, I hold these convictions and I dare to express them.
Now, Sir, we are all aware that railroads are a great blessing wherever they .are planted. We know that if we were to be deprived of railroads we would go back almost into an uncivilized condition. Therefore, we must have them, and the country must be developed. Consequently, where-ever there are no railroads it is the duty of the government to see that they are built, and that the country is opened up. I will not say now whether it is proper for the government to push forward this scheme at this particular time, not knowing anything about those vast regions that we have heard of ; although some gentlemen undertake to tell us how many trees, how many streams, how many mountains there are in that stretch of country 3,000 miles long. I have not seen one person yet that has ever been over tlie line. But we believe that sometime that country will be developed, and that there is room enough in the region to be traversed by this railroad to plant 10,000,000 of people, on a strip 20 miles wide each side of the road. The people of Europe are waiting to go in there, and we are told here that we cannot wait any longer for this road. The people of Europe are waiting for us to bring them out here and plant them on these fertile plains of the Northwest. But whether this is the proper time to build the road in the way proposed, is another question, and I am not now discussing whether the proposition is right or wrong, though those who have introduced it and have thoroughly studied it, ought to know. But speaking of the millions coming out to this country, or waiting to come, why, Sir, if the children of Israel, when the [ Exodus took place, and who had so much difficulty in crossing the Red sea, had known about this glorious heritage that we have on this continent, they would never have settled in Palestine, which is about the poorest land under Heaven, but they would have come out to this country, and we would now have Jews for our neighbours. Why, the people generally don't know what a giorious heritags we have here. If that land is as good as it is reported to be, then we shall want more than one road, and we shall want them built by the government. I do not mean to say that the operation of the road should be carried on by the government, because we do not want to see every man who works on that road a mere government hack, who is put there to vote as the government tells him to vote. I am strongly opposed to that. The exMinister of Railways said that the Intercolonial should not be placed under a commission. I think that every government railway should be operated by a -commission. We do not want to see every man who works for the government obliged to vote

just as the Minister of Railways tells him to.	.
Now, speaking of railroads and their advantages, the first time I had the pleasure of travelling through the North-west, there were no railways built, and to get there I had to go through American territory. 1 struck our boundary at Emerson. Winnipeg was not very large then, it was called old Fort Garry, a little while before, and it would be old Fort Garry yet if the Canadian Pacific- Railway had not been built. So you see the great good that has been done by that railroad in building up the North-west. That country has been called the great lone land, and if we had not had railroads built through it, it would be a great lone land yet, whereas it is now blossoming like the rose, with thousands of miles of railroad running in every direction.
The Canadian Pacific Railway was a very costly affair for Canada when it was built. I do not say that the promoters of that road did not act to the best of their light, according to the best knowledge they had, lint they made a great mistake. We are all apt to make mistakes, but when they recognized a syndicate of men and granted them large bonuses of money, and lands, and railroads already constructed, amounting altogether, I think, to some $145,000,000, they created an enormous corporation, and I think they then made a mistake. They had the courage to secure the building of tlie road by a company, but they should have had courage enough to bond that road, and gone to England and borrowed the money on their own responsibility, and then tlie people would have owned the road. As it was they became responsible for the bonds. Then we would have owned that road ourselves, and every acre of that land, and a great portion of that country would not now be under the control of a corporation. But you have lost that opportunity, and now that another opportunity presents itself equally favourable, I hope the government will not let it pass. You have had one unfortunate experience of that kind, and don't have another. I say that $145,000,000 of money would have built that road, every inch of it ; it did not cost $50,000 a mile ; then you would not have a wealthy syndicate composed of Lord somebodies, and of great noblemen to look up to, but you would have had instead a railroad owned by yourselves. I have great sympathy with the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) who moved that amendment yesterday, and talked so logically and with so much good sense.
I am sure other lion, gentlemen who have spoken on this question will excuse me when I say that it was the best speech yet made in this House since this debate began.
This proposed Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will not pass through my constituency, it will not come within several hundred miles of it. At the same time, the people of my constituency are broad minded, and Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
are willing to help their neighbours to develop this country. They want to see this country something more than a mere fringe along the American border, but I do not think they will complain if this road is built and owned by the people themselves. X do not think they are anxious to see another great syndicate formed, having such vast power in this country. By this tiro-position you are creating an incubus which you propose to place upon your own necks, something that will be a damage to the public interest. Why, Sir, with these two large corporations, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Company, to say nothing of this new Grand Trunk Pacific Company, if they were to unite their forces at the next election they could elect nearly every man they wished. They have influence and power enough in almost every constituency to elect nearly every man who comes to this House, and they will elect such men as will serve their purpose. They are not Grits or Tories, they are looking after their own interests. The other day a member of this House said to me, I am just between the devil and the deep sea, or words to that effect. He said, ' There are a thousand Grand Trunk votes in my constituency, and if I vote against that measure the Grand Trunk Company will use all its influence against me ; and if I do not vote against it, then the farmers will all vote against me.'
It was something like the juror who was sitting on the trial of the seven bishops in the reign of James II. This juror who was a brewer was much concerned and he said : Oh Lord, I am ruined anyhow ; if I give a verdict against the bishops I will never brew any more beer for the people, and if I do not, I will never brew any more beer for tlie king. That poor brewer was in jeopardy, and that is just the way with the members of this House who are under the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway the Grand Trunk Railway and all tlie other railways. Now, Sir, we want to get out from that position. So far as I am concerned I don't care for any of these corporations. I will do my duty. This country is not so old that we cannot retrace our steps and start on the right track. We Started wrong s me years ago ; let us start right now, and we have excellent advice how to do it. The member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) took strong ground against government ownership ; the member for Hants (Mr. Russell) followed him in the same strain, and tlie Minister of Justice supported these two gentlemen. But unfortunately for tlie Minister of Justice lie brought some evidence in which altogether he did not like. He supported his case against government ownership by quotations from Sir John A. Macdonald, lint I do not think he would swear on John A. Macdonald for every thing ; however he used him because it suited his purpose. John A.

Macdonald was bound hand and foot to the Canadian Pacific Railway syndicate and could not help himself-it is quite possible that the gentlemen on the treasury benches are in the same fix to-day with other railway corporations. Now, Sir, I do not wish to take up the time of the House.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Go on.

This is about the time that I usually conclude my speech, but if the House is determined to say ' go on ' I will have to be polite. You would think that the member for Westmoreland lived in the western part of Canada and knew nothing about the Intercolonial Railway. He does not seem to know that it cost $70,000,000 and that it is doing excellent service in its own way. He forgets that the [DOT]country through which, it runs is unsettled and that it is almost impossible to make the Intercolonial Railway pay commercially. Why, it was never intended to pay commercially. It was built as a military road, and we all remember that the Trent affair helped to bring about its construction. However, it has connected the colonies and we could not get along without the Intercolonial. It is one of the grandest things in Canada although it does cost something. I would like to see more of it. If the Intercolonial railway does not pay the Dominion in cash, it pays the people of the maritime provinces, and generally speaking it pays us all to have it.
It has been argued by gentlemen on the treasury benches that the government could not operate a railway in the public interest. I am sorry the Postmaster General is not present, because I would like to tell him that he his discharging a public duty very well, and we hear no complaints. Hundreds of thousands of dollars go through his hands and millions of people are reached, and reached pretty accurately through the instrumentality of the post office, if the government can run the post office right, what is the matter with them running the railways right. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) said it would take $50,000 a year to pay a magnate to look after a government railway. Well, Sir, there is no danger of him getting the j b. If it takes $50,000 a year to pay a railway manager, I do not wonder that the shareholders get no dividend. I think $50,000 a year is more than one man can earn. I think there is a mistake in that regard, but the hon. gentleman may know that they get $50,000, I do not. It is admitted that the Postmaster General runs the post office, or at least it is run to the best of the Postmaster General's ability through his deputy. We have other institutions run by the government which I suppose you gentlemen have no experience of and I hope you never will ; I mean the penitentiaries. I understand that the penitentiaries are run well enough. Then there are the asylums and other institutions managed by the government all over the country, and there is no reason why the railroads should not be managed by the government. Of course it will take some time to get into it; some time to get the right men, but we have boys growing up in Canada who will be quite competent to run our railroads and we need not go to the United States or any where else for them. Now, as to the bonding privilege, I felt plea'sed the other day to hear the Prime Minister with all his eloquence expound the idea that we should be. independent of the Americans. But the hon. gentleman has the Intercolonial Railway over which we can bring all the stuff" we want in bond. I do not think we need fear any threats about the bonding privileges. I hate to be threatened ; I am just as sensitive as the Prime Minister as to that, but this threatening does not amount to much, and so long as there are such presidents as Roosevelt there is no danger of any injustice being done to us Canadians. But, Sir, if we should happen to get a crank as president as we had some years ago. then we might perhaps be in jeopardy. I do not know that I need mention his name for you gentlemen are well enough posted to know who I mean. If we are in jeopardy from that cause we cannot get straight to the ocean simply because the land that our forefathers fought for, was given away by a certain Lord Ashburton, and consequently we are hemmed in and cannot get in a straight line to our ocean ports.
I remember reading some time ago of a legislator in the United States who was very anxious to do some great good for Canada. So he cudgelled his brains and got up a resolution to have .the Senate of the United States and the President and the whole machinery put into operation in order to buy Canada from Great Britain and hand it over to the United States. I believe there was one fool enough in the world to attempt to do that. I am not so big a fool as that; I will not go so far; but if out government were to appeal to the American government and tell them that there is a piece of land down there lying near our orchard which once belonged to us, and that we are willing to pay a fair price for it, I think the people living in that part of the state of Maine would be glad to come under the old flag which has waved a thousand years, and which represents more civil and religius liberty than any other flag in the world. I think we might buy that part of the state of Maine, and then we would have a straight road to St John. I think it would be just as rational for us to propose to do that as for the United States legislator to propose that the United States should buy up Canada.
While we have the Intercolonial, there is no difficulty about getting to the sea; but you profile will not wait long enough to get there; you want to hurry to New York or Boston, because it will save you a few hours'

time. I think we ought to patronize our own ports, and carry as much of our produce as possible over the Intercolonial. I got a copy of the Intercolonial Railway tim '-table this morning, and I see that six trains run a day on that railway, and many others could be run. We are told by members of tips House that it Is one of the best roads in America, with the easiest grades, and that although it Is a little longer, it makes as good time to the seaboard as other roads. If that is so, the question of the bonding privilege is settled. We can ship our own products over our own road through our own territory. So that I do not think we have anything to complain of so far as independence of the bonding privilege is concerned. But, as has been well argued here, the Americans themselves ai-e not anxious to abrogate tiie bonding privilege, because they make a profit out of it; and the American people are not willing to give up anything that they make money out of-my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) knows that.
Now, Sir, we had a discussion here the other day On the trwo-cent-a-mile rate. Railways should be compelled to carry passengers for two cents a mile That would be easily accomplished if the government owned the railways. There would not be any begging of the railway magnates to do justice to the people of this country, because the government would then see that the people got justice. The railways to-day are masters of the situation, and their mandate has to be obeyed. I have had opportunities of knowing that. Some years ago the people in my section applied to this House for a charter to build a railroad through the southern counties of Ontario ; they came here year after year, but they met with the direst opposition from the railway companies and the other parties interested. But finally they obtained a charter to build the road, and they built it. The Canada Southern owned it for a time, but finally leased it, I am told, to the Michigan Central for 999 years. So we are sure whose hands we are in during our time. There are managers and superintendents of railroads who are very courteous and try to accommodate the people, and to oblige them; but at other times they are not just so obliging. Some members of this House wept scalding tears and showed a great deal of sympathy for the ex-Mlnister of Railways and Canals because he left the cabinet. Well, Sir, I did not weep any tears, simply because I found that that hon. gentleman, while he was the Minister of Railways and Canals, was the guardian angel of the railways; and whenever the farmers of this country asked for justice from the railways, that lion, gentleman stood by them as if he owned them, and he was master of the situation. So I did not shed any tears. A town in my constituency, a growing and thriving place called Dutton, near the cen-

tre of the thriving township of Dunwich, has but one railroad crossing in the town. The people of that place appealed to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to have another road built some sixty rods from the first one, so that the farmers might ship their cattle, draw their grain to the mill, and do other business. They sent maps and plans and letters, showing the necessity for the change. There are two railway tracks there parallel and close to each other, and when I tell you that very often a train goes thundering along one track at the rate of a mile a minute while cars are standing on the other, you will realize why the people there wanted another crossing. Their request was so reasonable that I thought no Committee of the Privy Council would refuse to grant it.
I appeared before the Committee of the Privy Council and appealed to them on the subject, but my appeal had no effect whatever. The present crossing is a very dangerous one, a number of people having been killed there. The government sent their engineer, and the railway company sent its engineer, to make an examination, and I went and met them. The councils of the township and town both petitioned for another crossing; but they did not get it, and have not got it yet.
The other day I brought up the question of protecting farmers and drovers in connection with the shipment of cattle, and stated that some of tne wealthiest and best men in our part of the country had been killed; and when I asked the late Minister of Railways and Canals if he could not put something in the Railway Commission Bill to protect the farmers, he just laughed at me. Well, I think the men who pay a heavy price for shipping their cattle on the railroad ought to be protected against negligence or carelessness. But the minister ignored my request altogether. If we had government ownership, do you not think something would be done to remedy the grievances of these peopl; ? Only last session I asked the Minister of Railways and Canals to compel the railway companies to make the farm gates in such a way that a small boy could go down through the farm and bring the cattle' across from the other side of the track. He said he could not do it now because a great many of them, instead of swinging on hinges, were rolling along on slides and often in snow three or four feet deep, so that the children could not open them. I asked him to provide that railway companies would have to make these gates swing on hinges. And the large member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser) came to his rescue, and of course our request was not granted. We know that in everything the farmers have applied for, they have been snubbed. We know how long the cattle-guard question was discussed in this House, session after session, and how long the farmers

have been trying to have the railway companies obliged to pay them for their injured and killed cattle. But the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals would never yield an inch until forced to do so by members of his own party. Even on the question of drainage across railway tracks, he set a determined front against the railways being obliged to contribute to the expense, but I am pleased to see that in the new act this obligation is imposed on the railway companies, and the ex-minister was the only one who voted against the amendment to this effect. I am therefore not going to shed any tears because the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals is out of the cabinet.
I had no intention of making these references to the ex-minister, but it becomes my duty to do so as advocating the government ownership of railways.
I am strongly in favour of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), but I am afraid that the people are not far enough advanced to adopt it. You cannot get the people advanced in a very short time. The hon. member for Winnipeg is many years ahead of his time; and in that respect perhaps he resembles the bon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), who has been advocating the same thing for years, and whose voice no doubt will be heard on this Bill before the debate is closed.
I wish to make an appeal to this House on behalf of the farmers. We have been here since the middle of March and have had to neglect our harvest. It seems to me that this House ought to meet in January.
I moved last year an amendment to a resolution, and by my amendment I asked that the House should meet in the middle of January, but it was laughed out of court. But just as soon as we have a majority of farmers in this House, we will meet the first week in January and will quit for harvest. If the farmers were represented here in proportion to their wealth and numbers, they would run this House to suit the greatest industry in this country, the agricultural interest, but they unfortunately allow the wire-pullers to run this country. No doubt some of the men here are earnest, hard workers, regular in attendance, and anxious to get business done, but there are a great many others who would give Rudyard Kipling plenty of opportunity for the exercise of his satire. We know what Kipling wrote about the English dudes, who neglect their business, squander their opportunities and waste their time. He said that they were ' flannelled fools at the wicket and muddled oafs at the goal.' If he were to see how half the members of this House fill in their time-one hour in the chamber and then dawdling around the lobbies, he would hit them off pretty sarcastically. I say this in all kindness, because I do not wish to hurt anybody's feelings, but we should do something to get on with business and go out
and help the country. Our farmers are paying $2 per day for harvest hands, and half the members of this House are able-bodied men who would be williug to take a job in the harvest field. They would' be better employed in that work than dawdling around here, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will use your influence to have the work of the session forwarded and to induce the government to take up the policy of government ownership of railways as soon as possible.

I desire, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the hon. member for West Elgin, who has just spoken, upon the arguments he used in favour of government ownership of railways. He arrives at the_ conclusion that because the government can run penitentiaries and lunatic asylums it can run railways. That seems to have been one of the leading arguments in support of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee).
Before going into the details of the proposition before the House, I desire to offer my sincere congratulations to the government for having grappled with this railway problem in a strong and fearless manner-in such a way as not only to do justice to the west and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but also to the maritime provinces which have been crying out so long for better communication with the rest of the Dominion. Some people are surprised that the maritime provinces should have put up the fight they have in order to have this railway built into those provinces. But if those people lived in the provinces down by the sea, if they knew the difficulties under which we have laboured since we came into confederation, they would find no cause to wonder that our constant endeavours have been to bring ourselves in as close communication as possible with the central provinces. Such a policy appeals to our hearty support because we recognize the position in which we have been placed by confederation. It is to be regretted that we could not have this railway problem discussed without bringing in extraneous matter, but the hon. gentleman, who has left the cabinet and who held the portfolio of Railways and Canals during seven years, took upon himself to bring into the discussion matters which had nothing whatever to do \vith the problem before the country : and while I have been, and I am still, a personal friend of the hon. gentleman, I must say that I do not think it was to his credit, when he discussed this question, which should be discussed on a high plane, to have brought in the name of Senator Cox. What has Senator Cox to do with the railway problem ? As a matter of fact, he only consented to become an associate wdth the' Grand Trunk Railway in this matter

The government of that day gave to the promoters of that railway completed railway to the value of $30,000,000, they gave cash subsidy to the value of $25,000,000, they gave to the company 25,000,000 acres of selected lands in Manitoba and the Northwest. Of course, it is difficult to estimate the exact value of those lands, but when asking for a loan from the government in 1884, 1 Mr. Stephen, now Lord Mount Stephen, said the lands which up to that time had been sold, had produced on an average $2.36 per acre. They were given, for instance, the privilege of importing their rails and other supplies for that railway free of duty. That proposition is as follows :
The government pays interest for seven years and guarantees the interest for a further period of forty-three years at three per cent on bonds of mountain section up to three-quarters of the cost but the total amount not to exceed $30,000 per mile. The old Grand Trunk Railway guarantees the balance of cost for construction; the government will take a first mortgage on the road and on the rolling stock. The old Grand Trunk Railway with its $150,000,000 of assets in order not to suffer loss must protect the government. It has been shown by actuarial calculation that the total amount of money for the payment by the government of seven years interest could be provided by the present sum of $2,334,575.90.
On the prairie section the government guarantees interest at three per cent for fifty years on three-quarters of the cost of the road, the total amount not to exceed $13,000 per mile. The eastern section from Winnipeg to Moncton is to be built and owned by the government as the neck of the great western bottle. This is to be a common highway for all railways, the government reserving right of way for the traffic of the Intercolonial Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific to be given a lease of this line for a period of fifty years and to pay the government three per cent upon its total outlay after seven years. The government therefore borrows the money, pays interest for seven years, and after that interest will be paid by the Grand Trunk Pacific for a period of forty-three years, when the road improved and developed as it must be will revert to the government. The amount required to pay the total interest for the seven years is computed by actuarial calculation to be $8,853,504.
The total amount, therefore, required at the present time to pay all the interest as above for seven years on the mountain section as well as on the eastern section amounts to $11,188,079.90.
