According to this despatch, Mr. Blair stated in the committee that he did not object to the connection, but that there should be provision made to reach St. John so that there should be a nearer Canadian port to which to bring that traffic from the west. At a later date in the Railway Committee when the hon. member for Sunbury and Queen's (Mr. Wilmot) moved that the city of St. John be substituted for the city of Moncton as the Atlantic terminus of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, the hon. Mr. Blair voted at that time in favour of the terminus of the railway being at St. John. Now, I come to. the St. John ' Sun.' a leading Conservative paper. In an editorial on May 8th, it says :

we going to compel the maritime people to travel over a road 35 per cent longer than another simply because it happens to have been built in the wrong place some thirty-five years ago ? From Moncton to St. John, the distance is 90 miles. From Moncton to Montreal via the Canadian Pacific Railway the distance is 512 miles, and by the Grand Trunk Railway and Intercolonial Railway, 537 miles. So that the only difference between via the Intercolonial Railway and Grand Trunk Railway to Montreal and via the Intercolonial Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway to Montreal is 25 miles. I know that these figures are wearisome, and I shall not quote any more, but I only want to show that we are building a line which will bring a maritime province winter port 205 miles nearer western Canada, over Canadian territory, than any road we have at present.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, was somewhat bothered over this Quebec to Moncton proposition. I suspect that that was the cause of his delay in addressing this House. He was between the devil and the deep sea, and the deep sea, I may say, is at Halifax. Finally he concluded that if a road is to be built at all from Levis to Moncton, it should be built by the government, and owned and operated by the government as part of the Intercolonial Railway. Before this proposition was submitted by the leader of the opposition, the building of any line at all from Quebec to Monc-tori had been condemned, in all the moods and tenses, by all the hon. gentlemen opposite, more particularly by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), and the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart). The hon member for South Lanark said :
We have accumulated deficits on the Intercolonial Railway during a number of years at the rate of $1,500,000, if what should be charged for revenue were charged to revenue and not to capital account. Now you want to make it so that the people will have to pay increased deficits on the Intercolonial Railway. A madder scheme never entered into the mind of man. It is a useless destruction of property already owned by the government.
Now. however, this hon. gentleman has to eat humble pie and follow his leader who wants us to build a road to Moncton as a government road, and operate it as part of the Intercolonial Railway. By the proposition before the House, the government propose to build the line to Moncton and lease it to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, who will pay 3 per cent on the cost of its construction, and who will bring over it the transcontinental freight of the country-freight from all the northern part of Quebec and Ontario, not to speak of the products of the west. This scheme the hon. member for Lanark described as a mad one. But if it be an insane project, what will he have to say of the project of his leader ?

The ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) said that there would be no local business for the road in connection with any other road. I may say that our proposition is to make this road part of a transcontinental line, and to give running powers over it to the Intercolonial Railway. I would like to know what more benefit the leader of the opposition could get from a road which would be operated by the government ? We propose to build the road as a part of a transcontinental scheme. We propose to bring more business to the Intercolonial Railway at Moncton to be carried by the Intercolonial from Moncton to Halifax. But the scheme submitted by the leader of the opposition would bring in no transcontinental traffic and would have no connection anywhere.
What have we to-day ? We have a transcontinental railway provided for. In the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway it is provided that all freight originating upon any part of this line in Canada or its branches, shall be carried to Canadian ports, unless otherwise routed. What does that mean ? The reply was made that the Grand Trunk Railway would give better rates to Portland, and that people would route their freight that way. But the government forced the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to enter into an agreement not only to carry the unrouted freight, but all freight to Canadian ports at the same price as to American parts. Have we no Canadianism in this country ? Are the farmers of the North-west devoid of patriotism ? Have the people no national feeling ? Is it to be supposed that when they can ship their goods as cheaply by Canadian as by American ports, they will send them to the latter ? I refuse to believe that there is any such lack of national spirit in this country. But the contract calls for more than that. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the Grand Trunk Railway will arrange with a steamship line to carry freight cheaper from .Portland to Liverpool than from a Canadian port. But here again they are met by a clause which says that not only shall the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway carry Canadian produce to Canadian ports as cheaply as to American ports, but to the point of destination as cheaply. So that there will be no reason whatever for a Canadian whose soul is as big as a bean to send his products to Liverpool by an American rather than by a Canadian port.
We come to the question, what does this road mean to the Intercolonial Railway ? The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) says it means dismantling the Intercolonial Railway. But before passing to that, let me refer once more to tlie proposition of the leader of the opposition to build this road from Levis to Moncton to be operated as a government road. Let us see what this would mean according to the figures we have before up. Let us take the

Intercolonial as an example. The cost of construction of this road was $70,000,000. Interest at three per cent would be $2,100,000 a year. The average yearly deficit since the opening of the road has been $200,000. The cost of the new line according to the estimates of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals would be $15,000,000, the yearly interest at three per cent on which would be $450,000. If the deficit on the new line were in the same proportion- and even supposing it did not take traffic from the Intercolonial-there would be a yearly deficit of $53,333. Or, adding the deficit and interest of the two roads the old Intercolonial and the new road, you find a yearly cost to the people of $2,803,333. In addition to this, there will be new rolling stock required. But, according to my bon. friend from South Lanark, the true deficit on the Intercolonial is $1,500,000 a year. The Halifax ' Herald ' says it is $2,500,000. Let us take the less extreme statement of the hon. member for South Lanark. How, then, will it work out ? You have the old road costing $70,000,000, with interest at three per cent, say $2,100,000. You have a deficit of $1,500,000. The new line will cost $15,000,000 and the deficit on it at the same rate will be $400,000, while the interest will amount to $450,000. So, you have a total yearly charge upon the country, on the basis of the figures of the hon. member for South Lanark of $4.450,000 for the operation of the Intercolonial in the maritime provinces. And what do we get for it V We get scarcely a pound of through-freight down to the seaboard at St. John or Halifax. Why, Mr. Speaker, the people of western Canada do not realize the condition of affairs in regard to the Intercolonial. Go to Halifax and you see there an immense elevator almost touching high heaven, a standing example of the condition of affairs with reference to the through-freight of the Intercolonial. The same thing applies to St. John. These elevators are examples of the folly of prepai'ing for through-traffic unless we actually have a through-traffic road from the west. Our opponents may say that the Halifax elevator was built by the present government. So it was, but it was only built to supply the place of one built by the previous government, which happened to be burnt down. Now we do not want elevators as playthings, but as a part of our equipment in handling through-traffic by our own ports. Mr. Hays has stated, and he should be in a position to know, that there would be traffic enough to supply half a dozen harbours. Suppose Mr. Hays is correct what does bis forecast mean 7 It means increased traffic over the Intercolonial from Moncton to Halifax and from Norton to St. John. It means that the line from Norton to St. John will have to be double tracked and that the line from Moncton to Halifax will have to be double tracked. I have no doubt at all it will come
to this, unless, in order to avoid double tracking and severe grade, you run the line to the south of the Cobequid mountains passing near Parrsboro and thence by Five Islands, Economy and Truro. I have no doubt also that in order to shorten the line between Moncton and New Glasgow and to reach the harbours of Whitehaven, Country Harbour, Louisbourg and Sydney, there will have to be built a new line from Moncton to New Glasgow along the north shore of Westmoreland, Cumberland, Colchester and Pictou counties. This road will shorten the distance between Moncton and New Glasgow by at least thirty-nine miles.
It means that we must have lines of steamers to handle the traffic. The Grand Trunk has specifically agreed to supply lines of steamers at the maritime province ports. It means, and must mean eventually, the establishment of the fast line. It means the establishment of a great through-traffic carried by the Grand Trunk Pacific to the ports of St. John and Halifax. The exMinister of Railways and Canals has stated that this project will ruin the Intercolonial Railway. I can hardly think he was serious. I have here a statement prepared by the Intercolonial Railway officials which gives me the total amount of the earnings for last year. The total earnings for local and through traffic was $6,056,171.97. Of this, the total amount of local traffic was $4,327,626.88. Where is there a single pound of iocal freight that will be taken by the Grand Trunk Pacific ? They cannot get any of the local traffic from the Intercolonial between Montreal and Quebec. Nor can they get any from along the St. Lawrence and the north shore of New Brunswick. They cannot take the trade now brought to the Intercolonial by iocal roads such as the Atlantic and Lake Superior, the Bue-toueke and other lines, because they will not connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Intercolonial will not lose to the Grand Trunk Pacific a single pound of local traffic in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. As to the through-traffic, 1 have not as full a statement as I had hoped to have. The memorandum giving particulars has not reached me up to this time. But I would take the statement I have before me, which has been prepared by the Railway Department This, mark you, relates wholly to through-traffic and does not affect the $4,000,000 and odd of local traffic which the Intercolonial now has and which will not be interfered with. The traffic originating in Montreal and vicinity amounts to $560,000. I have no data to show where that trade goes. No doubt, a large amount of it is dropped along the Intercolonial Railway between L6vis and Moncton, while some goes into the province of Nova Scotia. Let us assume that one-third of this will be secured by the Grand Trunk Pacific. The traffic from Nova Scotia and New Bi'unswick to Montreal and vicinity

amounts to $304,975.20. X have no data to show where this originates. If it originates along the north shore of New Brunswick it will continue to go over the Intercolonial Kailway-the Grand Trunk Pacific cannot touch it. But suppose that the Grand Trunk Pacific can capture one-third of this traffic originating in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The traffic from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to Levis and Quebec and vicinity amounts to the paltry sum of $50,320.39. The traffic to points in Ontario and the west via Montreal amounts to $671,740.67. The freight traffic from Ontario and the west via Montreal amounts to $071,740.07; via Ste. Rosalie, $29,307.08; and via St. John, $79,938.07. The Grand Trunk Pacific would not capture the trade which at present is handed over by the Canadian Pacific Railway at Ste. Rosalie and St. John. Let me point out to the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals that when he took over the Drummond County Railway he entered into a hard and fast agreement with the Grand Trunk that every pound of freight coming from the west destined to Intercolonial points would have to tje handed over to the Intercolonial for a period of ninety-nine years. There is an item of freight traffic from Ontario and western points via Montreal of $671,000, and that must come via the Canadian Pacific Railway or Grand Trunk to Montreal. Of course, the Canadian Pacific Railway is not going *to hand over any part of its trade to the Intercolonial; but the Grand Trunk mast hand over all of its portion of this traffic to the Intercolonial under the agreement-and the exMinister of Railways and Canals stated that he would stake his political future on the statement that that agreement was hard and fast. Therefore, we need not consider that, for, so far as that trade is concerned, it is bound to go over the Intercolonial under that agreement. Let us admit we lose a part of the traffic originating in Montreal. I do not admit it as a matter of fact, but let us admit it for the sake of argument. Admit in the same way that we lose part of the traffic to points in Ontario and the west. With all this the Intercolonial would be deprived of only between $400,000 and $500,000 of freight business, and this out of a total traffic of over $6,000,000. And yet the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals says that the effect of the building of this line, which, at the worst, will take this insignificant part of the trade, will be to dismantle and destroy the Intercolonial Railway. Why, the Intercolonial will make more money carrying Grand Trunk Pacific freight between Moncton and Halifax in one month than it will lose on through-traffic in a year by the building of this new road. If the Grand Trunk bring to Moncton what they have promised to do. they will fill the road between Moncton and Halifax. Consider the effect upon Moncton.
What does it mean ? My hon. friend the Mr. LOGAN.
ex-Minister of Railways refers to the city of Moncton as going to revert back to a small village. But this means that it will become a great city in the near future, a central point for a number of railways in the maritime provinces. It means more than that, it means that every man in Moncton, in every railway workshop, every brakeman, every railway engineer, or conductor, every dispatcher and operator and other railway employee, will have more chances for promotion. will have more chances for getting increased salaries, because there will be more work to do and more pay for doing it by means of more competition between railways. Moncton being a divisional point, the Grand Trunk Pacific will have their repair shops there for their rolling stock, they will have their divisional offices in that city. But what will it mean to Moncton if the policy of the leader of the opposition is adopted, to extend the Intercolonial to Georgian bay 7 How long does he suppose that Moncton would retain the general railway offices and workshops ? How long would it remain the headquarters of the government railways of Canada ? Under such conditions of affairs, not one year would pass before Moncton would suffer a severe set-back, these offices would be removed to a more central point, perhaps Montreal or Ottawa, and then would come the dismantling of the city of Moncton, and the people of that whole section would have cause to regret that such a policy had been adopted.
Now, these are some of the local advantages that would come to the city of Moncton if we built this road. I said a few moments ago that if the policy of the leader of the opposition were adopted it would mean more money to railway magnates and railway companies. Now, it has been stated that there will be spent in this country, in five years by the government, between Moncton and Winnipeg and by the Grand Trunk Pacific, between Winnipeg and the coast, between $100,000,000 and $200,000.000. What does that mean ? Sir, if there is one industry in this country struggling for existence, it is the iron industry. I am not going to discuss the question of the iron industry, but I will say this, that if all the iron concerns in Canada were to work night and day from this time until the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific, they could not supply the rails and iron and structural steel required for the construction of the road. According to the terms of this contract, all their supplies must be secured in the Dominion of Canada. It means that more money will be paid Canadian workmen and Canadian artisans ; it means a great demand for supplies of all kinds of the products of the farm and the . forest : it means a great demand for lumber, a great demand for ties, a great demand for hay. for grain, for beef, for pork : a great demand for engines and boilers : a great demand for building material ; an immense

demand for woollens, for building stone, for cement, for boots and shoes ; a great demand for rolling stock ; a great demand for ears, passenger and freight ; a great demand for car wheels. Why, Sir, I have not the slightest doubt that within a very short time the car works in the town in which I live will be quadrupled in size to build the cars that will be required for the Grand Trunk Pacific. At the present time the Grand Trunk Company are not able, in its own shops, to produce the rolling stock required on their old line, and how could they produce the rolling stock required on this additional line which with branches will be over 4.000 miles in length ?
It means a great demand for an article of supreme importance to us in Nova Scotia, because it gives us our provincial revenue- it means a great demand for coal. In this northern country between Quebec and Winnipeg, while almost everything else is to be found that is for the advantage of man, there does not seem to have been discovered yet any good coal. There has been found some good lignite, but no good bituminous or anthracite coal. To-day in Nova Scotia we are not able to send our coal west of Montreal, we are not able to send our coal into the province of Ontario ; those places get their coal from Pennsylvania. Manitoba also gets its coal from Pennsylvania. But by the construction of this road from Moncton to the city of Quebec we will decrease the distance for coal carriage over 100 miles to that point. When we come to the northern country further away from the Pennsylvania coal fields, I believe as much as I believe that I am living that within a short time we will be supplying, not only the city of Quebec with Nova Scotia coal, but also that whole northern country, clear away to the city of Winnipeg, in competition with the Pennsylvania coal mines. What does that mean? It means that in the operation of this road alone from Moncton to Winnipeg there will be required nearly 1,000,000 tons of coal per year ; more coal than is produced to-day in the whole county of Cumberland will be used upon this road alone for locomotives. This road is particularly important to the county of Cumberland, which I represent, because that county will be the best able to supply the Moncton and Quebec division all the year round with coal. We can compete for Quebec with the mines of Cape Breton and Pictou, anl we can compete for the trade as far west as Winnipeg. It means another thing, so far as coal is concerned, and that is an immense quantity of bunker coal for St. John, Halifax and other ports to supply the steamers employed by the Grand Trunk Pacific. It means better wages for men on the Intercolonial, and a greater demand for labour all round.
Now. Mr. Speaker, I have to complete the remarks that I did not intend to make so long. But somehow none of us seem to be able to make short speeches upon this proposition before the House. I have had some experience as whip on the government side of the House in arranging for the speeches, and I have not yet been able to find any one who did not exceed the time he said he was going to speak by at least 100 per cent. I think I am following the example which has been set for me by those lion, gentlemen. I have only one thing more to say, and that is in reference to the bonding privilege, the necessity for which we are endeavouring to avoid. We do not want in this country any privileges from the United States, we want always to be able to stand on our own ground. Some of our friends opposite have been trying to make merry with the contention that we should have an all-Canadian route, in order to get rid of the need of this bonding privilege, the abrogation of which the Americans have been holding over our heads for so long. We are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that we are on very good terms with our American friends to the south of us, and that there is no danger of their withdrawing the bonding privilege. I do not deny that we are on friendly terms, but if we are going to remain a part of the British empire, we must take certain eventualities into account. We must expect that whenever the British empire gets into trouble in any part of the world the very first people who will hurrah for her enemies will be the people of the United States. We have found that in the Boer war, we have found it in every war in which Britain has been engaged. We need go back no further than the Venezuelan affair and the Fenian raid. They are in that state of mind that it only needs a match to set them aflame. I have the greatest possible respect for the American people and American statesmen, but there is a feeling in that country which is antiBritish. We are on good terms with them, but we do not know how long we can continue to be on good terms. As the Prime Minister said, the best way to remain on good terms with our neighbours to the south is to become independent of them. They refer to us continually as the spoiled child of the empire. They refuse to deliberate with us on a fair and reasonable basis. Take the present Alaska Boundary Commission. The proposition was made to them to appoint an arbitration commission so constituted that a majority of the commission should make a final decision. And that the majority report should be final. Did they agree to it ? No. Because they imagine that with an equal number of arbitrators in the tribunal there would not be a majority report and nothing would be done and they would eventually secure the territory in the north-west of this country that they are endeavouring to obtain. What are the facts to-day, Mr. Speaker, we have been imagining all along that we owned the country north from Hudson's Bay clear to the north pole.

But, now we have the astounding statement made by American newspapers that they have a right over parts ot' this country and propose to maintain it. We have today a party going to these northern climes -what fcr ? To assert the right of the British empire against the United States if they endeavour to encroach on our lands. We must be independent of the United States. Let us not be in the position that we fear all the,time that something is going to happen that will interfere with the prosperity of this country. I belive the policy of Canada for the future to be that we should not only have Canadian ports for Canadian traffic but that we should have a preference not in tariff alone but a preference in ports as well. Two or three years ago, I put on the Order Paper of this House a resolution to the effect that the British preference should only apply to goods coming into Canada by Canadian ports.
You never moved it.

I put it on the Order Paper and I will tell you why it was not moved. It was not moved because pressure was brought to bear on me, not by the government, but by certain parties who feared the bonding privilege would be removed if we granted a preference to Canadian ports. Every day American newspapers printed articles saying that if such a policy were adopted the bonding privilege would be taken away from us. lam not in a position to convey to the House the representations made to me at that time from official quarters, not of this country. X think I could produce evidence to prove to the House that the time has come that we should not have to ask the United States if we can give a preference to Canadian ports.
I believe when this road is built, and we have an all-Canadian route to Canadian Xiorts that that will be the time when we should adopt my resolution, and that the principle of that resolution will form a part of the policy of the Dominion of Canada. Let us have a British preference and let us have also a preference for Canadian ports, let us endeavour to build up our Canadian ports, to build up our Canadian trade and to develop Canadian territory.
You tell me the United States do not think anything of this bonding privilege and that it does not amount to anything. Let me read to you a paper, the New York * Scottish American,' a paper that is reliable and well known to many members of this House. Referring to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, it says :
First and foremost, such a railway-one from the Atlantic to the Pacific entirely on Canadian soil-would make Canada absolutely independent of the United States, so far, at least, as regards those bonding privileges upon which this country and its people generally calculate so very much. In this sense the proposed railway may be said to be indispensable to the proper maintenance of Canadian manhood. The Mr, LOGAN.
threat of removing these bonding privileges has been held by this country over Canada to obtain any desired concession. Even advocates for annexation are fain to handle it. Mr. Andrew Carnegie said, in effect, the other day, that Canada had better become annexed to the United States or the latter would remove the bonding privileges now enjoyed by the former ; and in saying this he was only voicing the sentiments of the people here generally.
Mark these words :
Once she had this proposed transcontinental railway Canada could afford to tell the United States to remove its bond privileges whenever it pleased, as she no longer needed them.
Now, Sir, in conclusion let me say that I am in favour of building this road for the reasons I have endeavoured to lay before this House. Sir, I represent a constituency which gave to Canada the man who was big enough to lift the curtain and look into the future of the Canadian west and to be the foremost mind in the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway which has done so much to develop that part of Canada. I am here to-day to say I admire Sir Charles Tupper for the part he took at that time in the building of that road. It is only just and fair and manly on my part if I believe that, to express my thoughts. The people of Cumberland, I believe, are behind me when I say that they favour at the present time as they favoured in the past the opening up of the west ; that they favour at the present time the opening up also of the great north land of this country to assist in making Canada a mighty nation. To-day we are described as a mere fringe along the United States border. We want thickness in this country. In a few years, Sir, we will have west of Lake Superior, probably ten millions of people and ten millions of people on the east of Lake Superior, but for a thousand miles between you have a mere ragged backbone of country without population. Let us while we are developing the west, while we are bringing people into the western country, at the same time fill up the middle of this country, let us have this country so developed that it shall have breadtli from the Atlantic clear through to the Pacific.

The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are supposed to lease the eastern division, and to put up security on that division in the shape of rolling stock. If my contention is right, they put $20,000,000 rolling stock on the whole road, of which $5,000,000 is to be on the eastern section. Every railway man knows that when rolling stock has been in use one year its depreciation in value, as a second hand article, is 20 per cent, and after four-years it is 40 per cent. If well renewed after that, for many years it may be worth 40 per cent of the first cost. In four years' time this $5,000,000 of rolling stock will be worth at the outside $3,000,000. If you take it that at the end of twenty-six years the capital of that railway is $280,000,000, and I am quite sure I am within the mark, I will not take the same relative proportion but I will double that for the twenty-five years. If at the end of twenty-five years we have had an expenditure of $280,000,000 or a doubling of the debt of Canada, then at the end of the fifty years we will have an expenditure of $560,000,000. and if the Grand Trunk Pacific Company carry out their agreement of operating this road, which I am very happy to say I do not believe they will do, we will have an expenditure of $560,000,000 upon this road, the Grand Trunk Pacific paying to the country three per cent of the cost.
The minister will have to get his actuary to work again.

This is a rule of thumb matter and does not require an actuary. Now then following that out I will read again the clause in which I have no doubt the Minister of Finance or the other members of the government, if I was wrong in assuming that the Finance Minister is the originator of this clause, was trying to leave a particular branch of free trade in Canada for fifty years as the record of his principles. If I am wrong in assuming that he drafted this clause, I am quite sure he did not know the meaning of the clause when he and other members of council passed it. Now, the government have agreed to build this road as a government road ; they have agreed with the Grand Trunk Pacific and through them in a roundabout way with the Grand Trunk Railway that the Grand Trunk Pacific are to pay three per cent on the net cost of that railway and no more. Now, then, the clause that follows, and this is the final clause I think iii connection with the government building the railway, because this clause is left out of the clause concerning the Grand Trunk Pacific building the western division. This clause (clause 17) provides that no addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to the capital construction account in respect of customs duties levied where there is direct importation of material or supplies by the government. Now, a bargain between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific is the same as a bargain between any two men ; each one will hold the other as far as possible to the bargain. The government have agreed with the Grand Trunk Pacific that they shall build this road and that so far as imports by the government in connection with the road are concerned there shall be no customs duties levied. Suppose the government take this technical point and say we are not going to import these things, there is no court in the land that will not say to the government that is the meaning of your clause, you have the power to import without duty, therefore you must import without duty. I do not think a man, the least familiar with business, can contradict or can disagree with the assertion I make that that would he the interpretation of that clause. Now, then, if it was affecting only the original construction of this road it might be said to be a matter that was only temporary, but this includes all the expenditure to be made by the government during the fifty years of this lease and of this contract. We will assume, because there is nothing in the contract apparently defining how it is to be built, we will assume that this road is built under a commission appointed by the government, that is by the government itself. The government perhaps may let out certain contracts, the contractors before they make the contract or the Grand Trunk Pacific before it consents to that contract will say the contract must contain a clause that if the contractor brings in materials they shall be free of duty. No other meaning can attach to that clause ; it covers the great bulk of the rough manufacturing industries that are now in existence in Canada. It covers steel rails. The minister will say that steel rails now come into Canada free of duty, but I

hope that when wiser and better fiscal ideas rule in this House instead of having that abortion of bounties we will have a correct and a proper system of protection where the individual manufacturer is protected on all the articles that he makes. We will, I think, without looking forward with too great hope, within a very short time-I think myself within a shorter time than my friends opposite will agree with me-find that those who have the sound fiscal policy of this country at heart and believe in protection will rule, and they will bring in a protective tariff. If this clause passes all the materials necessary for this railway in future will come in free and no law that can be passed will alter it, and all the supplies will come in free. Now, I read to-day a few of these supplies and this list will be extended indefinitely. It extends to all the rougher manufactures of Canada. I am not lawyer enough, I am not a lawyer at all, to say, that in connection with this very bounty that the government has established, if that clause was submitted to a court the government would not have to refund to the contractors a proportion of the bounty they give on steel rails if without the bounty they could buy steel rails elsewhere. It strikes me that is probably a very reasonable thing, but I am not able to say whether that is so or not. However, I assume that under that clause we will have admitted into Canada all the materials required for the construction of the railway, and all the supplies, all the pork and the beef and the blankets, and the rubbers and the boots, and it may be the clothing of the navvies who work on that road if they work under a government contract, because What is an easier matter than to put in a contract with a body of men that they shall be paid so much and shall be provided with their clothing and supplies which will be cheaper if they are imported free of duty. It would not affect all the supplies brought in for this railway, but the Minister of Customs is business man enough to know that if I have a contract for supplying $50,000 worth of materials, which I can get in free of duty, and another contract for $50,000 on which I have to pay duty, I can very easily compete with the local manufacturer and crush him out. That must be the effect of this contract if it is carried out. I think I have made myself as clear as possible on that point.
I want to repeat the statement I made in connection with the direct bonus which the government gives to this railway. I assume that the portion built by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will cost $40,000,000 which the government guarantee at three per cent, and that will save to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway one and a half per cent per year for fifty years. A sinking fund of one per cent a year for fifty years at that amount would realize at the end of that ime $62,446,000, or more than Mr. OSLER.
enough to pay the whole bonded debt of the company, and with the practical result that the government hand over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway the western section of the road free of cost. I am well within the mark when I say that the benefit to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway of the government guarantee is at least one and a half per cent per annum, because I can state as a positive fact that no railway on this continent has yet borrowed a sum of money like that at a less rate of interest than 44 per cent per annum. I say that no railway on this continent can now borrow the sum of money that is required for the construction of the western section of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway at a rate as low as 44 per cent per annum. The New York Central, probably the railway with the best credit on this continent, has lately borrowed money at 5 per cent per annum paying one per cent commission for the loan. Now, if I take 44 per cent as the interest the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway would have to pay for the money if it were not guaranteed by this government, then at the eud of the fifty years' term-which is a quite legitimate calculation because they can use that as a sinking fund to pay off their debt-the bonus you give them would amount to $93,000,000. And yet this government says that the whole cost to this country is only $13,000,000. I would like to suggest to the Minister of Finance that he should take this scheme as it is in its entirety, with all its contracts weak as they are, and ask the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company from whom this money is to come that is put in under second mortgage for the construction of the western section, and suggest to them that he will give them a bonus of $20,000,000 in cash if they will carry out the scheme which the government now proposes on all its lines, and I will be bound the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway directors and shareholders will turn it down without five minutes' discussion.
I do not like to see a misstatement made in this House and endorsed by a man of the position and the reputation of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), who I am sure will be the last man to countenance a statement which is outrageously wrong. The hon. gentleman quoted from the 1 Weekly Sun.' It has struck me during this debate that the greater part of the arguments made by the government and its supporters are arguments from the newspaper press of the country. It is not so very long ago that we heard the Prime Minister state in this House that he absolutely paid no attention to letters or articles in newspapers, and yet he himself in his speech took up nine columns of ' Hansard ' quoting from the New York ' Sun ' and yellow journals. I do not for a moment suggest that the hon. member for Cumberland did not quote from the ' Weekly Sun '

in perfect good faith, but he certainly quoted a misstatement. It is a farmer's paper and has often very good things in it, but it often shoots oil things which exist only in the imagination. This is what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) quoted from the ' Weekly Sun
The Candian Pacific Railway has just declared a dividend at the rate of six per cent per annum upon the original issue of $65,000,000 common stock. Of the proceeds of this stock not more than $8,500,000, according to Mr. Blake, ever went into the construction of the road. The remainder went to swell the profits of the shareholders. The dividend that has just been paid amounts to nearly fifty per cent of the actual cash expended by the shareholders on the construction of the railway.
That is an absolutely false statement. The original $25,000,000 of Canadian Pacific Railway stock was bought and paid for under an agreement with the government, and of course you cannot blame individuals for making the best bargain they could, although they did not make a good bargain in that case as it happened. They paid 25 cents a share or $6,250,000 for the original $25,000,000 of stock. All the other stock that was issued from that date to this has been issued on the market at the fullest market price. I am speaking from memory now as I had no time to verify the actual figures, but there was one case where a syndicate took $20,000,000 of stock at 55 cents or 60 cents on the dollar, and when the time arrived for the payment of that stock under their agreement, the stock was worth 10 per cent or 20 per cent less than the amount they agreed to pay. They had to pay for that, however, and that money went into the company's hand, and every other dollar of Canadian Pacific Railway stock issued after the original $25,000,000 loan was issued at the fullest market rate. The last $20,000,000 which was issued under the authority of this parliament was sold to the shareholders and produced par, and that money has been expended during the last year and a half on the road. Of the original $65,000,000 I think I am quite safe in saying that over $50,000,000 was put into the road in cash by the shareholders ; not the original men who took it, but the shareholders in England, Germany, America, Canada, and all over the world. I know that the member for Cumberland will be glad that I have given this explanation, although I have a great dislike to referring to anything connected with any company I am interested in. The hon. gentleman from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) made a very strong appeal in favour of this contract because of the great benefit that would accrue to the manufacturers of this country by reason of the money that will be expended. I say that if this contract is carried out in dts present shape it will be the greatest blow that the manufacturers of Canada ever have experienced, not excepting the abolition of the reciprocity treaty.
The bonding privilege question has been so often referred to that perhaps it is almost superfluous to refer to it again. But I have an idea on that subject which I believe is a sound one. It is something which I would not like to see carried out; I should very much regret jf the occasion should arise to necessitate it. If under any unfortunate circumstances causing friction between the two countries, the bonding privilege should he done away with, it would do more to make Canada a nation than all that the Prime Minister of this country has done since he came into power. What we have lacked and what this government has lacked more than anything else, has been the ability to grapple properly with the transportation question. Where are we weak and where are we strong in dealing with that question 1 We are proposing to spend $120,000,000 to shorten the route from Quebec and Levis to our sea ports, 120 miles according to some, forty miles according to others. In constructing that line we do not improve our position with reference to the bonding privilege one iota. We have now an all-Canadian route by a government road. All Canadian products to be shipped through Canadian ports can go over the Intercolonial Railway, if it is provided with sufficient rolling stock. What we want is to improve our waterways and lake ports, instead of building duplicate railways. These are very well in their place, but they are not the first needs to be considered. To make Canada free and independent we must make our ports as good as any on the continent. Building a hundred railways across the continent will not improve the St. Lawrence route, the harbours of St. John and Halifax or the Georgian bay and Lake Superior harbours. Go into the Department of Marine and Fisheries, -where 1 suppose you can see a marine map of the upper lakes and the Georgian bay ; look at that, and then be ashamed of the position we occupy and the little we have done to improve our ports. We shall see on the map three or four stars representing lighthouses on the Canadian shores from Port Arthur to Sault Ste. Marie, and from the Sault to the Georgian bay ; you can count them on your fingers. Look on the other side, and you will see lighthouses so thick that you can hardly count them. We have not a life-saving crew on our northern waters, and no attempt is made to put one there. No attempt is made to develop our natural channels for international trade. Make Fort William, Port Arthur, Midland and all the ports on the Georgian bay so perfect that the larger vessels can enter them, load and unload and tranship their cargoes at a minimum cost; and then improve the grades of your railways and double track them if youTike. But, after all, the key of the situation is the St. Lawrence route. Make the channel so safe, and the ports of Montreal and Quebec so good, that our ships can safely use

them. What has happened since we came to this House this year ? Vessel after vessel has gone ashore, partly because we have not proper lighting, partly because we have not sufficient foghorns, and partly because we have not a proper pilotage system, for all of which the government is responsible, and all of which can only be remedied by the action of the government. Let us first provide what we know will bring immediate returns, and then will be time enough to spend money for developing the interior and far off portions of the country. I agree thoroughly with my leader in saying that the Conservative party are not and have never been afraid of spending money, so long as it is spent properly. The people who have been afraid of spending money up to the time they came into power, are our friends on the other side of the House. They spend it now, but they do not spend it properly.
With regard to this contract, I do not like to speak harshly; I do not like to impute motives; but if I were to judge it by the weakness I see in it, though not being a lawyer and not understanding its intricacies, 1 would say that it was drawn by the solicitor of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Let me make a suggestion to my hon. friends on the other side of the House, that if ever they have another contract to make-and I hope they will not for many years-let them remember that the first principle of business between two contracting parties is that the party doing the favour should draw up the contract, and that the only modifications made in it should be those suggested by the other side. This contract has tlie appearance of having been drawn up by the solicitor of the men who were receiving the favour. It may have been supervised by the government and the government officials, and point after point may have come up and been conceded; but the main points in favour of the contractors are still embodied in it. I am quite sure that this is the basis on which this contract was drawn. It was the basis on which the contract for the Yukon railway was drawn; it was the basis on which the contract for the Treadgold concession was drawn; it was the basis on which the contract for the bottle nosed ships was drawn; and it is the basis on which the contract for this enormous expenditure has been drawn.

The policy of bonusing railways by cash and land grants from the Dominion government has become a fruitful source of jobbery, peculation and corruption. Under its operation favourites of the government have been enriched. Appropriations have been made for the sole purpose Mr. OSLER.
