The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) twitted me upon my opposition to government railway bonuses. I am not ashamed to say that as a rule I am opposed to these bonuses, but there are circumstances and conditions in which they may be properly given. In the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick, where it may be necessary to open up colonization roads into the public domain, in those sections where the country is not settled, and where there are timber or agricultural lands which will warrant the expenditure, it is good policy to aid the building of railways into such districts. Such a policy gives the government both an indirect and direct return. Many years ago, long before I was in politics, I was struck by the stupidity of the Ontario government in giving bonuses where they were not needed-in giving bonuses to aid the duplicating of railways -and I have studied up this question of government aid to railways. The hon. member for Hants gave many authorities, among others the United States, for the granting of bonuses. It is quite true that in the early years of the American republic, the state governments did grant bonuses, but not to the extent suggested by the hon. member. Over a year ago, I obtained the following report from one of the leading railway lawyers of the United States, with regard to the position of the various states of the union in this matter of railway bonuses. This report is headed ' State and Municipal Aid to Railways in the United States ;
Powers of Legislatures and Municipalities.' It states as follows :
In considering the subject of state and municipal aid to railways in the United States, tho following legal principles adopted by the courts with reference to the powers of legislature and municipal corporations should be borne in mind: (1) That the legislature has full power over the municipalities, and may, unless the constitution prohibits, authorize municipal corporations to aid railways by issues of bonds and otherwise. (2) That the municipal corporations have no inherent right to issue bonds or grant aid to railways. Such power must come from the legislature.
Perhaps it may weary you a little, but it will be interesting for future reference if I give a few more extracts from this report :
In the state of Maine, the constitution of 1S20, article 22, was amended in 1877. By this amendment the credit of the state shall not be directly or indirectly loaned. Municipal corporations are not prohibited from aiding railway companies, but no debt or liability can be incurred which, with previous debts, shall exceed five per centum of the last regular valuation of the municipal corporation.
New Hampshire-Constitution of 1874, part 2 article 5, amended 1879. Neither this state nor any subdivision can aid any private association or corporation.
Vermont-Constitution of 1793. No constitutional prohibitions.
Massachusetts-Constitution of 1780. There are no constitutional limitations for debt for state, county or city purposes. Aid to railways may be given by either.
Connecticut-Constitution of 1818, article 25, amendment adopted 1877. No county, city, town borough or other municipality shall ever subscribe to the capital stock of any railway corporation, or purchase its bonds, or make donations to, or loan its credit, directly or indirectly, in aid of any such corporation.
Rhode Island-Constitution of 1842. No prohibition against such aid, but restrictions.
Now mark. In nineteen cases out of twenty, the original constitution of each state authorized it to grant aid, and almost in every ease the amendment to the constitution prohibits the granting of aid absolutely.
Have you the mileage of the different states and their population at the time they ceased to bonus railways ?

No, but I shall give the hon. gentleman what he wants. In New York and New Jersey, the amended constitution prohibits aid to railway companies. In Pennsylvania, by the limitations to the constitution, neither the state nor a subdivision can aid a railway. In Maryland, municipalities are not prohibited from aiding a railway, but counties can give or loan their aid only when authorized by an Act of the general assembly, which shall be published for two months before the next election for members of the house of delegates. The state cannot, directly or indirectly, aid a private corporation. In Delaware there is no limitation. In the Virginias, the state

cannot assist a railway. In North Carolina, the municipalities may aid a railway, with the consent of the taxpayer. In South Carolina, state aid requires the consent of the people. In Florida, the state is prohibited from granting aid to railway companies and the legislature from authorizing any county, city, borough, township or incorporated district to become a stockholder in. or aid or loan its credit to any company or individual. In Georgia there is the same prohibition as in Florida. In Alabama neither the state nor any of its subdivisions can help a railway. In Mississippi the state is prohibited from aiding by pledge or loan, any person, association or corporation, or to become a stockholder in an association or corporation. The legislature is prohibited from authorizing municipalities to loan money or to grant aid to railways.
In Tennessee, the municipalities may aid railways, provided the proposition is submitted to the voters and receives a three-fourtlis majority. In Kentucky, the credit of the state can never be given to aid railways. The next state on the list is Illinois, and this is the state which the bon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) quoted as having been so greatly benefited through railways. It was my little knowledge and interest in the state of Illinois which caused me to take an interest in the question of municipal and state aid to railways. Large grants were made to various railways in the state of Illinois, not only by the state, but by the towns, cities and townships. Bonds were issued to the extent of millions of dollars, and these bonds were, to a very large extent, brought to Canada and sold. The late Mr. E. H. King, general manager of the Bank of Montreal, who had great knowledge of the west, bought $500,000 of Illinois county bonds to pay him 14 per cent, although at that time our bonds in Ontario were selling to pay 6 per cent. The scandal connected with railway bonuses in Illinois caused them, in 1870, the earliest time when it could be done, to amend their constitution, and they provided that neither the state, nor the county, city, town or township, or other municipality, could issue bonds to pay for the stock of a railway or other private corporation, or in any way aid such corporation. This provision did not appear in the previous constitution of 1848. The constitution was amended in this respect because of the absolute demoralization caused by this public bonusing. of railways.
Indiana.-Counties are prohibited from subscribing to the stock of railways or issuing bonds to assist them.
Ohio.-The state is prohibited from aiding railways, nor can the legislature authorize municipal corporations to do so.
Michigan.-The credit of the state cannot be granted to or in aid of any person or corporation.
Wisconsin.-The credit of the state shall not be given to any corporation or railway.

Arkansas.-The state or any sub-division of the state is prohibited from lending its credit for any purpose whatever.
California.-Prohibits the bonusing of railways.
Colorado.-Prohibits the state or any division of the state from bonusing the railways. Under a prior constitution of 1870, state aid could be given.
Idaho.-This state was created in 1889, and had no previous experience to guide it. But from the experience and knowledge of others, in its constitution, it prohibits the state from lending its credit to or bonusing or becoming a stockholder in any corporation.
Kansas.-The state shall not be a party to carrying on any work of internal improvement.
, Louisiana.-Prohibits the state from loaning its credit.
Minnesota.-Prohibits the giving of the credit of the state for any internal improvements.
Missouri.-The state is prohibited from loaning its credit.
Montana.-The constitution was adopted in 1889, and it prohibits the granting of aid to railways.
Nebraska.-This state was constituted in 1875. The constitution provides that no municipality shall make donations to any railway, unless authorized by the electors, and under certain restrictions as to amount.
Nevada.-There is no limitation.
North Dakota.-This is a comparatively new state, and when its constitution was granted it was not in anything like the condition of prosperity of our western provinces to-day, Manitoba, Alberta and the others. Its constitution prohibits the granting of aid to railways.
South Dakota.-This is not nearly so valuable a state as our Manitoba. Its legislature has never authorized aid to railroads.
Texas.-The constitution contains sweeping provisions against granting any municipal aid.
The Territories.-Are prohibited from aiding railways by Act of Congress.
Now, I call attention to these facts which, I think, are interesting and ought to be very useful. If the states to the south of us, with all their long experience, have come to the conclusion that it is a vicious thing for the state to aid in the construction of railways, we may be pretty sure that there is good reason in favour of that conclusion. That good reason was this :	During the
time of the early settlement of the western states, when the state government and municipalities granted bonuses to railways, Ihere existed such a state of corruption as lo absolutely demoralize the electors, insomuch that they have hardly got over it to this day. The results of that corruption were so serious that, in every case, after 1865, that is, after the close of the war- the great wave of railway building swept

over the United States from 1862 to 1868- almost every state amended its constitution, and almost the first clause put in was a clause prohibiting aid to railways. I do not go so far as that. But I have said that, on general principles, state aid to railways was wrong. I do not believe there is a single dollar of aid needed for the building of railways in the prairie portions of Manitoba and the North-west. The railway companies there will build as fast, or even faster, than the requirements of the people demand. This has been the case all over the western states. I believe that if you do not grant a dollar of aid to the Grand Trunk they will build into the Northwest faster, and be there sooner than if you do grant the aid.
But the Prime Minister, all through his speech rang the changes on the idea of a crisis. Now, we have not yet had any outside explanation as to what this crisis is.
I can only think that probably the crisis is the near approach of a general election and the discovery, on looking into the treasury of the various machines required for running an election, of balances which will not satisfy all demands. Is this government scheme, this magnificent expenditure of money, to be the government's way of meeting this crisis ?

The shortness of the time that I have allotted to myself to address the House will preclude me from devoting as much attention as I would like to the remarks of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier), and I hope he will not consider me discourteous if I do not attempt to refute all the arguments he has presented. He, like other hon. gentlemen on that side, insistently demand to know the meaning of the word ' crisis,' and demand to be told why there should be any call for speed in the carrying out of the project now before us. It is for the very purpose of preventing that diversion of trade into American channels that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) himself has warned us against to-night. He said that long before the government could complete the eastern section the western section would be completed by the Grand Trunk, and. for want of through connection by the eastern section, the trade would be diverted through American channels to American ports-and once caused to run through those channels it would be very difficult to bring it back again to our own side. It is to prevent that crisis and that diversion of trade that the government is now proposing to build a railway through Canadian territory whose terminals shall be Canadian ports. Our hon. friend found fault with the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Bogan) reading a list of letters from boards of trade, congratulating the government upon their attempt to build this railway, and he said they were endorsations of the Grand Trunk
scheme to build from North Bay to Winnipeg and into the prairie section. In that he has made a great mistake. These endorsations covered the construction ,of this very road that the government intend to build to prevent that diversion of Canadian trade through a foreign country and to foreign ports.
Now our friend tells us in the early part of his address that he is not a lawyer. I am not a lawyer either, but I hope I am a better lawyer than he is, and I believe I am quite as able to interpret a clause in this agreement. I differ entirely with him in his efforts to condemn the character of this agreement. If there is anything I felt pleasure in it was the masterly skill with which this agreement was drawn up. so that a layman could understand it without the intervention of lawyers. When it is necessary to get lawyers in the House to interpret anything that may be a matter of dispute, no two of them appear to agree; therefore, it is absolutely necessary that these agreements should be couched in such language that an ordinary layman can understand what they mean. Now this clause 17, that is such a direct blow to the manufacturing establishments of this country, that is such a. menace to the national policy which our good friend has so much at heart, I read in an entirely different sense from what he does. But he does not go quite far enough back. If he went to clause 16, in the Bill, which explains the motive of these particular clauses, he will find it says that the eastern section shall be built under the supervision of commissioners, and that it shall be let by public tender, and given to the lowest tenderer who can assure the commissioners that he is qualified to carry on that work. Therefore, this work will be carried on by public contractors, who will buy their goods in the cheapest markets in the world, I have not the slightest doubt, but will give Canada, as Canadians, very likely the preference, all things being equal. I take it that this clause was put in there to protect the Grand Trunk Pacific from being compelled to pay an unduly large amount for the use of this road. They say that should it be necessary for the government to import goods that go into this railway, the amount of duty that would ordinarily be collected from a contractor shall not be added to the cost price of this railway and thereby increase the annual rent to the company. That is all I see that this means. It is no blow at the manufacturing interests, it is no menace to the national policy, it is a wise provision put in, I presume, at the instance of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. The whole explanation of clause 16 is given by the Minister of Finance in his speech, it says that this eastern or government section shall be built under the supervision of commissioners, shall be let by public contract, and given to the lowest tenderer.

But our friend shows the excess of his imagination when he alludes to the liberality with which the government is treating the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in actually subsidizing them, or conferring a benefit on them, to the amount of $93,000,000 for building the western section of this road. He gets at it in this way, that by the guarantee of the government they are able to borrow money at 3 per cent which in other circumstances they would have to pay 4 per cent for, and, therefore, the government is giving them an extra 1 per cent which will amount at the end of 50 years to $50,000,000. He says that the government is giving them $50,000,000, while In reality the government is not giving them a single cent. Now that is an evident proposition, to every intelligent man in this House ; and I am surprised that a gentleman who is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who has a reputation as a financier, if not as a critic of railway construction, should deliberately, in the face of as intelligent a lot of gentlemen as I see surrounding me, make such an absurd statement as that we are going to give the Grand Trunk Pacific Company $50,000,000 when we are not giving them one single cent.
We are saving them $50,000,000.
We are saving them $50,000,000 if you choose to put it the way my horn friend does. But that is quite a different thing to giving it to them, is it not'!
It is just the same thing actually.
But is it the same thing to us ?
Yes, we take the risk.

But we do not lose the $50,000,000, and we cannot give them that $50,000,000, because we do not give them 50 cents. But our friend excels himself when he goes on further to explain this contract. Now this contract, if anything, is one of the things that he should have left alone. He might roam in the realms of imagination, he might make prophesies as to the future, but when he comes down to plain black and white, and the thing is there so that each one can see it for himself, it is so easy to refute such a statement that 1 am surprised our friend made it. He says we are going to construct a railway that will cost, from Moncton to Winnipeg, $80,000,000. That is the least sum that he has heard any one estimate as the probable cost. He could not have heard the Finance Minister, he could not have heard others speak from this side of the House. But assuming that he deliberately closed his ears, there are none so deaf as those who will not hear ; it may be that he heard no one estimate the cost of this railway at less than $80,000,000. But assuming he got no more accurate information than that, was he justified in Mr. HEYD.
telling us that this $80,000,000, before the 50 years will have expired, will reach the magnificent sum of $560,000,000 ? Because he said a railway when first constructed does not represent what that railway will actually cost, that It requires continuous improvement, and that improvement will go on for 50 years. I presume that is true, but that is all provided for in this contract that he intended to explain, because it says that when this road is handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific, from that time they must keep up its maintenance, they must make constant changes, and when that 50 years shall have elapsed, they shall turn it over to the government in a first-class condition, in harmony with the condition of railways, not now, but what they may be 50 years from now. And, therefore, that statement that a railway that was going to cost according to his estimate $80,000,000 now will represent a loss to the government of $500,000,000 is absurd because the very conditions that are to bring this about, according to the hon. gentleman, are all provided for in this agreement and after we once turn it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific and they accept it, from that time not a dollar can be added to it without the consent of the government, and when we do insist upon substituting say an iron bridge for a wooden bridge, it must be added to the capital and on that capital the Grand Trunk Pacific must pay interest.
1 could devote more time to answering certain objections that have been advanced, but I think it is hardly necessary. We on this side have arrived at that stage when we do not take the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) seriously, especially when he goes into the domain of prophepy. We have had experience before of what he is capable of saying on certain occasions, especially when it is a matter of politics. We remember that only five years ago we had an important discussion in this House as to the advisability of giving 3,750,000 acres of gold lands to the Mackenzie and Mann syndicate. Now, our hon. friend made a speech then magnifying all the dangers to the government and minimizing all the advantages that might accrue. Well, now five years have gone by, and we have an opportunity to-night of ascertaining whether he was then a true prophet or a false prophet, a prophet of Baal. Now, let us see what he had to say five years ago :
The man who has not the cash to pay, always pays more. I make the statement here and I defy contradiction, that if I went to London to-day with the contract which has been offered to these gentlemen, of the pick of 3,750,000 acres of the best mineral lands in the Yukon region, I could sell that land to-morrow for more money than the 25,000,000 acres of land granted to the Canadion Pacific Railway.
He made that statement in all seriousness in this House. He was applauded to the echo by his friends who sat around him. That 25,000,000 acres of land will certainly *

bring $75,000,000, and five years after that prophecy was made we have still got that
3,750,000	acres of rich gold land, and it is not worth 3,550 cents. I do not think our hon. friend would venture to say to-night that that land was worth $75,000,000, and five years from now, if his speech of tonight is referred to on some important question that may present itself for solution, he will be found just as far wide of the mark as we And him to-night with respect to a prophecy or a statement he made five years ago.
But, Sir, an important task presents itself to my mind. I shall try as briefly as possible to find out just exactly what we liave got in this government scheme and just exactly what there is in the other proposition advanced by the leader of the opposition, which was so vociferously applauded by his followers the other night, and to which to-day they appear to still hold so firmly. I do not intend to prove, Mr. Speaker, that we need another railway. That has been made abundantly manifest by the various speakers who have preceded me. We have the statement of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals himself, we have a letter addressed to the leader of the government only four weeks ago, in which he states :
I have no hesitation in stating that I am as much in favour of the construction of another transcontinental line as any other member of this parliament.
That is his very latest utterance on this question. Sir, the feeling that we ought to have another transcontinental line is not confined to a few people. There is a general feeling that we should construct another transcontinental line, and so much evidence has already been presented to substantiate that that it will not be necessary for me to do more than simply allude to the action of the Railway Committee itself. There were in the committee about 175 representatives of, all parts of this country. The Grand Trunk scheme, as I understood it, originally was to go from North Bay out into the west; that at the request of members of the Railway Committee was extended to Quebec, and there was not a dissenting voice; that was extended to Moncton, and there were very few dissenting voices. An attempt was made to extend it to St. John, and that the late Minister of Railways and Canals supported. At that time he was a strong believer in the necesssity of a transcontinental railway. He says himself in the letter which he presented to the House that there were three alternative propositions which presented themselves. He used these words in the letter which was dated July 13th, and read in the House on July 16th:
Let me state our position on the main question : My decided preference is for a government owned and government operated railway across the continent.
That is his position, but he says:
In this view I am practically alone, and therefore I admit at once that this proposition must be laid aside.
Did the hon. gentleman know what he was talking about on the 16th of July when he said ;
In this view I am practically alone.
He had the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee). He had one or two supporters of government owned and operated railways on this side of the House, but so far as the hon. gentleman knew he was alone in the government, he was alone on that side of the House, he was alone on this side of the House. Not one voice was raised in the Railway Committee in favour of a government owned and government operated railway, and it is only now, when some political capital may be created out of it by our hon. friends on the other side, that some few of them are beginning to adopt it.
Now, I only allude to that to show where the hon. gentleman stood with respect to government owned, government constructed and government operated railways, that he stood practically alone. An amendment has been moved in this House to the resolution that is before it by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) affirming the principle of government owned, constructed and operated railways. It may develop a stronger sentiment in its support than any of us were previously aware of. It might influence some gentlemen on the other side of the House to support it who a week ago did not know that they were supporters of government owned and government operated railways. We have heard of sudden conversions. I do not object to a sudden conversion if it is the result of conviction, but I do object to these sudden conversions that are not the result of a process of reasoning where conscience enters and dictates the course that a man should follow.
You should not rub it in to the member for North Norfolk so hard ; be easy with him.

The late Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) said that when the government scheme was first pro-poandea there was a sigh of relief among the supporters of the government. I am willing to confess that he exactly represented the state of my mind. I did heave a sigh of relief that his views did not predominate, and that the government did not commit themselves to construct and operate this railway from Quebec to the coast. There are others who entertain the views that I entertain. A resolution has been moved in the Senate by a Conservative Senator who has the confidence and respect of our friends opposite, and while I do not endorse the whole of his resolution there are certain clauses in it that are absolutely true, and this is one of them :

Resolved that governments do not operate railways as economically and with the same necessary close business attention as private companies ; that the country has had an object lesson before it in the partial failure of the Intercolonial Railway ; that this House should object in the most unqualified manner to railways being constructed and operated by the government.
I endorse these statements, and I breathed a sigh of relief when I found that these sentiments hadi prevailed with the government, and that the late Minister of Railways and Canals was alone in the possession of his sentiments. As an ideal sentiment, government ownership and operation is all right in itself, but 1 do not think the Canadian people have arrived at that stage of development where we can safely trust the management of so large a corporation into the hands of either the political parties in this country. I remember that for eighteen years every Liberal in Canada believed that our Conservative friends were running the Intercolonial Railway as a political machine, and we have applauded the Minister ot' Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) here when he alluded to the time when the old Intercolonial Railway issued their bundles of ' passes ' not to advance the pecuniary welfare of the railway so much as the political interest of their party. And for the last seven years we have heard our friends on the other side crriticising the management of the Intercolonial Railway ; charging it with falsifying the books and putting down to capital account sums of money that should be properly charged to working expenses. They have charged us with running the whole organization as a political machine ; and that belief is as widespread in this country as are Conservative principles. Let us extend the operations and the opportunities for running a railway of that kind as a political machine, and what would be the result ? How would our Conservative friends regard it if we the Liberal party were to run an organization of that kind ? They cnuld find no words strong enough in the English language to condemn it. But, Sir, when the Conservative party have arrived at that stage, that such men as Sir John A. Macdonald, John Abbott, Sir Charles Tupper are revered no more, and even the present leader of the opposition is incapable to be the bright and particular star at Conservative picnics ; when they shout great is the new Diana of the Conservative party ; when the leader of the opposition steps aside and allows one of his lieutenants to explain, that the lion. Mr. Borden is absent to-day because he is making the effort of his life down in Ottawa (and I don't think we ever saw him that day in the House ;) when in the meantime our friend from Manitoulin is exalted in his place, and the Conservative party bow down and worship him-a man who does not posses the confidence of the judges at least; a man who has been accused of peculating

documents from a bank, and a man who admits that he was inaccurate in his statements-when the Conservative party can worship that kind of an ideal, they are not in that mental condition to give us credit for the proper management of a large railway like this.
There lias been no criticism of the government scheme so effective as that made by the late Minister of Railways and Canals. There is no man on the other side of the House who is so well qualified to do it; who has so great a personal object in doing it and who, owing to the position in which he has placed himself, has so much to gain by doing it. Therefore we can assume that everything that can be said against this road has been said by him. He was obliged to confine himself somewhere within the limits of truth, because he had stiil some reputation for veracity to lose, and he would not and did not make such wild statements as have since been made by speakers on the other side of the House, who were not railway men, who were not financial men and who absolutely knew nothing about this business.
Now, what has our friend the late Minister of Railways and Canals called this scheme? He called it a hybrid scheme. He said :
At best it is but a hybrid scheme compromising to antagonistic principles. It will be difficult to explain why the government should build and own the lean section of this railway and provide the company with credit to enable them to build and operate the fat section.
Our friends on the other side enthusiastically applauded that. I want you Mr. Speaker, to bear in mind the word [DOT] hybrid,' because we have had a counter scheme presented by the leader of the opposition. This word ' hybrid ' was most enthusiastically cheered by our friends opposite, but we will be able to show by and by that this scheme that they are now enthusiastically applauding should not be entitled even to the appellation of ' hybrid ', but, that we might properly call it a mongrel scheme and be within the limits of the truth.
In what sense is this railway lean and fat ? The ex-minister told us that we are going to own the lean section and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway the fat section. If the government was going to operate and own the lean section, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway own and operate the western section, it might be a true definition. But, just as soon as this railway is leased, it becomes the absolute property of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for fifty years-as much their property as though they had built it and owned it; and it ceases then to be either lean or fat, and becomes one proposition for at least fifty years. And who will say that when the fifty years shall have elapsed the western section shall be the fat section and the eastern section the lean ? May the conditions not be reversed ? In any event,

we are not In a position to brand either portion as fat or as lean.
Now, 1 would like to get down in 'Hansard' what I think this railway will cost. I am not in a position to give any expert opinion. I am simply going to quote the opinion of a man whom I have looked up to with respect for the past seven years; a man who has never during that time deceived us in what he stated would take place with respect to financial matters; a man who has had the opportunity of being advised by the financiers of the government and also by the Railway Department of the government. I am quite satisfied to take the opinion of the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) on this question in preference to that of any other man in this House. He has a reputation to lose. He does not speak without the knowledge and the wisdom that are associated with his office. For seven years we have tried him, and when he has prophesied surplus after , surplus, they have come with unvarying regularity, and always a little larger than he prophesied. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have a right to assume that the same caution which has characterized his utterances in the last seven years still characterize what be says to-day. If he errs at all he errs on the safe side. We have seen with what liberality he has been prepared to increase his figures to make it absolutely certain that he was right; because he cannot afford live or six years from now to be confronted with statements showing him to be incapable of discharging the duties of the position he holds, and to be made such a spectacle of as some people would be were we to quote their speeches made five years ago. .
What does the Finance Minister say that this railway will cost ? He says the portion from Moncton to Quebec, 400 miles, will cost $10,000,000; the portion from Quebec to Winnipeg, 1,475 miles, $41,300,000; interest during construction, $3,390,000; or, a total of $54,090,000, which will be due in about fifty-five years from now. As bonds will be issued upon which we will pay three per cent-and after seven years the Grand Trunk Pacific Company agrees to pay that interest-that is the capital that we put into this scheme-not $80,000,000, as our friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) said; not $500,000,000, as he afterwards said it would grow into; and, if he had been speaking yet, it would have been by this time $15,000,000,-000-because these things grow. The Finance Minister tells us that during those seven years the interest on the Moncton-Quebec section will amount to $2,334,000; ou the bridge capitalized, to $324,000; and on the eastern section, to $8,853,000; or a total of $11,512,000 of a direct subsidy, as I would call it, to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That disposes of that question.
Very cheap.

That is what the Finance Minister said, and I would rather believe him than the hon. gentleman who interrupts me. If I wanted some advice as to how to buy merchandise, I would certainly take the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Wilson's) opinion : I would think he had a training in that direction; but on this subject he knows no more than I do, and I am willing to take the Finance Minister as my guide.
According to the hon. minister, the government guarantee on the prairie or fat section amounts to $16,900,000 and on the mountain section, to $14,400,000. These together amount to $31,300,000, which, together with $54,690,000, the cost of the eastern section, gives a total of government bonds and those of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, amounting to $85,990,000. Now, if my hon. friend has never heard before that the eastern section of this railway will cost not less than $80,000,000, he can go home and say he has heard it to-night, because I have certainly made it plain.
Are we safe in our investment on that western section ? That is the next question. We are guaranteeing the bonds of the company on what ? On the mountain section, which at $40,000 a mile will cost $19,200,000, and on the prairie section, which at $18,000 a mile will cost $23,400,000; interest during the period of construction, amounting to $2,400,000; and equipment, amounting to $20,000,000; or $65,000,000 .of Grand Trunk Pacific money, which is in that road, upon which we have a mortgage of $31,300,000, leaving us a surplus security of $33,700,000. That is what the contract says, and we are dealing with the contract. We are not dealing with an imaginary contract, .into which men can read whatever they like; but we are dealing with the-actual contract which we interpret according to our understanding of the English language and the intent of the parties to the contract. We do not need to worry over-that end of the undertaking, that is sure, We have no anxiety about it. That is the fat end, and in addition to the fatness of' the security we have a margin of $33,700,000.
That is not the only estimate that we have. That is the estimate of the Finance Minister, who is responsible, in consequence of the position he holds, to tell us what he believes to be the facts, and he is surrounded by those who are qualified to give him information that would justify his statement. But we have had another valuation of that road, that is, by the late Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair). Did he make that valuation while he was Minister of Railways and Canals, and while a certain amount of responsibility rested upon him ? Not at all. But he said something after he had ceased being Minister of Railways and Canals, and while he was still friendly to the present government, which will justify us in believ-



ing that he did not think at that time the road would cost more money.
On the 10th of July, speaking in this House, he quoted from his letter addressed to the leader of the government-not the first, but the second letter-and after he had plenty of time to consider the matter. In that letter he deliberately expressed himself as follows :
As I have said, I am in favour of the whole line being built and owned by the government, but having abandoned any expectation in that regard, I am equally in favour of the whole line being a company line. I am prepared

I want you, Mr. Speaker, to listen to this particular clause :
I am prepared, since Council has determined, to go forward with this undertaking at once,-
No need to investigate or to make surveys, no need to fritter away two or three years, he was ready to go on at once. He proceeded to say :
I am prepared, since Council has determined to go forward with this undertaking at once, to co-operate with my colleagues in guaranteeing the bonds over the whole line to an extent not exceeding three-fourths of the cost of constructing the railway.
He there deliberately wrote to the First Minister, and read the letter in this House, that he was prepared to support a policy of guaranteeing the bonds of this railway from Quebec to the coast to the extent of three-fourths of its actual cost, and that at a time when, according to his later opinion, we knew nothing about those regions except that it was an absolute wilderness. I do not think he could have thought so then. He only learnt that afterwards, because had he believed it then, he was certainly betraying the interests of this country in offering to guarantee the bonds of the company which was to build a railway through an unknown wilderness. Was he sincere? Did he believe then that we had sufficient information to justify the construction of this road ? He must have, or it would have been dishonest on his part to advise his colleagues to guarantee the bonds to the extent of three-quarters of the cost of the construction of that railway. He evidently did not think then that this scheme was going to cost as much money as he afterwards found it convenient to say it would. At what did he estimate its cost later when he was interested in increasing the difficulties which the government would have to surmount ? He said that the road would cost $121,000,000. and as I have shown, he had previously been prepared to approve of the policy of the government guaranteeing the bonds of this railway to the extent of three-fourths of its cost. Well, three-fourths of $120,000,000 is $90,000,000, which is a greater amount than the government guarantee by their present scheme, so that the government are not doing very badly in connection with this matter. The guarantee which the bon. gentleman was prepared to support

amounted to $90,000,000, whereas that given by the government does not exceed $84,000,000. But, says the hon. ex-minister;-
The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is being aided to a most generous extent. It cannot build its road without very liberal assistance. In giving aid the government might very properly impose terms looking to some financial advantage to the country in the future, and therefore I would insert that a share of the earnings-I would not say one-half, but I would not think it ought to be less than a third of the net earnings, or that portion of the net earnings which would not be required for the improvement or betterment of the road.
Aud he proceeds to say :
My decided preference is for a government owned and government operated railway across the continent, and my chief reason for favouring it is, that it will have an equalizing and regulating influence upon ail other railways throughout the western territories.
So that he puts himself on record as being willing to guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway from Quebec to .the coast to the tune of $90,000,000, and then to put his hand into the treasury of the company to the extent of one-third of their net earnings, making this country a partner in the enterprise, interested in the amount of dividends paid by that company, interested in keeping up high rates in order that we may have high dividends, and, by that very method, frustrating the chief object for which he is a supporter of the policy of government ownership of railways. Is his position as good a one as that adopted by the government ? He wants his pound of flesh. We are not so grasping. All we ask is the right, when the earnings of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will justify it, to insist on a reduction of rates. We will reduce the freight rates instead of taking one-third of the company's earnings. That one-third of the earnings we intend shall remain in the pockets of the farmers in the west and the manufacturers in the east, and in that way we shall regulate the freights on other railway systems. When the rates of freights on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are lowered, the Canadian Northern Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and other competing railways will have to follow suit. We are looking to the regulating and lowering of freights and not to dividends and high rates.
Our hon. friends opposite say that this railway will cost $121,000,000. The Minister of Finance says it will cost $84,000,000, and a subsidy of $12,000,000. There is only about $20,000,000 difference, but anybody who goes beyond the estimate of the ex-Minister or Railways can hardly fail to be charged with using reckless language. On the other hand, I do not think we should go below the estimate of the Minister of Finance, for although his estimate of the length of the road from Quebec to Winnipeg is 75 miles longer than that of the ex-Minister of Railways, his estimate of the cost is only

$20,000,000 less, which shows with what care he has spoken.
We hare heard many speeches made in this Hotrse decrying the country through which this road is to be built, and 1 can quite realize the position in which the manager of the road will find himself when he stands before the directors and stockholders of the Grand Trunk Railway and explains to them the reasons why they should go into this scheme. They will say to him : We have been reading the speeches of leading members of the opposition at Ottawa, and they say that this railway will pass through a barren wilderness, an unexplored country, a land of muskegs, that the scheme is a wild, mad one, and yet you come here and ask us to endorse it. It may be a safe scheme for the government of Canada, as they come first, but where do we come in ? We are behind the government. They will have a railway costing $54,000,000 and $5,000,000 of equipment, and the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Pacific for the eastern section. They will have $3,300,000 surplus as security for the western section. We will be obliged to' run that road fifty years and assume all that responsibility and loss. It is all right for the government of Canada, but what about the stockholders of the Grand Trunk Railway V We have read the speeches of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and the other leaders of the opposition. Well, Mr. Speaker, what do you suppose Mr. Hays will say in reply ? He will, no doubt, say in effect:	You are paying me
$50,000 a year for running the Grand Trunk Railway. I have been with you some years, and have raised it out of the mire into the position of a first-class railway. My opinions are backed up by all the officials under me. We pledge our reputation as railway men, who thoroughly understand the situation of affairs, that this is a good scheme for you to put your money into, and these men who are condemning the scheme are not familiar with railway matters and besides have a political interest in decrying it. Listen to the man to whom you are paying $50,000 a year, and do not listen to lawyers and farmers and merchants and politicians, who can not tell an air-brake from a steam engine. I suppose he would be justified in referring to some speeches made by these hon. gentlemen. He might take, for instance, our friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). He might say : Why, he is a very honourable man. He is. There is no doubt about his honour or about his profound wisdom. But when it comes to a matter of politics, wisdom leaves him and he becomes absolutely blind. Mr. Hays might say to his stockholders : I will read you some of the utterances of this hon. gentleman. He has condemned this Grand Trunk Pacific scheme, but on what ground? The language he usfed to-dav he has used 2924
before. Let us go back five years. By referring to page 1665 of the ' Hansard ' of 1898 you will see that this hon. gentleman advised the government to abandon the Mackenzie & Mann scheme in the Yukon, and five thousand miners would go in and locate
Five hundred thousand.

Yes. But I was almost afraid to mention that. Five hundred thousand miners would go in and locate. Two years would be the very moderate estimate of the time required for this according to the hon. gentleman. Only two years, and in that time 500,000 miners would come in and locate. Remember, Mr. Speaker, this is Mr. Hays reading the speech of the hon. member for East Grey to his stockholders who want to know what kind of mem these are. The hon. gentleman went on :
Now, 500,000 miners, at $10 apiece-what they want for a free miner's license-would be $5,000,000 for the right to go there and begin prospecting. This same amount would have had to be paid the following year. In order to take up this amount of land each miner must locate eight claims, making four million claims. At $15 each for locating claims, this would be $60,000,000. If they continue to work these claims the second year, they would pay $60,000,000 more. If they took an average of $100 of gold out of each claim-and that is moderate when you consider that men have claims that they can sell for $2,000,000, the royalty as compared to what Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann would pay, would amount to $9,000,000. This makes a total of $139,000,000. -from 500,000 miners, I would like to ask the Finance Minister if he has got that money ?
No, the surplus is not quite so large as that.

I would ask the Minister of the Interior where those 500,000 miners are ? They are still in the imagination of these gentlemen. But other hon. gentlemen who spoke concerning whom Mr. Hays might be asked. There was the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). He told us that the railroad would suffice to carry in the 60,000 or 75,000 people-incoming miners, I suppose-but the question was whether there would be boats enough to carry them. Then he quotes from am interview with a Mr. Bellew, whom he endorses as a practical miner, who says that the
3,750,000	acres of land given to this syndicate would make 750,000 claims, which, at $25,000 each would make $18,000,000,000. This is deliberately stated to the House as given on the authority of a practical miner. What will the stockholders of the Grand Trunk say when the opinion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) with regard to the Bill now before us is read to them ? But this estimate is a little too much even for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk). He confesses that this is a high estimate, but

says that So an acre is a low estimate. This .same gentleman in condemning this Grand Trunk Pacific scheme only three or four days ago, stated that the 25,000,000 of acres of land given to the Canadian Pacific Railway by the Canadian government years ago, were not worth anything, because there was no railway to develop them. But the land to be given to Mackenzie & Mann, which was away up in the Arctic regions, was worth $5 an acre though there was no railway. What do you suppose Mr. Hays would say when he was asked about that ? But that is not all. Now, hon. gentlemen opposite have found a mare's nest in the contract. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) spoke of it. In some mysterious way, the Grand Trunk Railway is to get possession of $25,000,000 worth of that common stock. We are told that they may buy it cheap. Of course, in some mysterious way, these hon. gentlemen do not seem to know how the Grand Trunk is going to be in this deal. That is quite easy to me. And it was just at this stage that our friend the late Minister of Railways and Canals showed his animus by alluding to the Grand Trunk as 1 the red-headed boy.' Without ' the red-headed boy,' this road cannot be built. We are dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific, but that company has not the means to build this road. They could not issue a dollar's worth of bonds and realize in the market unless somebody was to guarantee those bonds. And so the Grand Trunk, the yellow-headed boy, comes into this deal. The Grand Trunk Pacific guarantee that the Grand Trunk Railway shall take $25,000,000 of the stock. What for ? I take it that that will put them in a position to raise the money to build the western section of the railway. But the Grand Trunk will require to guarantee $20,000,000 of preference stock which will be sold to put the equipment on the road. I see in this quite plain, businesslike transaction. They become the custodians of this common stock and guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific, giving that company hard cash. How much money will they have in this road ? Mrith their share of building the western section and with the equipment, they will have over $31,000,000 in the road.
They have got to provide terminals, shops, hotels, ships, loss of bonds, if sold at a loss. They have got to provide to run their road for six or seven years before it becomes productive. I do not see that the $25,000,000 security they have to give will more than compensate them for guaranteeing at least $33,000,000 of bonds of this Grand Trunk Pacific, and no one else will do it. Behind that they have got to pay interest at three per cent. Now he says this is a bad scheme. Our friends on the other side, who are absolutely irresponsible, who do not apparently understand the agreement itself, have not the slightest idea of the actual cost, or if they have, they have got beyond the range of ordinary reason. We have them on the one side, and on the other side we have Mr. Hays, Mr. Wilson, Mr. Wainwright, Mr. Bell and the men that manage the Grand Trunk Railway in this country, telling their stockholders that this is a good scheme, and if it is a good scheme for the stockholders it cannot be a bad scheme for the people of Canada.
But, if you do not like this scheme, the leader of the opposition is prepared to give you a substitute. When he gave that substitute scheme he was vociferously applaud-

ed by our friends opposite. Let us analyze that scheme, and the same moderate figures that the Minister of Finance used in valuing the Grand Trunk Pacific will apply to this scheme. What have we got ? The leader of the opposition did not move it as a resolution, he did not like to commit his supporters to the quality of the scheme. They could talk without limit and no particular harm would be done, but if it was crystallized in the form of a resolution and they had to vote yea or nay they would have to proclaim themselves as something that X do not like to characterize a man that I have the least respect for, therefore I shall keep it to myself. He says : We will extend the Intercolonial to the coast, and begin by extending it from Montreal to Goteau a distance of 38 miles. Then he will unite with a little road down there, the Jacques Cartier, I think the road is called, some 38 miles of road, to meet the Intercolonial. Now to give a value to that 38 miles is a very difficult job. But as we know, a large portion of it will run right through the city of Montreal, if they built it, it cannot cost less than $2,000,000. He says we will expropriate the Canada Atlantic Railway from Coteau to Depot Harbour. He tells us that the Canada Atlantic Railway paid five per cent interest last year upon its capital stock. Now, looking into the railway book, we find that the actual cost of the Canada Atlantic Railway was a little over $20,000,000, that includes a branch that runs into the states. I presume if the government wanted that portion of the road from Coteau to Parry Sound they would have to pay just as much for it as if they took the whole outfit, for without that part the road there would be no good. Now, is that worth $20,000,000 ? for that is the actual amount of money that has gone into it. I think we can safely leave it there, because there were nearly $600,000 of a net profit last year. It is a good road, and will constantly increase in value. We will throw in the Canada Atlantic Railway transit line of boats, because they will have to be acquired, and that will help to make up the $20,000,000.
Now, we will take a little summer trip through the lakes in boats belonging to the government, and when we get to Fort William we find 431 miles of railway to Winnipeg in bad condition, with bad grades, with" bad curves, not one, but two such railways. Now our friend proposes to modernize both these railways, to lower the grades, to straighten out the curves, and make them first class railways. But how much will that cost through that rocky region V Is $30,000 a mile for bettering those two roads running through that rocky region a high figure ? If it is not, you will pay for them $12,930,000. Then we have got to give the Grand Trunk and all other rival roads running rights over it. We are told by our friends opposite that it is impossible for one company to own a road and allow
a rival company to run over it. On this particular section the title is going to remain with them, but all other roads are to have running rights. You say that is impossible, but you applaud the leader of the opposition when he says it can be done. What are we to believe ? When are you sincere and when are you fooling ? That is what we want to know. Well, when you get west to Winnipeg you find that one of these roads unfortunately runs through American territory, and you are actually going to expend more of our money in improving a road that does not all lie in Canada. We come now to the hybrid part of the scheme, we are owning a road from Montreal to Parry Sound, from Fort William to Winnipeg, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern come in. When we get to Winnipeg we are going to guarantee the bonds, I presume, of the Grand Trunk Railway who are going to build from Winnipeg to Edmonton, 690 miles1 at $13,000 a mile, making $11,700,000. Over the prairie section to the coast, 480 miles at $40,000 a mile, represent $19,200.000, and from Edmonton to where the Grand Trunk section begins, 300 miles at $18,000 a mile, representing $15,400,000. We are piling up the money, we are buying old roads, but we are not opening out a foot of fresh territory, because we can go to Edmonton by two railways already, and they tell us the road from Edmonton to the coast is not needed.
But if you do not take a summer journey, you find the lake frozen, and you have to deflect your road, and you are going to get over the difficulty, the leader of the opposition says, by expropriating the Canadian Pacific Railway from Fort William to North Bay. 634 miles. Now what is that railway worth ? That railway has arrived at that condition that it is worth twice as much as it was when it was built. 700.000	more. But they will not need the road to North Bay, and they are buying an

Do you suppose that can be justified by the people ? They talk about the fat side and the lean side, but we have not got through, because the hon. gentleman having accomplished all this, says we will make surveys and at once, as soon as it is determined that it is feasible, build the Quebec section, we will start from Quebec, and we will spend $44,0000,000 on that. Up to that time we have $168,000,000 stuck into it, and if we leave out the Quebec end, $124,000,000, and have not enlarged the- spout. Our friends will have a government owned railway there, a government operated railway there; they have got a hybrid scheme owned by one railway and operated by another, and you can hardly tell what nomenclature to apply to their scheme. 100.000	barns ? Let us build elevators so that instead of building barns, they can put their grain into elevators. 000 more there for elevators, but he has not yet finished, because he is going to have the government guarantee all the warehouse receipts to the farmers, but they do not need any such guarantee, any man with a warehouse receipt for 1,000 bushels of grain can deposit it in the bank and get ail the money he wants. We will make them all free. Where have we got at the end of all this ? Two or three hundred million dollars dropped at the Quebec end, and he is spending on this scheme millions more than we have, and has not enlarged the spout, and what lias he got on his hands? We talk about the lean and the fat. He has no tenant, he has no lease, he has the whole government responsibility, he lias no guarantee that the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk Railway will take advantage of the road or will pay interest on the investment. It is an absolutely blind venture, and he has built a railway from Montreal to go through a lean section at $2,000,000, he has bought the Canada Atlantic Railway for $20,000,000, that is fat; he has bought or subsidized the road from Fort William to Winnipeg, $13,000,000; he has built from Edmonton to the coast, $24,600,000, and he has bought from Fort William to North Bay, $31,700,000, and from Sudbury to Scotia, $3,600,000, and he has got $95,000,000 spent there. $20,000,000- is fat. the Canada AtlanticRailway, and $75,000,000 is lean, and it is not only lean, it is tough. Those are the actual conditions of his scheme as compared with ours.
Now, which would any reasonable man endorse? I have not exaggerated the cost of a single foot of that railway, the actual values that I put there harmonize with those given by the Finance Minister, not the exaggerated figures of our friends on the other side.
If our scheme goes through, and it will go through, because there is no legitimate argument that can be used against us, we are-absolutely safe in building the railway now from Quebec to Winnipeg, the risks of which will be taken by the Grand Trunk Railway for fifty years, and when it lias been made valuable it will come back to us. We control the situation after that and we control it until then. We can prevent rival roads going through there for fifty years, and for fifty years afterwards, and this very railway that may now be lean and may be run at a loss, which may be compensated for by the profit on the more productive sections of the railway in the west, may fifty years from now be one of Canada's most productive assets, and if the whole thing is a failure and the Grand Trunk Railway fails, we have got the government road that some of these gentlemen want, with

.$30100,000 of Grand Trunk Railway money in it. But the most important point is : Can we afford to go into this scheme ? We must not look at it from the standpoint of the present, hut from the standpoint of fifty years from now. Hare we any reason to suppose we will not be in a position to meet the obligations maturing then? Fifty-four millions, 64 millions, 74 millions, what is an increase of $70,000,000 to the debt of Canada fifty years from now when we compare it with the marvellous growth that has taken place during the past few years. 1 do not need to go back far ? Are we justified in going back and judging from the past what the future is likely to be? I will not assume the role of a prophet, but I will quote a few facts, and each can apply them for himself.
Take British Columbia that we have heard extolled so enthusiastically to-day. Twenty years ago it had a population of 36,000, now it has a population of 17S,000, not distant from us, separated from us by uninhabited wildernesses, but by a magnificent country, traversed with railways in every direction.
Take Manitoba, when it entered confederation thirty years ago, with its 2,000 whites and 10,000 half-breeds, and compare it with the Manitoba of to-day, with a population of 350,000, producing last year 100,000,000 bushels of grain. Take Fort Garry, into which years ago 117 immigrants plodded their weary way from Port Arthur. Today that distance is spanned by two magnificent railway systems, and Fort Garry is almost unknown, except as an historic relic. In its stead we have the magnificent city of Winnipeg, writh its population of 60,000. The North-west territory, which 20 years ago was but the home of the buffalo and the wild Indian, last year produced 25,000,000 bushels of wheat and is populated by 300,000 people. We have these two provinces, with their cultivated area of 3,500,000 acres producing 125,000,000 bushels of wheat, and what will it be when the other 200,000,000 acres becomes cultivated by a hardy and thrifty peojile ?
But we need not go so far as that to look for progress. There is a later day when our progress became marked, a day that has impressed itself on the mind of every member in this House. Bet us take the last eight years only and let us see what progress has been made. Take our population, take our railway development, take the progress of the trade of our country just for eight years, and see what is the result. Eight years ago the import trade of Canada was $105,000,000; last year $224,000,000; the increase, $119,000,000 or 113 per cent. Eight years ago the exports of the products of Canada amounted to $109,000,000; last year to $214,000,000; an increase of $105,000,000 or 97 per cent. Eight years ago the total trade of Canada was $215,000,000; last year it was $439,000,000; an increase of $224,000,000 or 104 per cent. Eight years ago
our revenue was $36,000,000; last year it was $66,000,000; an increase of 90 per cent. Eight years the railway earnings were $50,000,000; last year they were $83,000,000; an increase of 60 per cent. Eight years ago exports, the products of the mines, amounted to $8,000,000; last year they amounted to $34,000,000; an increase of $26,000,000 or 325 per cent. Eight years ago our export of manufactures was $9,000,000; last year it was $20,000,000; an increase of $11,000,000 or 120 per cent. Eight years the bank assets were $316,000,000 ; last year they were $581,000,000; an increase of $255,000,000 or an increase of 80 per cent.
But the only thing that has not maintained a proportionate increase has been the national debt of the country, which^during this marked period of prosperity, after we have spent $55,000,000 on capital account and subsidjizjimg rajilwiaiys, has Only Increased from $258,000,000 to $265,000,000. And yet, with these facts before us and with such a future in store for us as we can easily foresee, are we afraid of spending $50,000,000 in fifty years from now ? What will happen when these 16,000,000 acres of good clay soil are being tilled in New Ontario; what will happen when the magnificent land In northern Quebec is opened up by that railway which shall be studded with towns and villages from one end to the other ? Will we be afraid of adding $50,000,000 to our national debt, which if we quietly cease subsidizing railways for four years we can pay off out of our surplus without adding a dollar to our indebtedness ? I am not afraid of this scheme. Looked at from every standpoint I see in it a scheme that will redound to the welfare of this country and to the glory of this government. There is nothing in it that does not commend itself to me. We have heard our friends opposite say that the clause in the agreement which diverts trade to our Canadian ports is not worth the paper it is written on. Well, it might not be if it were only a statute, but this road which is intended to divert the trade from the west through our own territory to our own ports; this road is actually shorter from Winnipeg to St. John than any other railway that runs over this continent, and there will be no reason for the Grand Trunk Railway not to carry out its bargain. It is bound by the statute to do it, it is bound commercially to do it, it is bound geographically to do it; the Grand Trunk Railway cannot help itself unless it is willing to develop American ports at its own loss, and to carry its freight a longer distance than on its own road to Quebec and thence to St. John.
I look forward with hope and I look forward with confidence to the accomplishment of this project propounded by the government. I look forward with more hope and more confidence to it than our friends on the other side entertain, for this scheme to

whicli their leader has pledged himself and which will never be endorsed by the people of Canada.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) has well followed the Minister of Finance, who seems to have been his mentor, for the hon. member quoted almost the identical figures which the Finance Minister gave to the House the other night, glorying that the country ought spend all the money we had made. Logan) and other members opposite, have quoted Sir Sandford Fleming whom they are very anxious to quote as an authority but whom they never quote when he tells them that this line will only lessen the distance eighty miles to the city of Montreal. He intimated that the hon. ex-Minister of Railways had insulted Senator Cox. There was but one mention made of Mr. Cox in the speech of the hon. ex-Minister of Mr. HEYD.
Railways, but scarcely an hon. gentleman on that side of the House has risen since without talking Cox. It is quite evident that Mr. Cox needs defence, or they would not mention his name. The hon. gentleman ended with a grand peroration in which be complimented Sir Charles Tupper as one of the greatest statesmen of Canada, as one to whom was due the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; and then he drew himself up and said, I, as member for Cumberland, proposed this in the Railway Committee- behold a greater than Sir Charles Tupper. Now, Mr. Speaker, you are aware that for a number of years the question of improved transportation has been before this House and the country. It has been brought up here from time to time, and has been discussed by hon. members on both sides of the House-discussed more perhaps as it affected their particular constituencies Ilian from a broad national standpoint. It has been constantly brought to the attention of this government, perhaps with more persistency by the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) than by any other hon. gentleman. It has been the persistency of that hon. gentleman on this question as well as on the question of adequate protection that has probably forced the government to take even the action that they have taken at this late date. The press of the country has also been discussing the problem of transportation, from one point of view and another, until the government should have seen that it was necessary to take up the matter in some practical form. There has been not only this feeling in the country in regard to the transportation business, but there has been a very widespread feeling in regard to the way in which the people's money has been expended in years past without any adequate return in the form of a national scheme of transportation. We have expended money in a good many directions-some on harbours along the Georgian Bay and the great lakes, some in dredging the St. Lawrence, and in other ways trying to make that great waterway what it should be, and some for terminal facilities in other parts of the country. But these expenses have not been made with

any view to a general system of transportation. They have been made, some times wisely perhaps, but more frequently in the interest of some member who is a friend of the government, for the sake of saving his constituency to him at the next election. In addition to these expenditures, we have recently abolished the tolls on the canals. This in itself has been quite an additional burden on the tax-payers of the country, who, besides paying to keep the canals in proper condition, have now also to pay for their maintenance, which was very largely paid for in former times out of the tolls collected. So that the tax-payers have now practically to pay the amount of the tolls which have been abolished. But we have had no complaint from the people on account of this additional expenditure, because they believed that it was along the line that they wished to see adopted. They believed that it was along a line that would eventually lead to some national transportation scheme. I say that the present government, with the possible exception of the late Minister of Public Works, took very little interest in this matter. They seemed to lack the initiative in this, as they do in a great many other matters. They seemed simply to drift continually, without any prospect of change. But when this House was called to meet this year, we fancied that under the pressure of the late Minister of Public Works, there might possibly be some change ; for in the speech from the Throne, delivered on March 12, 1903, after reciting certain things that seemed to be necessary, they put these words into the mouth of His Excellency the Governor General :
The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
They had at last awakened to the fact that the country was looking to them to do something. Then, we had a return which perhaps supplemented this announcement. The first sounded something like business, and the second a little more so, and I am going to read a few extracts from this. By the way. I note that this report was made by the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). It will be interesting to know where that hon. gentleman is. He has not put in an appearance since the present resolution has been before the House. It may be, as has been suggested, that he is on strike, or possibly he may be away loading his gun to shoot at the 'dictation of his leader. This report says :
The minister submits that it may be assumed that grain and other products will naturally seek their markets by the cheapest routes, and therefore the method of attaining the object desired should be to make the Canadian routes cheaper and more convenient than competing routes.
It will be very desirable for hon. gentlemen who are backing up the present scheme to demonstrate to this House and the country how this alt-rftil route can be made a cheaper route, and it will be especially desirable to make that appear to the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton).
The Minister further states that the questions to be considered are complicated and involved, including among the objects to be sought the transportation of western products from place of production to the markets of the ivorld.
Further on he says :
It is obvious that before any satisfactory conclusion can be reached upon these questions a thorough and comprehensive inquiry should be made regarding the conditions of general shipment and the possibilities of improvement in the conditions surrounding these shipments.
Further on the hon. minister says :
In making such investigation attention should not be confined to routes and facilities which are at present utilized, but if necessary new surveys should be made to determine whether any more economical and satisfactory channels of transportation by land or water can be opened up.
Diversion of Canadian products through eastern outlets to Boston, Portland and other United States ports, should be investigated, and the best and most economical methods used by our competitors should be carefully studied and reported upon.
The minister apprehends that in these circumstances it devolves upon the Dominion government to consider and adopt the best possible means of promoting such measures as may enable Canada to control the transportation of its own products, and it is thought that the most efficient method of conducting such an inquiry and obtaining the required information is by means of a commission of competent and experienced experts who may be appointed and authorized under the provisions of chapter 114 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.
The right hon. gentleman then recommends three gentlemen, Sir William Van Horne, Mr. John Bertram and Mr. Harold Kennedy, as suitable to be appointed. He then proceeds to say :
I further recommend that such commission be authorized to employ such scientific and professional assistance as its members may decide.
You will readily see that It was not professional railway exploiters, but gentlemen who had some knowledge of the railway business that the government had then in view. I may say that after this policy was announced in the speech from the Throne, and repeated in this report, there seemed to be throughout the country a spirit of thanksgiving that the gpvernment had at last awakened to a sense of their duty, and I am confident that every hon. gentleman in this House will agree with me when I say that had the government carried out that . pledge to the people, made in these two do-

cuments, even had the route selected by the commission not satisfied particular localities, there is sufficient spirit of loyalty in this country to have induced the people as a whole to look on it with favour. I believe that the spirit of loyalty which has bound these different provinces and races into a great nation would have led every county and province to rise above any feeling of local jealousy and combine in giving every aid to the accomplishment of whatever proposal the commission would have suggested as the best solution of the transportation problem.
But, although in the speech from the Throne, the immediate appointment of this commission was promised, as the session progressed the government did not seem at all anxious to implement that promise.
