He needs the support in New Brunswick, of an hon. gentleman who, I understand1, is most interested in that particular line of railway and the company which is to extend it to the city of Fredericton. He gives us as a reason for this route that the magnificent mineral resources throughout that portion of New Brunswick, which will be developed by means of the construction of this line. Well, the poor fellows who have expended their money in exploring these mineral resources are still out of pocket. I hope that in the future some mineral resources may be found that will pay for their development. Among other things, he spoke of the magnificent coal area that will be developed, but he must know that we have magnificent water routes in that province, and that every chaldron of coal is carried down the river St. John from the head of Grand lake. From Chipman to Moncton is no doubt a fair country through which Mr. GANONG.
to build a railway, but it has no suitable port for ocean steamers and no suitable harbour for the terminus of a transcontinental railway.
We have heard -some question of competing lines, but it is evident that hon. gentlemen who speak of the advantages of competition are unable to see the difference between the building of competing lines by different corporations and tbe building by the government of a line to compete with one it already owns. What object can there be in building a line to compete with one which has cost the country some $70,000,000 V It is this competition by a new government road against the Intercolonial Railway to which we object.
The Minister of the Interior made an argument regarding the shipment of grain, which I need not combat. If I were living in Manitoba or the Territories, I would have his speech sent to every elector in those sections, to show on what little foundation the Minister of the Interior can base a wide conclusion. He takes an exceptional circumstance in connection with the Canada Atlantic Railway, he takes the lowest rate ever charged by that railway and a lower rate than can possibly be charged by any railway company, according to railway experts, and on that rate-made in very exceptional circumstances-he bases his contention that it will be possible to carry grain along the north shore of Lake Superior. If an hon. gentleman occupying the position of a Minister of the Crown cannot bring any better argument to support a policy which will involve an expenditure of millions of dollars, he ought not attempt to defend it at all. And the best condemnation of that policy would be to send abroad his speech without any attempt to controvert it. That argument would be sufficient to convince any elector that the hon. gentleman was talking of something he knew nothing about, and which, on the 27th of May last he admitted that he knew nothing about. I am not prepared to say that no grain will be carried along that route. It may be possible that some little grain may be carried over it, but only under very exceptional circumstances. On the Atlantic seaboard, we sometimes find that a vessel will bring out salt as ballast, but because a vessel, in default of being able to get paying cargo, will carry salt as ballast, that cannot be taken as any basis on which to calculate freight rates. The same thing occurs in the matter of Portland cement. Western cement has few sales down in the maritime provinces, because the Portland cement is brought there in the ships as ballast. Still if we were to follow the ex-ampie of the Minister of the Interior, we would figure out that a vessel, which loads cement or salt as ballast, could carry other cargo at the same rate.
As to the cost of this railway, we have an estimate made by the Finance Minister

and also one made by tlie ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, but the difference between tbe two is tliat tbe one was made by a gentleman who was simply figuring on something he had heard about, whereas the other was made by a gentleman who was figuring on something he knows about. We had the government admitting on the 27th of May, in this report of the committee of the Privy Council, that they knew nothing and would have to appoint railway experts to obtain information. On the 27tli of May their pin feathers of information had not started, but to-day they are birds of plumage; ready to be plucked ; and at the expense of the country, they will be plucked. When challenged across the floor of the House, there was not a minister who could come within ten million dollars of the cost of this proposed railway. The reason is evident. Men who know nothing can tell nothing. Had they appointed a commission, they would have been able to find out something. It is not against this railway that we are particularly objecting, but it is against the attempt to commit this country to something concerning which the government know nothing and concerning [DOT] which they have admitted they know nothing.
The Minister of Finance gave out the text, which every one of his followers, even the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) has taken up. He started out with the statement that we have a surplus. When he made that statement, I felt sorry for the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright). Only a few years ago that hon. gentleman declared it was a crime, a most outrageous thing, to have a surplus; and to hear his desk mate announce that he had a surplus of over $13,000,000 must have been gaul and vinegar to the hon. gentleman. I expected to see the hair of his head rise in horror; but even when the hon. Minister of Finance repeated we have a surplus and we shall have a greater surplus, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce remained apparently undisturbed in his lethargy. I expected to see him rise in his indignation and heap maledictions on his desk mate
If he did he would lose his job.

Of course he would. He was told by the First Minister that he must shoot in a certain direction or he would lose the office which he now fills and which he firmly said never should have been created. But this surplus evidently worried the Minister of Finance a good deal, and he concluded that one way to get rid of it was to give some of it away. He started in by saying that they could build all this road from Winnipeg to the west-that is they could adopt this redheaded boy, and it would only take $2,334,575 of the surplus. Then he looked around, he saw that they could have their own two boys representing 293
the road from Winnipeg to Quebec and Quebec to Moncton, and that they both could be supported by the country for $11,066,882. He found out about that time-it was a rather peculiar thing-that these boys should have been twins. And he had to afford relief to his political friends even at the expense of the poor taxpayer. He said : It will cost us $324,246 to make these Siamese Twins by taking over the Quebec bridge wrich belongs to our friends. And still we shall have a surplus, because the total will be only $13,725,703.
Two cents.

We should not forget that. How did the hon. gentleman get his figures ? He has an actuary. I never had an actuary in my line. If I had had one in my business thirty years ago, I suppose I could have been as rich as some of the Coxes and others. Why should we go any further ? Why not give the gentleman $13,725,703-and two cents-and let them build the road, own it and run it ? It would save the country great expense and trouble of managing it. I would suggest that we pay them even double that amount to build and own and run the line, and the country would be the gainer by it as compared with this contract. There is something wonderful about this actuarial business. It is fine to learn through an actuary that it will cost us just $13,725,703 -and two cents-to carry out this contract. We cannot be too glad that the Minister of Finance has an actuary. ' The Grand Trunk Pacific ought to have an actuary too; it is a good thing to have. Let me snow how this actuarial business works out. I have a clipping here from ' Hansard ' of the 13th of May last. The Minister of Finance answered a question put by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot). The hon. member for Bellechasse has changed his opinion somewhat. He had a little scheme of his own which has been taken out of his hands and now he is ready to shoot as the Prime Minister directs. The Minister of Finance said :
At the time of confederation the Grand Trunk Railway owed the province of Canada, according to the accounts of that province, $25,607,393.53, and this amount was taken by the Dominion as an asset, and still remains in the balance sheet of the Dominion at that amount, no payment having been made by the railway in respect thereof.
' Still remains ' as an asset. And every man knows that it is of no value. Why not wipe it out ? Suppose the Minister of Finance were to put his actuary on this problem, let us see iiow it would work out. On the 1st July, 1867, this amount stood at $25,607,393.53. ' Assume that this stood at interest of 5 per cent up to 1877, at 41 per cent from 1877 to 1887 ; at 4 per cent from 1887 to 1897 ; and at 3J per cent from 1897 to the present time and that the interest



was compounded half yearly, these being about the terms on which the government borrowed the money, how much do you suppose this would amount to ? It would amount to about $118,000,000. Why, this oppulent concern, this wonderfully strong company that is coming here to do us so much good, stands indebted to this country $118,000,000-every dollar of it owed as justly as a dollar was ever owed by one man to another. Suppose that the government had owed the Grand Trunk $25,607,393.53 on 1st July, 1867, what would have been the result to-day ? Why, the actuary would have got in his work and he would have come and said :	You owe us $118,-
000,000. And we are accepting the guarantee of this concern that already owes us this vast amount. This shows the business capacity of this business government, this combination of all the talents from the different provinces. Why, the Minister of Finance can build railways-it is no trouble to him, if his friends will pay this bill. He can build, according to his own figuring, eight transcontinental railways, and still have a surplus, if he will only collect what the Grand Trunk owes us. This indebtedness of theirs may be one of the reasons why they do not wish to acquire any more property, lest Canadians might know enough to ask them to pay their debts. I expect to see a boom in the actuarial business after this. Remember, this reasoning is not mine ; it is the reasoning of the Minister of Finance, the hon. gentleman who controls the moneys of this country, as he has done for the last six or seven years. It is the reasoning of a full-fledged, competent, experienced, scientific and pro-fesional railway expert-since the contract was signed, but one who did not know a thing about it until that time. This argument, first voiced b'y the Minister of Finance, has been repeated, as I said, parrot-fashion, by the rest of the gentlemen on his side who have spoken. But we have one gentleman who did even better than that. He does not propose to be outclassed even by the Minister of Finance. I refer to the hon. gentleman from King's (Mr. Hughes) who worked it all out that it would only cost us twenty cents a head to build this road from the mud-banks of the Petitcodiac to Port Simpson. Will hon. gentlemen on that side, who are presumed to have at least a modicum of common sense, accept such a statement as that ? Will they have the assurance to go before an intelligent electorate and attempt to cram such stuff down their throats ? I hope they will, for they will get their just deserts if they do. Since the Minister of Finance has blossomed out in the actuarial business I cannot but think of the change in him. ' A few years ago, you know, he favoured the factory of the cross-roads and the backwoods. Those were the days of his simplicity. Now, he finds

uo difficulty In granting a protective bounty to assist, as he says, a great iron industry that will cover half a township. So have his ideas grown. These are hopeful signs. I hope, should Providence treat this country so unkind as to allow the hon. gentleman to continue in his present position, that he will blossom out in a new direction. If he will get in his actuarial work and give us a statement of the losses to labour and capital by his own mistakes on tariff questions, he will show where money has been lost with which we might have built two transcontinental railroads had we so desired. It is to be sincerely hoped that the government will recede from these plunges that they have made. They have followed the Conservatives in a good many good things. I hope they will continue to follow the policy of the Conservative party on the question of transportation as laid down by the leader of the opposition. If they do, they will show some signs of a higher patriotism than that which fills the pockets of political friends.
Now, Sir, it cannot be said that we on this side of the House are against a judicious scheme of improving transportation facilities. All we have demanded in any instance is proper consideration of any scheme, instead of a plunge in the dark as mentioned by the Minister of Finance. We believe that the plan proposed by the leader of the opposition is a truly national one. It conserves the public interest in that it saves the great expenditure which is proposed by this other scheme without proper investigation. It saves the people's money, it gives the people a control of transportation rates that they can never hope to obtain under the scheme proposed by the government. It gives the great west what it requires more economically and more efficiently than the policy proposed by the government, namely, a scheme by which western grain may be carried through Canadian channels, ' and that cannot be done for five or seven years according to their scheme. The policy of the leader of the opposition makes it possible to carry this produce over a government railway to the harbours of eastern Canada. It becomes a patriotic scheme, as it will be a people's road, built by the people's money, and controlled by the people rather than a contribution of $125,000,000 to build up a distinctly foreign corporation over which the government can have no possible control.	*
